title: NFSU DNA experts begin assisting in identifying victims of Nepal flood disaster
full_text:
Gandhinagar (Gujarat) [India], August 30 (ANI): A 10-member team from the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU), Gandhinagar, Gujarat, the world's first and only university dedicated to forensic sciences, has begun the process of assisting in the identification of victims of the Nepal flood disaster.

As per a press statement, the 10-member NFSU team has reached Nepal and, in coordination with local authorities, has commenced work to assist in identifying the victims under the joint guidance of the Ministry of External Affairs and the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.

Centre of Excellence in DNA Forensics Coordinator, Malay Shukla, noted, 'A 10-member NFSU (National Forensic Sciences University) team has reached Nepal, led by Dr Bhargav Patel, along with scientific staff. They will collect samples from the deceased as well as their biological relatives so that DNA profiles can be generated and matched to identify the victims. Disaster Victim Identification is a crucial forensic process.'

It may be recalled that a devastating flood along the Nepal-Tibet border has resulted in significant loss of life. To assist in identifying the unidentified bodies, a 10-member team from the Centre of Excellence in DNA Forensics at NFSU, Gandhinagar, led by its Head, Bhargav Patel, departed for Nepal on Saturday evening, the press note stated.

Through Disaster Victim Identification (DVI), the families of missing persons can be assisted in identifying their deceased relatives, it said.

Shukla further noted, 'In cases where bodies are badly damaged, we try to collect teeth and other suitable samples for DNA analysis. The team will also support Nepal's forensic laboratory and help streamline sample collection and analysis. At NFSU, we have a Centre of Excellence with advanced DNA forensic equipment and the capacity to analyse more than 1,000 samples at a time. We will begin the analysis as soon as the samples arrive and make every effort to provide the results as quickly as possible.'

The Centre of Excellence in DNA Forensics at NFSU, Gandhinagar, is equipped with state-of-the-art facilities and an adequate supply of kits required for the identification of victims. (ANI)

title: US Says 85 Americans Are Missing in Tibet – Nepal Flood
full_text:
China says 18 U.S. citizens are among those missing on the Tibet side.

The United States said on Aug. 30 that about 85 Americans remain missing following last week’s devastating flood, which engulfed villages along the border between China and Nepal and wrecked critical infrastructure in the region.

The updates from U.S. State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott came hours after the Nepali authorities issued a fresh warning of a possible flood, and Beijing released its first country-by-country counts of those missing on its side of the border.

“As of 6:00 a.m. this morning, I can say we now have 85 Americans approximately that are unaccounted for,” Pigott told ABC News’s “This Week.” “We’ve also now seen nine Americans be safely evacuated. We are currently unaware of any U.S. citizen deaths at this time.”

The United States has activated $3.6 million in emergency humanitarian assistance, including up to three months of emergency food for up to 10,000 flood-affected households, according to Pigott. U.S. assistance will also be used to rehabilitate roads and mobilize specialized transport options to reach hard-hit, remote areas, he said.

“Our embassies in Beijing and Kathmandu are working 24/7 in terms of communicating and coordinating with local officials, trying to get that reliable information,” he said. “If any American is in the region, please register for the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program. That is so essential, so we know how to contact you, also know where you are.”

A U.S. disaster-area response adviser is on the ground, coordinating with Nepali authorities to offer any needed assistance, Pigott said.

“Our priority is the safety and security of the American people,” he said. “As you mentioned, the remoteness of this location makes getting reliable information difficult. But our dedication remains.” More Than 3,000 Missing The death toll from the flash flood on the Nepali side of the border has climbed to 781, and 2,502 people are still missing, according to an Aug. 30 statement from Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

In a separate social media update, the Nepal Tourism Board said as many as 591 foreign tourists are still “out of communication.”

Arun Sankar/AFP via Getty Images

Across the border, Chinese officials confirmed 16 deaths in Tibet, while 546 individuals, including Chinese citizens and foreign nationals, remained missing, as of the evening of Aug. 29.

At a press conference in Tibet, officials said 261 missing foreign tourists were from 23 countries, and they said the largest group was 104 Nepalese citizens, according to a transcript issued by state broadcaster CCTV.

Among the missing were 49 Indians, 33 Latvians, 18 Americans, 15 Britons, six Canadians, six Australians, and four South Africans.

The update was the first time Beijing released a breakdown by nationality of foreign nationals out of contact in Tibet.

Tibet is one of the most repressive regions in China. The communist regime has maintained a harsh approach against any dissent in the area since its troops seized control of the territory in 1951. Foreign journalists need a special travel permit to enter the region, which U.S. officials have said is rarely granted.

Since the flooding occurred last week, Chinese news agencies have largely relied on state media reports, making it hard to know the real situation in the remote Himalayan region beyond the official narrative.

Manan Vatsyayana/AFP via Getty Images

Initial Assessment of Cause The U.S. Geological Survey has The U.S. Geological Survey has determined that “a glacial collapse and debris flow” was responsible for “subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream” near the Nepal–China border.

At a briefing on Aug. 30, Su Pengcheng, a researcher at state-backed Chinese Academy of Sciences, offered a similar assessment in more detail.

At about 10:52 a.m. local time on Aug. 28, a glacier on the north slope of Langtang Lirung, in a subrange of the Nepalese Himalayas at an elevation of roughly 5,200 meters (17,060 feet), suddenly broke apart.

The falling ice and rock quickly descended to about 4,000 meters (13,100 feet), scraping and picking up mountain debris along the way and creating a “massive debris flow,” Su said.

It then moved along the rivers at high speed and hit Gyirong Port—a main border crossing between China and Nepal—at an elevation of 1,800 meters (5,905 feet).

The entire process took only six to seven minutes, Su noted.

It left approximately 173 acres of the area devastated, sweeping away about 27 buildings and associated facilities, destroying roads leading to the crossing, and cutting off communications and electricity, he said.

Prakash Mathema/AFP via Getty Images

Beijing’s Censorship In recent years, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has further tightened its control over the flow of information related to In recent years, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has further tightened its control over the flow of information related to disasters and tragic incidents; criticism of or questions about the official narrative often vanish quickly from social media. The regime also has a record of concealing information deemed harmful to its image.

Chinese media coverage has been centered on the CCP’s response to the flood. Footage and photos aired by domestic outlets showed soldiers, police, and other rescue workers wading through the mud to search for survivors, rather than the stories of those affected.

On Aug. 30, state broadcaster CCTV said that police had punished two citizens for spreading what the authorities called false information in the comment sections of flood reports.

Greg Baker/AFP via Getty Images

A 38-year-old man surnamed Zhou was given administrative punishment and ordered to delete comments that police claimed exaggerated death tolls and missing person numbers on a short-video platform.

Another 43-year-old woman, surnamed Xu, received “criticism and education” for allegedly “fabricating false explanations about the cause of the disaster,” CCTV said. It didn’t specify what Xu’s claim was, saying only that Xu had deleted her post and signed a pledge to comply with internet laws.

Nepal warns of possible fresh flooding as communities grapple with devastation

Authorities in Nepal warned of possible fresh flooding on Sunday and urged residents in flood-affected districts to remain on high alert after water levels rose in the Bhotekoshi River.

Flood warning notices were sent to people's phones early Sunday as rescue crews worked to clear a major highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas worst hit by Wednesday's catastrophic floods, which killed at least 1,000 people and left more than 3,000 missing in Nepal and Tibet.

Advertisement

Related video above: Massachusetts woman among the missing in Nepal after catastrophic flooding

The latest warnings came after Chinese authorities informed their Nepalese counterparts of increased water flow upstream, according to Dharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

The Chinese state news agency Xinhua, citing the country’s water resources ministry, said a new lake formed after Wednesday’s floods high in the mountains had largely drained.

But Xinhua said the ministry warned that a crater located 5.6 kilometers (3.5 miles) upstream, which held an estimated 1.4 million cubic meters of water, still posed some risk and required close monitoring.

The missing include hundreds of people from over a dozen countries who were in the region to work, visit the mountains or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak. On Sunday, Chinese state media said 261 foreigners were missing in Tibet, including over a hundred Nepalis and others from around the world.



Some are returning to what remained of their homes

In Dhading, one of the worst-hit regions in Nepal, some residents began returning to ruined homes to see what can be salvaged.

Residents sat in homes with walls washed away by the floods, shoveling sludge-like mud and rubble off balconies or window frames. Others scanned the ground for items they could pick out of the mud and rinse off. One man had returned for his chickens, which he found alive. He tied them up and put them in the cabin of his truck.

“Everything is finished. Nothing is left. Not even our home,” Sharmila Tamang, a Dhading resident who was trying to salvage items from her home, told The Associated Press.

At a key power plant that was severely damaged by the floods, workers started inspecting the facilities Sunday to survey the destruction. The plant serves over 20,000 people across four districts.

In the town of Galchhi, a group of residents sought higher ground on a nearby bridge and watched as the river roared by. Some pointed to enormous rocks washed downriver during the earlier floods, while others standing on a suspension bridge were warned off with whistles.

Along the river, homes, vehicles and farm tractors could be seen jutting from the thick gray-brown sediment that enveloped entire villages in some areas. Parts of rice terraces along the riverside had dropped into the river after landslides hit them.

Residents are receiving constant flood warnings

Homes and businesses left intact after the flooding were still without electricity on Sunday, as twisted power line poles and wires lay tangled in the mud.

Residents of flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they've received since the initial floods.

“Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain,” said Govind Shreshta, a resident. “It’s really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mom. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It’s going on like this for those who are still alive.”

Large concrete and smaller suspension bridges were destroyed, leaving communities on the other side of the river with less easy access.

“Those who are there are now stuck there. Those who are here are stuck here. It’s going to be very difficult,” said Sattan Singh Tamang, 47, who was working near a bridge when Wednesday’s floods came.

Minister says Nepalis have become victims of climate change

Wednesday’s flash floods started after a glacial collapse high in the Himalayan region. Scientists who studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake.

The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.

Related video below: Comparative satellite image of Nepal-China border

Nepal’s foreign minister called for a global response to climate change, saying Nepal was bearing a disproportionate share of its impact.

“Despite having only 0.1% contribution to the global emissions, people of Nepal have become major victims of climate change,” Shisir Khanal said Saturday.

Scientists have said it is too early to draw a direct connection between global warming and Wednesday’s catastrophe. However, they said that as Earth’s temperature rises because of human activities such as burning oil, gas and coal, the chances of such disasters increase, especially in the Himalayan mountains, which are warming considerably faster than many other parts of the world.

Meanwhile, Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Sunday his country will send a search-and-rescue team to Nepal to assist with relief efforts and help evacuate Malaysians affected by the disaster.

Malaysia has also pledged $1 million in financial aid to Nepal, he said in a statement.

___

Associated Press writers Aijaz Hussain in New Delhi and Shristi Kafle in Kathmandu, Nepal, and video journalist Shonal Ganguly in Dhading, Nepal, contributed to this report.

title: Nepali Community Hosts Vigil Honoring Victims of Devastating Floods
full_text:
Flickering candles lit up Dublin’s O’Connell Street as Ireland’s Nepalese community gathered in grief — and in support — after catastrophic flooding tore through parts of Nepal.

Around 100 people attended a candle lit vigil at the Spire, organised by the Non-Resident Nepali Association of Ireland to honour those who have died and to raise funds for rescue and relief operations.

Avishek Bogati, a vice president of the association, comes from one of the areas struck by the deluge that hit on Wednesday after a glacier collapsed.

He told RTÉ News that “my uncle is also still missing”.

The vigil in Dublin was just one of several events planned around Ireland

Mr Bogati said uncertainty is still widespread as families wait for news.

“Nobody knows how many people are missing and how many people have died.

“Maybe after two weeks or after a month they will figure it out.”

He said his mother was airlifted by a military helicopter and brought to Kathmandu.

His village, he added, is among several left in ruins.

“There are three villages and 90% of the people are missing, 90% missing,” he said, adding “they still don’t have any information”.

Ireland is home to around 3,000 Nepalese people, most living in the Greater Dublin Area, with others based in counties Galway, Limerick and Cork.

Hundreds are employed on dairy farms, drawing on skills they previously developed while working in Gulf states.

The gathering in Dublin is one of a number of solidarity events planned nationwide.

Prajaya Neupane, a Nepali living in Co Limerick, said a fundraiser will also take place tomorrow night at Hunters Sports Bar in the city, offering food and drinks.

He said all proceeds will be sent to support those affected by the disaster in Nepal.

‘Something unprecedented’ – Nepalese man on flash floods

Mahesh Kushwaha originally thought the incident was a monsoon flood

Separately, a Nepalese man who recently returned to Dublin from Nepal said that while Kathmandu is already struggling under pressure, the wider response has provided some hope.

Mahesh Kushwaha, a PhD candidate at DCU, said he initially assumed the flooding was linked to the monsoon — an annual threat he described as both regular and worrying.

But as videos began circulating, he said he quickly understood the true magnitude.

“It was massive, it was something unprecedented,” he said.

Authorities said the death toll in Nepal and Tibet from last week’s floods has hit 797 with more than 3,000 missing.

At least 781 people died in Nepal, its disaster authority said, with 2,502 people missing as rescue efforts continue for a fifth day.

Chinese state media earlier confirmed 16 dead in Tibet and 546 people missing following the disaster, taking the overall toll to 797 dead and 3,048 unaccounted for.

Nepalese man says the situation in Nepal is ‘pretty dire’

Mr Kushwaha said conditions on the ground remain “pretty dire”, with bridges swept away and homes buried by debris.

“It’s really difficult to even get the rescue efforts and teams up in the worst affected areas,” he said.

Even once rain eases and water levels become less dangerous, he warned it will take a “lot of time” to reach those still missing or trapped in the hardest-hit locations.

He said his family are from the southern part of the country — “pretty far” from the flooded areas.

Speaking on RTÉ’s This Week programme, he said: “So, I do not have any of my immediate family or friends directly affected by it.

“But I personally know three to four people who are still missing in the flood from my village, which is quiet far from the affected areas.”

He said work patterns tied to the border economy mean people often travel into the regions now impacted — including to drive trucks or take jobs as civil engineers, among other roles.

Mr Kushwaha said the new government responded quickly, and described it as “quiet uplifting to see”.

He said the prime minister and the home minister were “on the ground”, adding “they’re working with the people”.

While some social media posts have framed this as a stunt, he said: “As a whole the government is seen positively right now, especially with regards to the rescue efforts.”

Mahesh Kushwaha said the response to the floods ‘has been quite uplifting’

He said hospitals in Kathmandu are receiving both survivors and the dead.

“Kathmandu’s infrastructures are already being overwhelmed … especially by the dead bodies,” he said.

“We don’t have specialised storages for those bodies.”

Mr Kushwaha said: “The overwhelming response from the people as well as from the international community has been quite uplifting.

This, he said, is “because we have seen billions of dollars being pulled in for rescue efforts”.

He said the Nepali diaspora has also mobilised to support relief efforts.

“But still, it’s so devastating,” he said.

Mr Mr Kushwaha said Nepal is one of the “smallest contributors in the world when it comes to carbon emissions”.

But he added the nation is “among the most vulnerable countries when it comes to climate change”.

“People are slowly seeing that these events are not just natural disasters out of nowhere it’s being linked to climate change,” he added.

On Sunday, Chinese state media said 261 foreigners were missing in Tibet, including over a hundred Nepalis and others from around the world.



Some are returning to what remained of their homes

In Dhading, one of the worst-hit regions in Nepal, some residents began returning to ruined homes to see what can be salvaged.

Residents sat in homes with walls washed away by the floods, shoveling sludge-like mud and rubble off balconies or window frames. Others scanned the ground for items they could pick out of the mud and rinse off. One man had returned for his chickens, which he found alive. He tied them up and put them in the cabin of his truck.

“Everything is finished. Nothing is left. Not even our home,” Sharmila Tamang, a Dhading resident who was trying to salvage items from her home, told The Associated Press.

At a key power plant that was severely damaged by the floods, workers started inspecting the facilities Sunday to survey the destruction. The plant serves over 20,000 people across four districts.

In the town of Galchhi, a group of residents sought higher ground on a nearby bridge and watched as the river roared by. Some pointed to enormous rocks washed downriver during the earlier floods, while others standing on a suspension bridge were warned off with whistles.

Along the river, homes, vehicles and farm tractors could be seen jutting from the thick gray-brown sediment that enveloped entire villages in some areas. Parts of rice terraces along the riverside had dropped into the river after landslides hit them.

Residents are receiving constant flood warnings

Homes and businesses left intact after the flooding were still without electricity on Sunday, as twisted power line poles and wires lay tangled in the mud.

Residents of flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they've received since the initial floods.

“Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain,” said Govind Shreshta, a resident. “It’s really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mom. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It’s going on like this for those who are still alive.”

Large concrete and smaller suspension bridges were destroyed, leaving communities on the other side of the river with less easy access.

“Those who are there are now stuck there. Those who are here are stuck here. It’s going to be very difficult,” said Sattan Singh Tamang, 47, who was working near a bridge when Wednesday’s floods came.

Minister says Nepalis have become victims of climate change

Wednesday’s flash floods started after a glacial collapse high in the Himalayan region. Scientists who studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake.

The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.

Related video below: Comparative satellite image of Nepal-China border

Nepal’s foreign minister called for a global response to climate change, saying Nepal was bearing a disproportionate share of its impact.

“Despite having only 0.1% contribution to the global emissions, people of Nepal have become major victims of climate change,” Shisir Khanal said Saturday.

Scientists have said it is too early to draw a direct connection between global warming and Wednesday’s catastrophe. However, they said that as Earth’s temperature rises because of human activities such as burning oil, gas and coal, the chances of such disasters increase, especially in the Himalayan mountains, which are warming considerably faster than many other parts of the world.

Meanwhile, Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Sunday his country will send a search-and-rescue team to Nepal to assist with relief efforts and help evacuate Malaysians affected by the disaster.

Malaysia has also pledged $1 million in financial aid to Nepal, he said in a statement.

___

Associated Press writers Aijaz Hussain in New Delhi and Shristi Kafle in Kathmandu, Nepal, and video journalist Shonal Ganguly in Dhading, Nepal, contributed to this report.

title: School principal saved at least 900 pupils during deadly Nepal flooding
full_text:
Rajendra Dawadi was inside his classroom at Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School when the school’s accountant rushed in to warn that floodwaters were racing through Nepal’s Trishuli Valley, tearing apart homes, bridges and entire villages.

Then, a teacher received another warning by phone. Moments later, a parent arrived to take her child home.

Rajendra Dawadi took the decision to clear Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School (AP)

The danger had not yet been confirmed, but Mr Dawadi had little time to act. He rang the school bell and ordered pupils and staff out of the building and to move towards higher ground.

“I immediately decided to stop … school and (get the children out),” he told The Associated Press.

As he followed them to a nearby hill, the floodwaters rose behind him.

From the safety of the hillside, he turned to watch the school where he had once been a pupil – and where he had spent years teaching – disappear beneath a torrent of water, mud, boulders and debris. Two staff members could not make it, and remain missing.

The death toll in the catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet climbed past 900 on Monday, with more than 4,700 missing.

Mr Dawadi’s decision to evacuate the school saved at least 900 students from last week’s devastating flash floods in Nepal, unleashed after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas. The disaster killed more than 900 people across Nepal and China, while more than 4,700 remain missing.

As Nepal grapples with the catastrophic natural disaster, Mr Dawadi’s story has emerged as a striking example of foresight and courage.

The Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in the Trishuli Valley of north-central Nepal had 1,643 pupils.

At least 900 were on campus that morning, while some students were still making their way to school. Mr Dawadi ordered those already there to leave and called bus drivers, telling them to only stop at safer places.

One bus, packed with students, had already reached the school when Mr Dawadi told the driver to turn back, he said. The bus crossed a newly constructed bridge and, moments later, the old bridge beside it collapsed.

For Mr Dawadi, the scale of the destruction has become personal, as the school had been both his workplace and a large part of his life.

The search for survivors continues (AP)

“I have no words. I got education from that school. And I gave education at that school,” he said.

The destruction of Mr Dawadi’s school was not an isolated loss.

Across northern Nepal, the floods have left thousands of children without classrooms, disrupted their education and raised fears that the disaster could cost them months of schooling.

Charity group Save the Children said in a statement that at least 69 schools in northern Nepal have been completely destroyed, putting the education of nearly 19,000 students at risk.

Mr Dawadi’s quick thinking and swift response during the disaster have been hailed as an act of heroism. When he returned to the site of the school days later, parents embraced him as they thanked him for saving their children.

“Their parents hugged me, they cried with me,” he said. “They were emotional.”

Pupil Suvina Tamang, 14, said the school’s three-storey building was swept away shortly after all the students had been evacuated.

“I will thank him when I see him” for saving my life, she said.

But Mr Dawadi is reluctant to accept the role of hero. For him, rescuing his students was his responsibility. Now he says, students will need psychological counselling. Then, lessons must begin again, even if the school must temporarily relocate.

His appeal to the Nepalese government is simple: rebuild the schools and get children back to classes.

title: Nepal must work to avert the next disaster instead of just responding to it
full_text:
Open this photo in gallery: Members of the Nepal Army paddle an inflatable boat on Monday to retrieve bodies that were washed away by the recent flooding.Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters

Brabim Karki is a writer and columnist based in Nepal.

It has been a terrible week in Nepal, and the numbers alone don’t begin to tell the story.

On Wednesday, a giant torrent of water, mud and ice swept away villages and destroyed roads and infrastructure near the Nepal-China border. By Monday, the death toll in Nepal had climbed to at least 903, with more than 4,000 people still unaccounted for, with 592 of them foreigners, according to the latest data released by the government of Nepal. And on the Tibet side of the border, at least 16 people have been killed with 500 missing, according to Chinese authorities. Nepalese officials said on Monday the focus was on reaching the 900 workers believed to be trapped inside hydropower tunnels and various projects.

The U.S. State Department said on Sunday that about 85 U.S. citizens were missing, adding that nine had been rescued; Canada’s foreign ministry reported that 30 Canadians in both Nepal and Tibet were among the missing. Ottawa announced $5-million in humanitarian assistance funding to support emergency relief efforts, and after initially announcing a $500,000 contribution, Washington eventually announced more than US$3.6-million in humanitarian aid Saturday.

Force of Nepali flash floods leaves little chance of survival for missing pilgrims, organization says

What’s more, this is the second time in 13 months that this stretch of the Trishuli River has drowned the same villages. A flood on July 8, 2025, which also originated upstream, killed at least nine people, swept away the bridge linking Nepal and China and wrecked the Rasuwagadhi dry port.

The response to both disasters by the Nepalese government has been swift, as Prime Minister Balendra Shah has followed the same script as his predecessor Khadga Prasad Oli: an emergency cabinet meeting, evacuation orders, sending helicopters as the waters rushed. But what this disaster demonstrated is not a lack of ability to respond. What is troubling is that reacting quickly remains one of the few tools available, and only once a disaster is already under way.

Scientists are still working to determine the actual cause of the flood. Officials initially assumed it had crossed into Nepal from a glacial lake that burst in Tibet, but satellite analysis by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, working with counterparts in Nepal and China, now points to an ice-and-rock avalanche that fell into the Lhende Khola, a tributary roughly 40 to 50 kilometres upstream of the border, damming the river until the accumulated water broke through. A magnitude 4.4 earthquake was also recorded on the Tibetan side minutes before the flood hit, and researchers are still trying to determine whether the tremor triggered the avalanche or was itself generated by the mass of falling ice and rock. Meanwhile, danger still hangs in the air, as officials on the Chinese side have stated that a barrier lake at the confluence of the Tsogyal and Purupqiangzangbu rivers was overflowing and could also burst.

Open this photo in gallery: Nepalese police officers carry a survivor of the flooding to safety in the village of Devighat.Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters

The 2025 floods wiped out the stretch of road connecting the village of Syabrubesi to the border crossing at Rasuwagadhi. This vital corridor was only partially rebuilt, but every rupee spent on that reconstruction was a bet that the river would behave. It didn’t. Rebuilding the same infrastructure in the same fragile location, without better early-warning systems, is not resilience. It is merely repetition, and expecting different results.

Bigger changes need to be made to try to avert the next disaster. While a China-Nepal flash flood early-warning system exists, the upstream monitoring stations were swept away before alerts could be sent. Kathmandu cannot compel China to share real-time hydrological data on its own territory to create a more effective warning system. Bilateral data-sharing agreements on transboundary rivers exist elsewhere in the region, including with India, so Nepal doesn’t need to guess what one would look like; it just needs the will to negotiate one before the third flood. But even if Kathmandu succeeds in doing so, it must also understand that no warning system will ever be foolproof when dealing with a border that sits on some of the most unstable glacial terrain on Earth.

Syabrubesi will rebuild, as it did last year. The road will reopen. The hydropower plants along the riverbanks will be back online, and life along the Trishuli will settle back into its routine. But Nepal will not be meaningfully safer unless policy-makers start treating the transboundary watershed as a standing security and disaster-preparedness problem rather than a recurring emergency.

title: Nepal floods test PM Balen young government
full_text:
A year after Gen Z-led protests swept Prime Minister Balendra "Balen" Shah to power, deadly floods are testing his government's ability to manage a national crisis.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, an ex-rapper popularly known as "Balen," is facing the enormous task of rebuilding communities and critical infrastructure following last week's deadly flash floods.

The floods, carrying rock, ice, mud and debris, swept through areas near the Chinese border, ravaging entire towns and damaging hydropower plants.

More than 900 people have been confirmed dead and nearly 4,800 remain missing, authorities said Monday, as rescue efforts entered a sixth day.

The devastating floods struck the Himalayan nation just days before the anniversary of the Gen-Z-led anti-corruption protests of September 8-9, 2025 that toppled the previous government and swept Shah to power.

Now, the 36-year-old prime minister and his largely inexperienced cabinet face their first major national crisis in what is shaping up to be the country's worst disaster in a decade.

Anxious relatives await news from flood zone

Rescuers, including Chinese and Indian experts, believe hundreds of workers are trapped in tunnels at hydropower sites under construction that were buried in mud by the catastrophic flooding.

Nepal floods trap hundreds in hydropower tunnels To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Sushila Giri was waiting for news of her son, Sishir, a Kathmandu University student completing an internship at one of the hydropower projects.

"I came to know that my son, along with others, was at the quarter of the hydro project when the disaster happened," she told DW. "Please help me find his whereabouts."

Gen Z activist Raksha Bam expressed concern about delays in rescuing workers trapped at hydropower projects and urged the government to seek specialized assistance from the international community.

Across affected districts, family members gathered in hospitals and temporary aid centers hoping for news of missing loved ones.

Indra Adhikari lost her home and paddy fields in the floods. Four of her relatives remain missing. She said rescue and relief efforts appeared concentrated in areas accessible by road and where media were present, particularly along one side of the Trishuli River.

"Most of those who have come to Trishuli Bazaar are not rescuers but onlookers," she told DW. "Remote settlements farther upstream and across the river remain difficult to reach."

Nepal: Rapper-turned-politician set to become next PM To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How is the new government handling the crisis?

The administration itself has acknowledged that it was not fully prepared for a disaster of such scale, which is the deadliest for Nepal since a 2015 earthquake killed thousands and injured many more.

"On the very first day, we got a bit confused as to how to deal with the crisis," Bikram Timilsina, minister for information and communication, told DW after visiting the flood-hit area. "[From the] second day onward, we have been putting all our efforts into swift search, rescue and relief works."

Security agencies have received praise for their response, particularly their efforts to reach people in inaccessible areas via helicopters. But the disaster has also exposed questions about the government's crisis-management capacity and its relationship with Nepal's provincial and local governments.

"Given the scale of devastation, the government's efforts and promptness to deal with the crisis are commendable," Madhu Raman Acharya, a former foreign secretary of Nepal, told DW. "The preliminary search and rescue efforts, especially coordination among security agencies, are commendable."

Nepal flood survivors still searching for some 3,000 missing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Govinda Pokharel, a former chief executive officer of the National Reconstruction Authority which oversaw post-earthquake reconstruction, however, has a different take.

He said the federal government had attempted to manage the crisis largely on its own, without adequately involving local and provincial governments. This is particularly significant because Shah's ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party has no presence in local or provincial governments.

Pokharel also questioned whether the government's lack of experience had affected its ability to gauge the scale of the response required.

"Our neighboring countries like China and India were willing to lend help for rescue, especially for tunnel rescue from the very outset," he told DW, adding that the government failed to decide in time whether to allow them to deploy, costing three crucial days.

Can Balen's government deliver?

Nepal initially maintained that its own rescue teams were capable of handling the operation.

But by Friday, Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal told the media that the government had decided to seek international expertise, including from China and India, for tunnel rescues, DNA testing and forensic examinations.

The shift highlighted one of the central challenges facing the new administration: whether the government can act quickly and effectively during a rapidly evolving national emergency.

Pokharel said the government's decision to raise substantial funds domestically for disaster relief demonstrated public confidence.

Nepal starts mass burials of hundreds ⁠of flood victims To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"One good thing is that the government is collecting a huge sum of public money domestically on the Prime Minister's Disaster Relief Fund," he said. "It shows the public trust in the government that doesn't misuse its funds collected in the name of relief."

By Saturday, over 5 billion Nepali rupees ($34.7 million/€29.9 million) had been collected in a government-run disaster relief fund for flood victims, according to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers.

Prabha Bogati, deputy mayor of Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot, said local authorities had limited scope to act during the crisis because the federal government adopted a centralized "one-door" approach, requiring relief activities to be coordinated through a single command structure.

"In previous crises, local communities and volunteers used to be mobilized in search, rescue and relief efforts," she told DW.

Bogati added that helicopter rescues have been effective, but local stakeholders have not been brought into the response and have not been allowed to recover bodies or perform final rites.

Government spokesperson and Education Minister Sasmit Pokharel defended the administration's response, saying all available resources were being mobilized for rescue, relief and rehabilitation.

"In the first phase, our priority was to save citizens' lives by using the available human resources and means," Pokharel told reporters. "A process has also been initiated to better organize the mobilization of volunteers."

Edited by: Keith Walker

title: Nepal floods leave 500 workers trapped in tunnels as 43 Australians remain missing amid China disaster
full_text:
A devastating flash flood disaster in Nepal has claimed the life of at least one Australian, with 42 others still missing.

A devastating flash flood disaster in Nepal has claimed the life of at least one Australian, with 42 others still missing.

Rescuers in Nepal are racing against time to reach hundreds of workers feared trapped inside massive hydropower tunnels as the scale of the catastrophic flooding across the Himalayan region continues to grow.

More than 950 people have now been killed across Nepal and China, while more than 4,400 remain missing, including 43 Australians whose whereabouts remain unknown.

In Nepal, attention has turned to hydropower projects devastated by the flash floods, with a private-sector association representing power companies reporting at least 900 workers remain unaccounted for across 12 sites in the Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.

About 500 of those workers are believed to be trapped underground in tunnels used to control the flow of water.

Four bodies have now been recovered from three mud-filled tunnels, according to Nepal’s army, as rescuers desperately try to reach those who could still be alive.

NSW man Michael Keats has become the first Australian confirmed to have lost his life in Nepal’s flash flood disaster.

He was travelling to India for a spiritual retreat, according to his heartbroken family, which is now asking for support.

His partner Emily Boyd posted a grim update to her GoFundMe, confirming the worst on Monday evening.

“My partner, Michael, was tragically killed in the devastating floods in Nepal,” Ms Boyd posted.

“Michael was my partner and an incredibly important part of our family. He was also my young son’s stepfather, although he was the only father he has ever known. His loss has changed everything for both of us.”

In her crowdfunding post, Ms Boyd said she was asking for funds to travel to India with the couple’s son to engage in a spiritual ritual to honour the South Coast man.

“There’s a bittersweetness knowing that there was nothing more that Mike wanted (than) to know God, and to merge with the divine,” Ms Boyd posted to Instagram.

“He was a mystic, a medicine man, a teacher, leader, partner, father, brother, son, uncle and dearly beloved friend.”

Some workers were able to make calls for help when the disaster struck last Wednesday, while survivors who escaped told authorities and relatives that many of their colleagues remained underground.

Camera Icon BHARATPUR, NEPAL - AUGUST 30: (EDITOR'S NOTE: Image depicts death.) Police and army personnel bury unidentified bodies recovered from the flash floods at a mass burial site in the Devghat Forest on August 30, 2026 in Bharatpur, Nepal. Authorities said the flash floods were triggered after a mass of ice, mud and rock collapsed into a Himalayan river near the Nepal-China border, leaving hundreds dead or missing and causing widespread damage in affected districts. Authorities continued the gruelling search for victims, many buried under metres of mud, as both China and Nepal issued fresh flooding alerts. (Photo by Ezra Acayan/Getty Images) *** BESTPIX *** Credit: Ezra Acayan / Getty Images

However, it remains unclear whether rescuers have established contact with any of those trapped since the initial calls.

Six days after the disaster, Independent Power Producers’ Association Nepal president Mohan Kumar Dangi said fears were mounting that some workers may have suffocated.

Race against time for workers trapped in tunnels

Geoscientist Jakob Steiner said the enormous size of the tunnels could offer some hope.

“These tunnels are big enough to drive trucks through,” he said.

“And from what we understand, they have managed to get oxygen to some of those stuck inside and are trying to rescue them now.

“It’s a race for time, though, as people need food and water.”

At the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in badly hit Rasuwa, at least 576 people remain missing, with about 300 believed to be trapped inside the project’s tunnel.

Crews at the Trishuli-3 Hydropower Project are attempting to descend about 15 metres into another tunnel to reach workers feared trapped below.

Elsewhere, workers have been shovelling mud from a flood-ravaged power station in Dhading that provides a crucial electricity connection for more than 20,000 people.

Nepal’s disaster agency said on Monday that 939 people had been confirmed dead in the country and another 3,925 remained missing, including 592 foreigners.

Camera Icon An aerial view shows a torrent of muddy water surging past houses and through the Trishuli river in the aftermath of flash floods, at Betrawati in Nepal's Nuwakot district on August 29, 2026. More than 3,000 people were listed as missing on August 30, with another 768 confirmed dead, after the flash floods and landslides that hit the Nepal-Tibet border. Credit: Prabin Ranabhat / AFP

Chinese authorities had reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing as of Sunday, with state media reporting 261 of those missing were foreigners.

Grave fears grow for 43 missing Australians

Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong said there were now grave concerns for the 43 Australians who remain unaccounted for.

“We are urgently seeking to ascertain their whereabouts … we do hold grave fears, grave concerns for their safety,” she told 7.30.

Ms Wong said authorities had confirmed nine of the 43 missing Australians had crossed the border into China when the disaster struck.

“What we don’t have as yet, confirmed from any of the authorities, is any information about the 43 in total,” she said.

“This is such a difficult time. It’s incredibly distressing.

“We are working to do whatever we can and to provide any information we obtain.”

Camera Icon NYTSELECTS — A resident surveys houses destroyed by the flash flood next to the river in Devighat, Nepal, on Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. Five days after an angry deluge tore through the mountain passes of Nepal, family members arriving after long journeys looked for something — anything — that could identify their loved ones amid the hundreds of mangled bodies. (Atul Loke/The New York Times) Credit: ATUL LOKE / NYT

An Australian Air Force C-17A carrying humanitarian supplies, equipment and personnel is due to travel to Nepal on Tuesday as part of the Federal Government’s $8 million humanitarian response.

What triggered the catastrophic Himalayan floods

Across the border in China, crews are attempting to rebuild the road leading to the Gyirong Port crossing between China and Nepal.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed trucks carrying huge rocks as workers attempted to repave part of the road beside fast-moving floodwaters following days of rain. Sections of the road are now under two to three metres of water.

Scientists examining satellite imagery believe the devastating floods began when bedrock beneath a glacier high in the Himalayas collapsed, bringing part of the glacier down with it.

The enormous rockfall registered as a magnitude-5.2 seismic event.

Rock, debris and meltwater then surged into rivers below, creating a devastating torrent that swept away buildings, bridges and earth as it tore through Tibet and Nepal.

title: In disaster aftermath , Nepal battles a flood of misinformation
full_text:
September 1, 2026

KATHMANDU – Hours after the Bhotekoshi floods swept away settlements in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts on Wednesday morning, social media platforms were inundated with dramatic clips purporting to show the destruction.

Some depicted genuine disasters, but from other countries or earlier events. Others were digitally manipulated. Several appeared to have been created entirely by artificial intelligence.

The scale and speed of misinformation has complicated an already chaotic information environment at a time when families are desperately searching for missing relatives and authorities are struggling to establish the full extent of the disaster.

For social media users chasing views and virality, the flood has also become lucrative content.

At 7:26 am on Saturday, a Facebook page called Dudhauli FM posted a 20-second video claiming to show Home Minister Sudan Gurung inside a tunnel at the disaster site.

“Home Minister Gurung’s unique style: He reaches inside the tunnel at the incident site to join the rescue,” the caption said, praising what it described as the minister’s proactive involvement.

The page later amended the caption.

The video quickly spread across Facebook, TikTok and X.

But it was not from Nepal.

Fact-checkers established that the footage showed a tunnel rescue operation in Uttarakhand, India. The uniforms worn by the rescuers and the surroundings matched those seen in the original footage, which had been posted by the Fire Service Uttarakhand Police’s Facebook page on August 14.

The false attribution was only one example of misleading content circulating after the disaster.

As rescuers race against time to reach people trapped in tunnels and communities cut off by the devastating flash flood, a torrent of fabricated videos, recycled footage, artificial intelligence-generated imagery and cruel online commentary has bewildered a wider populace.

On August 27, at 7:54 am, an X account named Prakash Kunwar posted a 10-second video showing what appeared to be a catastrophic flood.

“No one imagined this would happen… What can anyone do when nature goes mad! May all those caught in the disaster be rescued safely,” the caption said.

The video had received more than seven million views, over 4,100 reposts and around 15,000 reactions at the time of reporting.

Yet the dramatic scene was not real.

When analysed using Hive Moderation, an AI detection tool, the video was assessed as 97.2 percent likely to have been generated by artificial intelligence. X’s community notes also flagged the clip as artificial, while BBC Verify independently debunked it.

Another viral video posted later that day showed a bridge apparently collapsing amid a raging flood. The user who shared it wrote: “If this video of the Nepal-Tibet flood is true, I have never seen anything like this in my lifetime…”

The clip, analysed through Hive Moderation, was assessed as entirely AI-generated.

International fact-checkers have also joined efforts to trace misleading visuals linked to the disaster.

Nepali fact-checking website Nepal Fact Check recently debunked a video that purported to show a glacial lake outburst flood, or GLOF, in Rasuwa. The clip showed a violent torrent of water and carried the English text: “This is a GLOF.”

The footage had no connection to Nepal.

Fact-checkers traced it to a glacial outburst flood at Columbia Glacier in Alaska, United States.

Similarly, a pair of “before and after” photographs claiming to show a picturesque settlement destroyed by the Rasuwa flood went viral on social media. Both images were fabricated, according to an independent verification by the Australian Associated Press fact-checking unit.

The false videos and manipulated images are only one part of the digital disorder surrounding the disaster.

Graphic footage of bodies, injuries and devastated communities has also spread widely, often shared by personal social media accounts without warnings or consideration for victims and their families.

The Nepal Press Council, the country’s media regulatory body, says it has been monitoring online content related to the disaster. Over the past four days, it has instructed 72 social media users to remove inappropriate content, most of it posted through personal accounts.

The council has also opened a dedicated portal, titled “Special Complaints on the Bhotekoshi Incident”, through which members of the public can report misinformation and graphic material.

By 5 pm on Saturday, the portal had received 101 complaints, according to Umesh Shrestha, chairman of the Press Council.

“It was found that 67 personal accounts had posted gruesome scenes. Similarly, complaints have been lodged against some online news portals and their social media pages,” Shrestha said.

He said mainstream media organisations had largely avoided publishing misleading information and excessively graphic visuals.

“This is a positive takeaway,” he said.

For fact-checkers, the Rasuwa disaster illustrates how artificial intelligence has made an old problem more difficult to contain.

Chetana Kunwar, assistant editor at Nepal Fact Check, said misleading visuals connected to the Bhotekoshi flood were increasingly being created with AI.

“AI-generated content and manipulated ‘before and after’ visuals make it significantly easier to create false impressions, which can be extremely difficult for the general public to detect,” she said. “At the same time, videos from disasters in other countries are deliberately being circulated as if they were from Nepal.”

The spread of false information during disasters is not new. Old photographs and videos have long been recycled after earthquakes, floods and other major emergencies. But generative AI has added another layer to the problem, allowing convincing images and videos to be created from scratch within minutes.

The result is an information ecosystem in which even genuine footage can become difficult to verify.

The information vacuum

Why does misinformation spread so rapidly during disasters? Shrestha, a former editor of Nepal Fact Check, points to the intense competition for attention that follows major emergencies.

“Some people post such material for views, while others are driven by the desire to go viral,” he said. “During a crisis, public attention is heavily concentrated on one event, creating a strong emotional response. People begin liking, commenting on and sharing posts without verifying them.”

Deepak Adhikari, an investigative journalist and editor of Nepal Check, says an “information vacuum” often emerges immediately after a major disaster.

When verified information from the ground is delayed, incomplete or contradictory, social media users begin filling the gaps themselves.

“People start crowdsourcing photographs and videos and sharing them without verification, which makes the problem worse,” Adhikari told the Post.

At the same time, he said, social media influencers and content creators face constant pressure to publish material that attracts attention.

“As a result, they share visually striking graphics and videos without properly verifying where they were recorded,” he said.

The dynamic is particularly dangerous during a fast-moving disaster, when official information can take time to emerge and the public is searching urgently for news about relatives, roads, rescue operations and possible further threats.

Kunwar said people were particularly vulnerable to misinformation during such periods.

“When there is an information vacuum, people often do not stop to assess what is right or wrong. They tend to believe whatever information reaches them first,” she said.

Social media algorithms can amplify the problem, she added. Once users engage with disaster-related content, platforms often recommend more of the same, regardless of whether it is accurate.

The consequences can extend beyond confusion.

Shrestha warned that circulating old or fabricated footage as current events could create unnecessary fear and panic, not only among the public but also among rescue and relief workers operating in difficult conditions.

Adhikari said misinformation could directly interfere with emergency operations.

“Someone may already have been rescued and moved to a safe place, but people might continue sharing an old video showing that person trapped somewhere,” he said.

“The primary focus should be rescue and relief, but many people appear more concerned about promoting themselves and posting photographs and videos.”

For survivors and families of the missing, false information can repeatedly reopen trauma.

Rumours suggesting another flood is imminent, or that the disaster is about to repeat, can further frighten people who have already lost homes, relatives or livelihoods, Kunwar said.

Government agencies are now attempting to respond. The government’s Social Media Regulation and Management Committee, which has been tasked with addressing graphic content, AI-generated misinformation, fake QR codes and other forms of online deception, has begun discussions with social media platforms.

But controlling misinformation after it has gone viral remains a formidable challenge.

A crisis of empathy

The information crisis surrounding the Rasuwa flood has also revealed something more troubling: a striking absence of empathy.

A video showing a woman tearfully appealing to the government to speed up the search for her husband, who is missing inside a tunnel, has drawn a stream of cruel and abusive comments.

The woman, visibly distressed, pleads for authorities to rescue her husband. Instead of offering sympathy, some users mocked her grief. Others criticised her for speaking only about her husband or attacked her for blaming the government.

The cruelty was often casual and anonymous, delivered from behind screens to someone facing the possibility of losing a loved one.

Comments questioning why her husband had taken the job and suggesting that she was secretly happy about his disappearance turned an expression of grief into another spectacle for online consumption.

Such reactions have become an unsettling feature of Nepal’s social media culture during the disaster, where genuine suffering is sometimes treated as entertainment, political ammunition or an opportunity for engagement.

For journalists and fact-checkers, the combination of misinformation and insensitivity presents a broader challenge than simply identifying fake videos.

Disasters create an extraordinary demand for information. They also create a market for attention.

The faster the information circulates, the less time users may spend asking whether it is authentic. And when a video provokes fear, outrage or shock, the incentive to share can overwhelm the instinct to verify.

That is why responsibility cannot rest solely with authorities, technology companies or fact-checkers, Kunwar said.

title: Family of New Zealand woman missing in Nepal flash flood dismisses false rescue reports
full_text:
The family of a New Zealand woman who is missing in the deadly Nepal flash flood has called on rescuers not to stop searching for the 44-year-old after conflicting reports of her status emerged online.

Suhasini Reddy was among five New Zealanders who have been reported missing following Wednesday's flash flood at the Nepal-China border.

Reddy's brother, Rajeev, and his wife, Lauren, have urged people to keep searching for survivors in a Facebook post.

"Please do not stop searching for her and please continue to share her information," the post said. "We will continue to do everything in our power to bring Suhasini home."

The couple told The Australian they decided to make the post on social media after seeing local outlets in India falsely report Reddy had been found alive.

They have arrived in Nepal to assist with the search for Reddy, according to media reports.

A spokesperson from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade said Tuesday there had been no change to the status of the five missing New Zealanders.

"While various information is circulating online of those rescued and recovered, there is still no new verified information on the missing New Zealanders," the spokesperson said.

"This is likely to take more time to emerge. Unfortunately, reports of the situation on the ground remain bleak."

Rajeev told RNZ last week that his sister, a mother of two who has been living in Australia for the past four years, was believed to have been in the Dhunche area heading towards the border on Wednesday morning local time when the flood struck.

The software engineer had been on a guided tour with Kailash Journeys with friends from Australia, her brother said.

More than 900 people have been killed and nearly 5,000 are still missing from the flash flood, according to latest wire reports.

Three hundred and fifteen foreign nationals have been rescued to date, according to the latest update from the Nepal Tourism Board early Tuesday morning.

New Zealanders Dejan Kuzmic, Shweta Mhatre, Mihir Patel and Kinnari Patel are also unaccounted for after the flash flood.

Here's what we know about them, as the search for those missing following the disaster continues.

Dejan Kuzmic Supplied

'Selfless' man dreamed of sacred pilgrimage for years

Dejan Kuzmic was part of a group of 77 Isha Foundation hikers who had just completed the pilgrimage to Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar.

Kuzmic came to New Zealand from Bosnia and Herzegovina as a refugee when he was 10 years old.

Nepal's Tourist Police confirmed Kuzmic's name to RNZ on Thursday morning.

Kuzmic's flatmate, Alicia Gimelfarb, told RNZ on Monday that Kuzmic had just turned 44.

"He was very selfless, very generous, and very ... affectionate," she said.

"He was always cheerful and, you know, wanted to make everyone smile and laugh."

She said he was always helpful and went the extra mile for people.

The pair met through school and had been flatting together for the past five years.

Gimelfarb said he had been "dreaming" and planning to go to Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar to do the sacred pilgrimage for several years.

Kuzmic has not made contact since the flash flood and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade had opened a consular case for him.

Missing Auckland woman travelled in Kuzmic's pilgrimage group

Auckland woman Shweta Mhatre is believed to be missing, following the devastating flash floods.

Close friends of hers told RNZ that she was in Nepal on a pilgrimage.

None of them had heard from her since the flash flood.

A former partner of hers, as well as her neighbours, had not seen or heard from her.

RNZ confirmed Tuesday that Mhatre had travelled in the same Isha Foundation pilgrimage group as Kuzmic.

The Isha Foundation told RNZ on Friday that Mhatre's emergency contacts had been notified about her situation.

Sadhguru, founder of the Isha Foundation, posted a video on social media saying two New Zealanders were missing from his pilgrimage group.

Mihir and Kinnari Patel Namaskar Gujarat NZ News

'Only a miracle can save them'

Mihir and Kinnari Patel, who own the Best Value Urlich Ave Dairy in Hamilton, have also been reported missing in Nepal.

Kinnary Patel's brother, Chirag, said the family remained hopeful the couple would be found.

"We're praying and that's all we can do," he said.

Chirag Patel said his 76-year-old mother was returning to New Zealand to support their two children.

He also remained in constant contact with the children in New Zealand.

He said he would attend a meeting organised by Richa Tours, which had organised Mihir and Kinnary Patel's pilgrimage to the Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar region.

Sixty-one people who were travelling with Richa Tours were missing, Patel said.

He said the couple had been celebrating Kinnary's 50th birthday while on the pilgrimage.

"They were planning to stay here for 10 days as well," he said, speaking from Vadodara in the Indian state of Gujarat.

Patel said the couple were always happy and made sure those around them were happy as well.

"I just want to say to everyone in New Zealand to pray for my Kinnari and Mihir," he said. "Only a miracle can save them."

Meanwhile, a family friend who declined to be named said the Gujarat community in New Zealand was standing behind the Patel family.

"We are just praying for Mihir and Kinnari's return home safely," he said, adding that the community had been doing all it could to find information on the couple.

"Unfortunately, no luck so far."

Their eldest son, Drishya Patel, told RNZ last week he was holding onto hope his parents had left the area before the disaster struck.

"They're just on a trip to go visit some of the mountains in Nepal. It's like a pilgrimage of sorts," he said.

"They were having a good time."

His mother had messaged him on WhatsApp about 5.30am local time to say they were leaving. The flash flood began unfolding around 8.40am local time.

The couple have not been heard from since.
