title: Nepal Hydropower Tunnel Rescue ; 500 Workers Trapped in Flood - Proof Structures
full_text:
Five days after a glacier collapsed on the Nepal-Tibet border and unleashed a flood that has killed more than 900 people, rescue teams from three countries are focused on one of the most operationally complex high-altitude tunnel rescue efforts in recent Himalayan history: reaching an estimated 500 workers who may still be alive inside the same hydropower tunnels that were designed — and built robustly enough — to survive the disaster around them. The Nepal flood death toll has reached 903 in Nepal and 16 in Tibet, with hydropower workers trapped in tunnels at 12 affected projects in Nepal's Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.

The engineering situation is described precisely by Arnold Dix, an Australian geologist and former ITA president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, who played a leading role in saving 41 workers from the 2023 Uttarakhand tunnel collapse in India and is now advising the Nepal operation remotely from Melbourne. "Normally, they collapse and I'm trying to get people out," Dix told CNN on August 30. "This time, they haven't collapsed, but everything around them has, and I'm trying to get in."

That distinction — tunnel structurally intact; tunnel entrance buried under meters of Himalayan debris — is the defining challenge of an ongoing rescue effort across at least 11 hydropower projects in Nepal's Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts. The Independent Power Producers' Association of Nepal, or IPPAN, which represents private power developers, reported that approximately 900 workers remained unaccounted for across 12 projects as of Monday morning, with its president, Mohan Kumar Dangi, estimating that 500 workers believed in tunnels. Nepal's government disaster agency, NDRRMA, put its NDRRMA missing hydropower worker count at 933.

How a Mountain Fell and Sealed the Tunnels

The flood began before dawn Nepal Standard Time on August 26, when a mass of glacier ice and bedrock detached from the northern slope of Langtang Lirung — a 7,234-meter (23,734-foot) peak on the Nepal-Tibet border — and plunged roughly 1,200 meters (3,940 feet) into the valley below. The U.S. Geological Survey, which initially detected the event as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake, re-examined seismic waveform data and satellite imagery and USGS reclassified the glacial collapse: no earthquake had occurred. The seismic signal was generated by the collapse itself, reclassified as a magnitude 5.2 glacial landslide.

The falling ice and rock temporarily dammed the Lhende Khola, a river draining toward the Nepal-China border crossing at Gyirong Port. When that debris dam failed, a surge of water, rock, and liquefied sediment tore southward through Nepal's Trishuli River system. At one monitoring point, the river rose 9 meters in minutes — nearly 30 feet in 30 minutes. The flood carried some victims 240 kilometers (150 miles) downstream into northern India.

By Monday, 903 dead and 4,247 missing had been confirmed in Nepal and 16 dead in Tibet's Gyirong County, with 546 more missing in China. The dead span citizens of at least 39 countries; 590 foreign nationals still missing, according to Nepal's foreign ministry.

Why the Tunnels May Have Saved Hundreds — and Why That Complicates Everything

Nepal's hydropower industry relies on large-bore tunnels bored directly through Himalayan rock to divert and carry water from river intakes to turbine chambers. These tunnels are engineering accomplishments built to exacting specifications for one reason: Himalayan rivers carry sediment, boulders, and seasonal floods that would destroy above-ground structures. The Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project — the site where the largest number of workers, roughly 300, are believed trapped — has a 9,490-meter headrace tunnel breakthrough 2025, with a 7.5-meter (25-foot) horseshoe cross-section, constructed by POWERCHINA through difficult geological conditions and completed in late 2025. The tunnels at other affected projects are similarly sized — large enough, as Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz in Austria, noted, "to drive trucks through."

That structural robustness is now both the source of hope and the source of difficulty. If the tunnels themselves survived the flood — as Dix believes is likely — then workers who were inside them when the surge hit may have had protection from the worst of the debris flow. But the portal entrances of those tunnels, which open onto the valley floor, were buried under the same debris that destroyed surface infrastructure across the flooded corridor. To reach anyone inside, rescuers must first clear those portals, which can involve moving tens of meters of packed boulders, mud, and rock under live monsoon conditions with active barrier lake secondary flood risk from two barrier lakes that formed upstream.

At the Trishuli-3A powerhouse in Nuwakot District, the tunnel portal was completely buried. Heavy excavation equipment had to be disassembled and airlifted in by helicopter to reach the site. On August 29, a controlled blast broke into tunnel in the upper section, allowing rescuers to pump in fresh air and lower a camera — a moment of cautious relief. Dix, advising from Melbourne with access to technical drawings, satellite images, and aerial video, warned that once inside the portal, rescuers still faced an unknown: "We don't know how much of that tunnel is full of mud or water," he told CNN. "So, we might only have to dig 10 meters [33 feet], or we might have to dig 100 meters [330 feet]." He also flagged a separate turbine room emergency shutdown risk: if the plant's emergency shutdown systems failed when the flood hit, the turbine rooms themselves could have flooded, potentially drowning any workers sheltering there.

At the Upper Trishuli-1 site in Rasuwa District, the numbers are larger and the status less clear. IPPAN's Dangi said as many as 576 workers were unaccounted for at that project, with an estimated 300 workers believed in tunnel. By Monday morning, 208 workers had been rescued from a third Trishuli project on August 29 alone — 43 of them foreign nationals, including 38 Chinese and 5 Indian workers — and a combined total of approximately 361 workers accounted for August 31 through rescue or self-evacuation across all affected sites.

Nepal's Army spokesman, Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet, was direct about the Nepal Army's challenge opening tunnels. "A large amount of debris has been deposited, and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels," he told Reuters on Monday. "Our main focus is on opening the tunnels."

What a Teacher's Decision Tells You About the Warning Gap

While the tunnel rescue dominates Monday's rescue effort, what happened at a secondary school in Nuwakot District illuminates how little warning time communities had. Rajendra Dawadi, headmaster of Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School, ordered the school evacuation 10 minutes before flood — evacuating more than 900 students approximately 10 minutes before the flood reached the school. By any measure, that decision saved hundreds of lives. By any engineering measure, 10 minutes is not a warning system — it is a headmaster's judgment call.

The absence of a structured warning has been documented before in this same watershed. In July 2025, a glacially triggered flood swept away the Nepal-China border bridge at Gyirong, killing at least nine people. After that event, Nepal and China verbally agreed to establish a cross-border data-sharing system for river levels and glacial flood risks. As of August 26, 2026, that cross-border data agreement never signed — it had never been formalized.

Survivors Speak

Among the workers who escaped, Ram Chandra's six-hour tunnel escape has become emblematic of what those inside faced. He grabbed hold of a rung bolted into the ceiling as water churned around him. "The water was rising and it was difficult to move my legs," he said. "If I had let go from that rung I would have fallen." He and five colleagues spent six hours making their way toward the portal, passing a sheet of tin between them as an improvised foothold, emerging without the clothing the floodwater had torn from them.

The Madan Singh Budha flood account was starker. He had finished a night shift when the water came. He looked out and ran uphill. "Those who weren't able to climb up were swept away," he said.

Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, were buried in shallow graves as decomposition accelerated in Nepal's late-monsoon humidity. Relatives gathered at mass burial sites in Chitwan, some searching faces for their missing, others in grief over those already recovered.

Three Nations Dig

Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who initially declined broader foreign assistance, Nepal reversed foreign assistance decision as the scale became clear. By Monday, approximately 21,000 security personnel were deployed across affected districts.

China mobilized more than 2,100 rescue workers and disbursed 220 million yuan in relief funds — approximately $33 million USD. Chinese teams deployed thermal cameras and acoustic detection equipment specifically designed to locate signs of life in enclosed underground spaces. Chinese President Xi Jinping, speaking from Bishkek, Kazakhstan, on Monday, Xi confirmed Beijing's search efforts for both Chinese and foreign nationals.

India sent tunnel rescue specialists — 18 army officers trained in tunnel operations — alongside six forensic teams equipped for DNA-based identification of flood victims. India also supplied prefabricated Bailey bridges to reconnect communities severed from the road network when the flood washed out crossings, and delivered four tranches of humanitarian aid including generators, water purification tablets, tents, and medicine.

International support has also arrived from the United Nations, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, Australia, South Korea, and the United States. The Red Cross estimated that more than 90,000 people had been affected by the disaster.

Secondary Flood Threat Hangs over the Rescue

The disaster has not stabilized. Two large barrier lakes formed from debris deposited by the initial flood in the upper Lhende watershed. The lower lake subsequently drained through natural outflow; the upper barrier lake half drained, according to China's water ministry. But Nitesh Khadka, a Nepali physical geographer who specializes in glacial floods, warned that a sudden failure of the remaining upper lake could send a surge directly into the active tunnel excavation sites — into the same spaces where rescue workers are operating.

Chinese state media additionally warned that glaciers near the original collapse site on Langtang Lirung could be further destabilized, raising the possibility of a second collapse event.

On Sunday night, monsoon rain temporarily flooded excavation sites across several tunnel locations, halting work before conditions eased. A Nepal Army statement confirmed that teams had army resumed drilling and excavation using "drilling machines, excavators, hydraulic cutters and other equipment."

Warming World, More Workers at Risk

The Langtang region was devastated by an ice-and-rock avalanche during the 2015 Nepal earthquakes. Glacially triggered floods struck the same corridor in 2025. A comparable glacier-flood event destroyed the Upper Bhote Koshi Hydropower Plant in 2016. Analogous disasters struck Chamoli, India, in 2021 and Blatten, Switzerland, in 2025.

Scientists are explicit about the limits of attribution: no single event can be directly linked to climate change without specific causation evidence. What the broader record does show is that the Himalayan region is warming considerably faster than the global average, and as it warms, the permafrost that once stabilized mountain slopes thaws, glacier tongues thin and retreat, and the mechanical foundations of peaks that have stood for millennia begin to fail. The ICIMOD glacier ice loss doubled since 2000, according to the organization's March 2026 glacier assessment of the Hindu Kush Himalaya region.

"Rising temperatures are changing the Hindu Kush Himalaya region and melting glaciers," said Saswat Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at ICIMOD. "We have to be cautious and not draw a connection yet. However, the chances of such disasters increase." That cautious climate change attribution statement reflects the scientific consensus: individual events resist direct attribution; the accelerating pattern does not.

The pattern matters for what Nepal has built. Academic research has documented for years that hydropower projects across High Mountain Asia face compounding, climate-driven hazards: glacial detachments, rock-ice avalanches, permafrost-triggered landslides, and the outburst floods of glacially and landslide-dammed lakes. The 2026 Nepal disaster has brought those risk assessments to catastrophic life. As researchers at The Conversation noted this week: as countries build more infrastructure in these places, the hazard risk rises because more people and assets are exposed.

What the disaster has also revealed is that Nepal's tunnel-heavy hydropower construction model — built for a mountain environment — created an unintended and undesigned form of worker protection against glacial flooding. The tunnels held. But no protocol existed for warning workers inside them to evacuate, because no early-warning system exists for the category of glacial hazard that triggered this flood, and no systematic evacuation plan has been required for tunnel workforces in Nepal's hydropower licensing framework.

What Comes Next

Nepal's energy sector faces a difficult reckoning. The 27 hydropower plants damaged or destroyed represent a severe blow to a national grid already struggling to meet demand. As Prime Minister Shah acknowledged, a full damage assessment remains impossible while active rescue operations and secondary flood threats continue.

For now, everything depends on the tunnels. Whether the emergency shutoffs functioned, whether the workers inside have air and dry space, and whether the portals can be cleared before monsoon weather closes in again are questions whose answers will determine not only the fate of hundreds of individuals but the political reckoning that Nepal's hydropower development strategy will face in the months ahead.

"Just to find the tunnel is a miracle," Dix told ABC News Australia on Monday. The search for what lies inside it — and who — continues around the clock.

Currency conversions are approximate and based on rates at time of publication.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many workers are trapped in Nepal's hydropower tunnels, and are they likely still alive?

As of Monday, August 31, approximately 500 of the 900-plus hydropower workers still missing are believed to be inside tunnels at 11 to 12 affected projects in Nepal's Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, according to Mohan Kumar Dangi, president of IPPAN, the private sector hydropower industry association. The IPPAN estimate of 500 trapped comes with significant uncertainty. Survival depends on whether the tunnels' emergency shutdown systems operated correctly when the flood hit — if they did, the turbine halls may be dry; if they did not, flooding inside could have been fatal. Australian geologist Arnold Dix, advising the operation remotely, noted that the tunnels' structural integrity is likely intact — the critical unknown is what is inside them. After six days, the urgent concerns are oxygen availability, dehydration, and the physical condition of anyone who survived the initial flood surge. Dix's assessment that Dix advised on tunnel survivability offers measured hope: the structures built to withstand Himalayan floods may have done exactly that for those inside.

Why couldn't rescuers reach the tunnel entrances sooner, and what is making it so difficult?

The portals — the entrances to the tunnels — were buried by the same debris cone that destroyed everything else on the valley floor. At the Trishuli-3A site, the portal completely buried by debris required dismantling heavy excavation equipment and airlifting it to the location by helicopter. A controlled blast on August 29 broke through to the upper section of the tunnel. But after entry, rescuers still face an unknown length of potentially mud-filled tunnel before reaching the powerhouse area where workers may be sheltering. Rain and secondary flood risk from an upstream barrier lake have repeatedly paused work. The engineering paradox, as Dix put it, is that structures built to survive a Himalayan flood did survive — and are now the hardest thing in the valley to reach.

What is the risk of a second flood while rescue teams are inside the tunnels?

Two barrier lakes formed from debris deposited by the August 26 flood. The lower lake has since drained naturally; the upper lake more than half drained, according to China's water ministry. But Nitesh Khadka, a Nepali glacial flood specialist, has warned that a sudden failure of the remaining upper lake could send a surge directly into the excavation sites and — potentially — into the tunnels themselves. Rain on Sunday night temporarily flooded excavation areas, a demonstration of how quickly conditions can change. Rescue teams are monitoring river levels continuously and have suspended operations multiple times this week due to rising water and weather.

Why weren't the workers warned before the flood arrived?

No early-warning system exists for the specific category of hazard that caused this disaster. Himalayan monitoring infrastructure is built around glacial lake outburst floods — events that originate from pre-existing lakes that can be watched with water-level sensors and satellite imagery. The August 26 event was a rock-ice avalanche from a steep glacier face, which requires a fundamentally different monitoring approach: satellite-based radar measurement of glacier surface velocity, seismic detection of mass movements, and cross-border river gauge data from the Tibetan portion of the Lhende watershed. Nepal's Flood Forecasting Division received no advance warning from China in either the 2025 or 2026 flood events on the same river system. A cross-border data sharing never finalized — an agreement was promised after the 2025 flood, but it has never been signed.

What does the disaster mean for Nepal's hydropower sector?

Nepal poured billions into hydropower as its primary development and export strategy, harnessing Himalayan rivers to address chronic domestic power shortages and sell electricity to India. The 2026 disaster struck 27 of those plants — damaging or destroying them and knocking a significant share of national generating capacity offline. Beyond the physical damage, the disaster has exposed a structural vulnerability in Nepal's development model: the same tunnel engineering that made hydropower possible in a Himalayan environment created an unplanned and undesigned form of worker exposure during precisely the glacial hazard events that climate scientists have been warning about for years. No evacuation protocol existed for tunnel workers facing a glacial flood. No GLOF warning system covered the type of event that occurred. The political and regulatory reckoning over Nepal's hydropower strategy — and the safety standards required for workers inside mountain tunnels — is likely to define the sector's governance for years ahead.

title: Nepal Flood Death Toll Surpasses 900 as Missing Persons Rise
full_text:
Nepal is grappling with a mounting catastrophe after flash floods and debris flows tore through communities near the Chinese border, pushing the death toll beyond 900 as rescuers worked through the night to reach people feared trapped in blocked hydropower tunnels.

At least 939 people have been killed in Nepal, the country’s disaster authority said, adding that the number of missing had fallen to 3,925 six days after the disaster.

Chinese state media earlier confirmed 16 dead and 546 people missing in Tibet, bringing the combined toll across the border region to 955 dead and 4,471 missing.

The disaster — an extraordinary surge of ice, rock, mud and debris along the Nepal-Tibet border — struck last Wednesday and has been blamed on a glacier collapse.

In Nepal’s plains, hundreds of bodies, many still unidentified, have been laid to rest in shallow graves as humid conditions accelerated decomposition after victims were swept down from the mountains by the torrent.

Officials said Nepal’s missing list includes 592 foreign nationals.

In its latest update, the disaster agency put the number of missing Nepali citizens at 3,333.

Among those still missing are 45 Nepali army soldiers, 38 police officers and 18 customs and immigration officers.

Across the border in India, authorities in Uttar Pradesh state said they had recovered 17 bodies from rivers flowing down from Nepal, and believe they are flood victims.

Those bodies are being identified by Indian authorities and are not included in the official toll.

Nepali officials said efforts were now heavily focused on reaching hundreds of workers believed to be trapped inside roughly half a dozen hydropower project tunnels, which were sealed by mud and rock debris.

The number of hydropower workers listed as missing — projects that took the brunt of the torrent — fell to 639 from an earlier count of 933.

Images and videos circulated by rescue teams showed earth-moving machinery digging and clearing mud and rock under floodlights in the darkness, while workers looked on.

Soldiers, using torchlight, searched a large pit they had excavated in hopes of finding an opening into one tunnel.

The Red ‌Cross has estimated that more than 90,000 people are likely to ⁠have been affected by the disaster, which China has linked to the effects of climate change.

Police personnel work at a mass burial of flood victims at Devghat in Nepal

Assessment of damage challenging, says Nepali prime minster

“A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Reuters. “Our main focus is on opening the tunnels.”

Prime Minister Balendra Shah described the flood as an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and said compiling a complete picture of the damage remained difficult.

“Despite the adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing risks, we are moving forward with determination to save the lives of our citizens,” he said in a Facebook post late yesterday.

A drone provides supplies along the Trishuli River, in Devighat, Nuwakot, Nepal

He said nearly 21,000 security personnel were engaged in rescue operations, alongside civilian workers and volunteers.

Rescuers in Nepal use a digger to find those missing

Since Friday, rescue work has been halted several times because of poor weather and fears that a lake created by the disaster across the Nepal-China border could unleash another wave of flooding after it began spilling into Nepal’s rivers.

In Devighat, a holy town on the banks of the flooded ⁠Trishuli river, residents moved through the remains of homes, trying to retrieve possessions from the wreckage.

Overnight rain and rising river waters hampered rescue operations

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV said the flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, calling it a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere disasters” on the Tibetan plateau.

title: Nepal - Tibet floods : Amid the devastation , fake content and scams thrive
full_text:
A bomb dropping on a dam, glitchy flood waters destroying an entire village street, and an elephant rescuing a man are some of the fake images circulating online.

The cause of the floods was a glacier collapse triggered by a vast flow of icy debris, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS). But if you're scrolling on social media, you might've instead seen the narrative that it was caused by a bomb being dropped on a dam.

The fake AI-generated clip was actually published in May 2026, with early copies of the video labelled with an AI watermark.

Associate Professor at the Queensland University of Technology Paula Dootson told SBS Examines AI labels can easily be missed, causing people to share posts before they realise it's fake.

"For any more obvious visual content labels, it's quite possible it's AI accounts or bots that are sharing these rather than human accounts. And we know there's a lot of those."

Dootson said mislabeled content is the most common type of problematic visual that response agencies deal with.

"How that visual gets there is not always clear," she told SBS Examines.

"Sometimes it could be because maybe you and I, we search 'landslide' or 'flood' and an old video pops up, and we don't check the metadata and we just share it. And then of course it gets momentum. The algorithm picks it up as being the first search response.

"But it could also be because the synthetic content is labelled, but content from a past event isn't. So it's harder to distinguish what you are sharing," Dootson added.

Implications for understanding disaster

Fake and mislabeled content can impact how people understand the scale of an event, such as the damage to infrastructure and how many people and communities are affected.

Dootson said misleading visuals can be used to push political or organisational agendas and to shift public conversations, by "aiming to really confuse the public and create uncertainty."

She added that financial incentives could be driving the spread of such content.

Following the devastating floods, many social media posts have prompted users to scan a QR code to donate to relief efforts. But it can be difficult to tell where the donations are actually going.

Independent cyber security expert Nittesh Bhatta told SBS Examines there's been a rise in scams.

"Not so much organised groups ... but more lone actors looking for easy money and fame in the name of donations and support."

The Nepal government has a 'one-door policy' to streamline donations and distribution, via the Prime Minister's Disaster Relief Fund.

Experts are urging people to verify content and look for AI-generated labelling. Credit: Facebook/AAP FactCheck

The Nepali Police have warned people to beware of fake QR codes and links to donate to Nepal flood relief efforts.

Police said scammers could be exploiting the disaster by using social media and other platforms to divert relief donations or obtain people's banking information, as reported by The Kathmandu Post.

Bhatta said scammers are also exploiting photos of missing people to get payments through private messaging apps

"Friends who were searching for a 22-year-old missing person were targeted by an individual on a Whatsapp chat, who had used photographs of the missing person to impersonate them and requested money."

Ask questions to verify content

Dootson encourages viewers to ask themselves questions in order to verify the content they see online.

"Where was it posted? Who was it posted by? Can we look for any inconsistencies and what's out there? And can we just ask ourselves more broadly, has this been used before? And we can use tools like reverse image lookup for that," she said.

"So if we're both consciously looking at what content's being spread and making sure we're not part of the problem, then we can hopefully have a situation where only the real verified visuals are being shared about an event."

title: Nepal death toll rises to nearly 1 , 000 amid fresh flood alerts
full_text:
Kathmandu: Over 1000 people have now been confirmed dead following last week’s devastating floods in Nepal, even as bodies swept away continue to pile up along riverbanks in different districts on Tuesday, September 2.

The number of bodies recovered so far has reached 1003, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said in its latest update. The highest number of bodies — 321 — were recovered in southern Chitwan district, followed by 216 in Nawalparasi East.

Authorities estimate that 3,916 people, including 583 foreigners, remain unaccounted for as security personnel, including those from the Nepal Army, intensify search and rescue operations in the affected areas.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), 321 bodies were recovered from Chitwan, 216 from Nawalparasi East, 170 from Nawalparasi West and 95 from Nuwakot. Sixty-five bodies were recovered from Gorkha, 55 from Dhading, 38 from Tanahun and 27 from Rasuwa.

As many as 639 people working at various hydropower projects along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river corridors have remained out of contact since last week’s disaster.

Relatives can submit DNA samples to identify victims: Indian Embassy

The Indian Embassy in Nepal on Tuesday issued a detailed procedure for the identification and repatriation of mortal remains of foreign nationals, including Indians, killed in the devastating flash floods in the country.

The Government of Nepal has laid down a nine-step procedure for handing over mortal remains of foreign nationals, including documentation, recording photographs and details, post-mortem examination, verification of the cause of death and formal identification, the embassy said in a press release.

The process also includes collection of fingerprints, DNA and other forensic samples, verification of the deceased’s passport or identity documents, completion of embassy or consular coordination, and issuance of a handover or release memo and receipt, it said.

The first four steps of the procedure will be carried out by Nepali authorities, the embassy said.

If relatives are able to identify mortal remains through photographs and descriptions uploaded on the Nepal Police website, the Indian Embassy will assist in coordinating with local authorities for their handover and repatriation.

The Government of Nepal has temporarily interred a large number of mortal remains to prevent health risks, the embassy said, adding that identification of such remains would require DNA matching with first-degree relatives.

A first-degree relative is a biological family member who is exactly one step away in the family tree. This category includes parents (biological mother and father), full siblings (brothers and sisters who share both biological parents), and children (biological sons and daughters).

In cases where identification is not possible, or the remains have been temporarily interred, Nepal will facilitate DNA matching, it said.

Nepali authorities are collecting DNA samples from the mortal remains to create their DNA profiles. First-degree relatives of the deceased can send their DNA profiles through email or provide blood samples along with preliminary information required by the Nepali authorities, the embassy said.

The embassy said relatives could also share DNA profiles with it for facilitation in coordination with Nepali authorities.

It also provided three helpline numbers with WhatsApp facility for further assistance and enquiries regarding the identification and repatriation process.

Over 11,000 rescued from flood-hit areas in Nepal

More than 11,000 people have been rescued from flood-affected areas in Nepal so far, with over 22,000 security personnel mobilised for search and rescue operations, officials said.

Unidentified dead bodies have been kept at 21 locations for identification and proper management. According to the latest update, 11,884 people have been rescued so far. Search and rescue operations are continuing in the flood-affected areas, with security agencies using helicopters and other resources to reach stranded people.

A total of 21,314 security personnel have been mobilised for search, rescue and relief operations, according to the NDRRMA. The mobilised personnel include 9,199 from the Nepali Army, 7,912 from Nepal Police and 4,203 from the Armed Police Force.

Also Read Nepal floods: Families struggle to identify victims amid crisis

At least 16 helicopters have also been deployed for search and rescue operations in the affected areas, National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) spokesperson Shanti Mahat said.

More than 11,000 people have been rescued so far, he said, adding that the government has intensified search and rescue efforts in the flood-hit areas.

Over 22,000 security personnel, including those from the Nepal Army, have been mobilised for the operations, Mahat said.

So far, 254 labourers and technicians have been rescued from the Upper Trishuli 1 Hydropower Project sites, while search operations continue with the involvement of Indian and Chinese tunnel rescue experts.

According to the latest figures, 927 bodies have been sealed, of which 51 have been handed over to family members following identification, while 726 remain unidentified.

As many as 413 unidentified bodies have so far been managed or buried in accordance with standard international norms, officials said.

The authorities have arranged temporary shelter for 2,970 displaced people at various holding centres.

Nepal issues fresh flood alert

Nepalese authorities issued a fresh alert over the risk of floods in several districts across eastern, central and western parts of the country, urging people living near rivers to remain vigilant and take precautionary measures.

There is a high possibility of flash floods in Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts, where water flow in smaller rivers and streams is expected to rise, according to a notice issued by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

There is also a risk of rising water levels and a moderate risk of flash floods in several districts, including Taplejung, Sankhuwasabha, Solukhumbu, Khotang, Okhaldhunga, Ramechhap, Dolakha, Sindhupalchowk, Kavrepalanchok, Lalitpur, Bhaktapur, Kathmandu and Dhading in eastern and central Nepal.

In western Nepal, the districts under alert include Gorkha, Lamjung, Dolpa, Rukum East, Rukum West, Jajarkot, Darchula, Baitadi, Dadeldhura, Doti, Kailali and Kanchanpur, the authority said.

The NDRRMA urged people living along riverbanks and in other vulnerable areas to remain alert and take necessary precautions in view of the forecast.

title: Nepal floods a climate warning signal - foreign minister
full_text:
A devastating glacial collapse on the China-Nepal border that unleashed deadly floods was a "warning signal" over the growing risks climate change poses to the Himalayan nation, its foreign minister said.

"We believe that this disaster should be seen as a warning signal to the risk that climate change poses to Nepal," Shisir Khanal said, nearly a week since the tsunami-like wave of freezing water, rocks and debris hit.

More than 1,000 bodies have been recovered, and nearly 4,500 people are missing in Nepal as well as across the Chinese border in Tibet.

Mr Khanal invited international support based on climate justice rather than charity.

He noted that his largely rural nation of 30 million people contributes a fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions compared to industrialised nations.

"We call upon the international community to take the changing climate in the Himalayas in an urgent light," he said.

"The support to Nepal should not be just seen from an angle of aid or charity but should be seen from a perspective of climate justice as well."

Families and relatives of those missing in the Tibet-Nepal flood check the names and images of those missing at the Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal

The disaster has affected people's lives but also public infrastructure, the minister said, underlining the need for long-term support to help Nepal adapt to and mitigate the growing challenges of climate change.

While the exact cause of the glacial collapse is unclear, climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.

Scientists say the Himalayas, the world's highest mountain range, are melting faster as global temperatures rise.

"We have to seek not just the preservation of mountains but also seek support for adaptation and mitigation of the challenges that climate change is bringing to Nepal - and this region as well," he said.

"In the longer term, it will have even further impact downstream, in the entire South Asia, as the ice melts."

China and India also affected, says foreign minister

Glaciers in the wider Himalayan and Hindu Kush ranges are a crucial water source for around 240 million people in the mountainous regions, as well as for another 1.65 billion people in the South Asian and Southeast Asian river valleys below.

Collapsed buildings are seen in a town hit by the flash floods along the Trishuli River, Nepal

"It impacts the entirety of Himalayan region's civilisation," Mr Khanal said.

"We are a downstream community for China, and an upstream community of India, and the Himalayan rivers impact all of us," he added.

The glacial collapse has highlighted the need to speed up data sharing mechanisms to send out alerts about any similar catastrophes, the minister said.

"Since the disaster, China has shared a lot of data, especially for this region where this particular disaster occurred," he said.

"This disaster does give more impetus and urgency to us to build the mechanism in a much significantly faster timeline."

While Nepal is now in mourning, Mr Khanal said people should still come to visit.

"We're in a moment of sorrow and grief," he said, adding: "But this is very resilient nation ... Nepal still remains open."

According to relatives, it was also about this time – 8.40am to 8.50am – Sydney’s Sreedharan Iyer, 53, his wife Lakshmi, 49, and their two gifted sons, Rishab, 23, and Rudhra, 20, were checking out from the Royal Himalaya, a hotel on Syabrubesi’s lower section. The Hindu pilgrims were on a family trip of a lifetime with 11 other Australian friends to see Mount Kailash, the earthly abode of Lord Shiva. A photo with most of the group a day before the flood shows them beaming in matching blue T-shirts with mountain print from Himalayan Glacier, the tour company. The Iyer family, from left to right: Rudhra, 20; Sreedharan, 53; Lakshmi, 49; and Rishab, 23. The Iyers appeared in a tour group photo. smiling and wearing matching shirts, a day before the floods hit. None of the 15 have been heard from since Wednesday morning. More than 1050 people were killed – and some 4500 are still missing, including 38 Australians – when the floods hit Nepal and Tibet. The smack of two raging water courses came about 9am, Tamang says, sending buildings “rolling and rolling in the flood”. “After half an hour, everything was similar to what we see now,” he says. That is a silver silt pan, where a village once stood.

Advertisement

The vantage point of Sano Bharkhu offers clear views of a handful of buildings still standing in the upper section of Syabrubesi, and more are obscured by a mountain. But the entire lower half is gone, including Tamang’s home. Images circulating of the village post-flood suggests the Royal Himalaya is too. Most of Syabrubesi was swept away or buried. Kate Geraghty Where the Iyer family was at the time is unclear. They may have spent time in the village after check-out getting organised or sourcing coffees before getting in their car to be driven about 15 kilometres north to their friends at the doomed Hotel Kailash, which was swept away. If they had left immediately after check-out, they would have been roughly halfway between Syabrubesi and Timure on the road running directly alongside the soon-deadly Trishuli.

Advertisement

Timure was destroyed, too. That’s where Tamang’s nephew, Lama Sanam Tamang, 28, a husband and father, was killed. His five-year-old girl, Sonam Dolma, is being minded in Sano Bharkhu by her grieving grandfather, Maywan Tamang. She is playing with a soft drink bottle and scratching at the road with a stick. “We haven’t told her her father is dead,” the grandfather says. “She keeps asking where he is.” Maywan Tamang says his granddaughter Sonam doesn’t yet know her father was killed in the flooding. Kate Geraghty The road the pilgrims took between Dhunche, the small capital of Rasuwa district, and Syabrubesi is destroyed from the point it crosses the Trishuli River. Upstream and downstream, the river’s bridges are gone, leaving survivors and residents of undamaged villages on the other side cut off from the main towns and the capital, Kathmandu. Nepal’s private fleet of helicopters have been commandeered for the rescue, aid and salvage efforts, but it is still not enough. A staging point in Dhunche for helicopter rescues and distributing aid. Kate Geraghty

Advertisement

A temporary morgue has been set up on the outskirts of Dhunche. Kate Geraghty At Dhunche, helicopters fly in and out, laden with sacks of food and other supplies, in perpetual motion. “But people keep asking for more,” a rescuer says. Nepal has declined offers from other nations for search and rescue teams, ostensibly because the devastating 2015 earthquake proved it was too unwieldy. It has walked back the initial hardline, however, and is asking for specialised technical teams in matters like DNA testing and tunnel rescues. Close to 900 hydropower station workers remain trapped in various tunnels across the impact zone with uncertain access to oxygen, food and clean drinking water. Time is running out, if it hasn’t already. Destroyed buildings in Betrawoti. Kate Geraghty Body bags lay on the roof of a destroyed building in Betrawoti. Kate Geraghty The flood barrelled on through Syabrubesi to the town Betrawoti, about 40 kilometres south. Unable to make the sharp right turn in the river bed, it smashed into a mountain.

title: Meet Captain Priya Adhikari : Nepal first woman helicopter captain who flew 100 rescue missions in six days amid devastating floods
full_text:
Meet Captain Priya Adhikari: Nepal’s first woman helicopter captain who flew 100 rescue missions in six days amid devastating floods.

Captain Priya Adhikari’s name has a weight to it in Nepal: not just because she found herself at the center of one of the country’s worst-ever disasters, but because she rewrote the rules for what’s possible in the air. When flash floods and landslides ripped through Nepal’s northern border with Tibet, she spent six relentless days above the chaos, flying close to 100 rescue sorties. For anyone watching from the ground, helicopters were often the only sign that help still existed.The official numbers of Nepal's flash flood aftermath tell the story’s grim side: Over a thousand people are dead, nearly four thousand are reported missing, including foreign travelers cut off with no way out. Helicopters swooped in as the roads disappeared and bridges, the lifeline for so many mountain communities, just ceased to exist. Emergency crews scrambled, but it was in the sky, up where the valleys are tight, the air is unpredictable, and mistakes mean disaster, that the most dramatic story unfolded.As reported by CNN, Captain Adhikari was everywhere, piloting her chopper through debris-clogged air, threading between jagged slopes, and hovering while landslides still thundered in the distance.At one point, nearly 20 helicopters squeezed into a single narrow valley, each crew alert, talking constantly on the radio, watching as each landing spot promised risk: solid-looking patches of mud that could trap a helicopter or collapse beneath its weight. Every touchdown was a gamble, and there was no room to get it wrong.By September 1, she’d completed close to 100 flights, not just ferrying survivors to safety, but retrieving bodies from remote places no road could reach. She described the operation, simply, as exhausting, and one could hear fatigue but also quiet determination in her words. “We’ve been trained for this.”However, per ABC News, Priya Adhikari’s journey began far from those flood-choked valleys. At first, she was deep into environmental science studies and working as cabin crew for a small domestic airline. Her life shifted completely the day she stepped into a helicopter on a frigid morning for a routine ride. Something clicked. She saw not just the mountains but possibility: if she could learn to fly, those skies could be hers.She chased her ambition all the way to the Philippines for flight school. Her family stood behind her, even when the idea seemed almost wild. Back home, almost nobody saw women flying helicopters. To become a captain, you needed not just training but hours: long, often grueling, and mostly male company. She became Nepal’s first full-time female helicopter pilot in 2017, then specialized in the kind of flying that makes most people’s pulses quicken: high-altitude rescues, shuttle runs to Everest, and missions where a single mistake means disaster.For Priya, this wasn’t just about breaking into a male-dominated industry and collecting “firsts” for the record books. Sceptics circled around her, whispering that the job was too hard for a woman, that she’d break under pressure. She brushed it off, keeping her focus on her flying. Her family mattered more: a father proud of five daughters, a house where ambition was encouraged.She’s spent years flying the Himalayas, facing the worst: unpredictable winds, oxygen running low, survivors trapped in impossible conditions. She still remembers the chaos after the 2015 earthquake, when rescue flying became one long, uncertain marathon over broken roads and shattered towns.None of it could quite prepare her for the scale of the August 2026 floods, which were a disaster triggered when a glacier collapsed and sent a wall of rock, ice, and water roaring into the valleys. In spots like Timure, she navigated through crowded airspace as pilots coordinated over staticky radios, trying to squeeze multiple helicopters onto scarce landing sites. From above, the earth looked solid, but appearances lied. Sometimes the mud was deep enough to swallow a helicopter’s wheels. From the cockpit, she saw the toll with her own eyes: bodies littered in places where the flood hit hardest, survivors waving frantically for rescue.Emotionally, it never got any easier. She’d carry the living to safety and bring out the dead, making the journey for families who just wanted their loved ones found — no matter what. It’s a responsibility that doesn’t leave you. But as she put it, “We’ve been trained for this.” Maybe that’s how she manages, turning what used to be impossible into routine.In the course of these few days, as she navigated her way into the valley, rescuing those in need, Captain Priya Adhikari’s helicopter became something more than metal and rotors; it’s the one thing that can break through when roads vanish and the ground can’t be trusted. In a place like Nepal, where a few minutes in the air make the difference between hope and heartbreak, her work and her courage mean a way back from disaster, a way home for some, and closure for others.

Security forces have recovered 348 dead bodies from Chitawan district, 218 from Nawalparasi East, 208 from Nawalparasi West, and 155 from Nuwakot. title: No time to issue a warning : Experts on what caused Nepal flood and what needed to improve preparedness
full_text:
With the death toll over 1,000 and thousands still missing, the human tragedy of the Nepal flooding disaster is undeniable. Some estimate the costs of reconstruction could equal up to a tenth of the country’s entire economy.

ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT

Now attention is turning to what caused the disaster and how to prevent devastation on such a scale when “unprecedented” events like this happen again which, scientists say, they will.

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah has linked the disaster to climate change, saying: “The flood in the Bhote Koshi River in Rasuwa was not an ordinary flood. It was one of the region’s major disasters, triggered by an avalanche of snow and ice in the Himalayan region.”

In the social media post, he went on to say, “It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change.”

It would be reasonable to assume he is referring to the rich, industrialised countries which are responsible for the vast majority of carbon emissions, unlike Nepal which is a largely rural country.

“Nepal is paying the price for a crisis it didn’t create. This is a moment for countries not just to understand how much climate impacts can play havoc but also how much is needed urgently in terms of putting climate action front and centre of development policy,” urges Aarti Khosla, director of research consultancy Climate Trends.

A Nepali police official stands next to a row of bodies of flash flood victims laid in a mass grave for burial in Kathmandu, Nepal, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. AP Photo/Dar Yasin

What caused the Nepal flood?

On 26 August, a sudden flood swept through Nepal’s Rasuwa district after a massive chunk of glacial ice and rock broke off from an altitude of about 5,200 metres and plunged roughly 1,200 metres into the valley below.

Inter-governmental body the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), based in Kathmandu, has concluded that the flood was most likely triggered by an ice-rock avalanche, rather than a glacial lake outburst flood.

It’s important to remember that attribution studies take months and researchers are still examining the precise sequence of events and whether long-term changes such as permafrost degradation and rock-slope instability played a role.

Glacier at heart of disaster had been retreating for decades

It has emerged that the glacier that collapsed in Nepal had been in retreat for decades, like many glaciers across Europe.

“The failed glacier retreated by approximately 450m between 1990 and 2020, potentially reducing the mechanical support provided by the glacier to the underlying rock slope,” says Professor Maria Shahgedanova, a climate scientist researching climate impacts on mountain glaciers at the University of Reading in the UK.

It has been known for decades that climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters. Scientists say the Himalayas, the world’s highest mountain range, are warming at an unprecedented rate and losing ice faster than the global average.

Nepal has lost almost a third of its ice volume in 30 years, with glaciers melting 65 per cent faster in the last decade than in the previous one, according to the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).

Rising temperatures induced by climate change are quite literally melting the glue (permafrost) that holds the mountains together. Kyoko Yokosuka UNDP Resident Representative for Nepal

"Rising temperatures induced by climate change are quite literally melting the glue (permafrost) that holds the mountains together," Kyoko Yokosuka, UNDP Resident Representative for Nepal, tells Euronews Earth.

"As temperatures rise and glaciers retreat, these frozen ice sheets that stabilise mountain slopes loosen, triggering catastrophic landslides and floods downstream."

This, Yokosuka explains, is creating "a dangerous chain reaction: small, isolated pockets of meltwater on top of glaciers are growing, merging into massive lakes, and putting immense pressure on the moraine" – the collection of rocks, soil and sediment left behind by a moving glacier – which can trigger "catastrophic glacial lake outburst flooding".

"When these dams burst, millions of lives downstream are put in immediate peril," she adds.

Shahgedanova says the recent disaster demonstrates how climate-driven changes in the cryosphere can change conditions that make hazards in high-mountain regions even more risky for people in the area. "Such events cannot be prevented, but their impacts can be reduced through systematic hazard assessment and monitoring,” she says.

Would early warnings have helped in Nepal?

It may be of some comfort to families and friends of the victims that experts believe that it would have been “very difficult” to predict the disaster. But better preparedness could have helped.

“This was an unprecedented and unexpected disaster. There was simply no detection and no time to issue a warning. The event was a sudden-onset hazard that could not be captured by conventional warning systems,” explains Dr Farooq Azam, senior cryosphere specialist and intervention manager at ICIMOD. “In such rock-ice avalanches, establishing a warning system is very difficult to ascertain the place of the breakpoints, which can sometimes be below the bedrock or glaciers and not easily visible with satellite or eyes.”

Still, UNDP says that continuous monitoring of glaciers, lake volumes and moraine dam stability using satellite and sensor technologies is critical to assess future risks.

"Governments need the systems and coordination mechanisms to anticipate rapidly evolving risks," Yokosuka adds. "Communities in downstream areas need warnings they can act on – clear evacuation routes, identified safe areas, and regular exercises."

European countries may be able to assist by bringing "technology solutions, such as precise engineering and avalanche-mitigation technologies used in the Alps directly to the Himalayas," as well as by scaling-up financing for risk prevention and early warning systems, says Yokosuka.

What does Nepal need to do to be more prepared for disasters?

ICIMOD says there are three immediate priorities to improve the region’s preparedness for global warming-related disasters. Firstly, make sure clear policies are in place that determine what land can be used for, particularly in areas close to rivers, slopes and mountains.

Secondly, assess how the environment can impact infrastructure using Environmental Impact Assessments before it is built, as well as assessing how environmental conditions could affect infrastructure over its lifetime.

Thirdly, bring Indigenous knowledge back into risk planning. Historically, communities often lived on higher ground and away from river channels, while newer development has increasingly moved closer to riverbanks and, in some cases, onto riverbeds. Indigenous knowledge should inform contemporary disaster-risk and land-use planning, ICIMOD says.

UNDP says interventions like physically managing high-risk lakes and strengthening vulnerable slopes could be considered but require careful assessment.

“If this heartbreaking tragedy can help countries realise the need for a shared approach – for building adaptation and resilience, early warning signals, and transboundary monitoring – that will be a step ahead for humanity in the fractured world order we are living in today,” says Khosla.

title: When roads end , drones carry dead home in flood - hit Nepal

Kathmandu, In the flood-ravaged hills of Nepal, drones are doing something far beyond their traditional role of taking aerial photographs or mapping -- carrying the dead home.Seven bodies were airlifted by drones this week from Devighat-3 in Nuwakot to Devighat-5, from an area so difficult and dangerous to navigate that rescuers could not safely reach it, according to a report published in The Kathmandu Post newspaper on Wednesday.It was "perhaps their most unusual role yet", the report said.The drone team included personnel from Nepal Police, Nepal Army, and drone manufacturing company GarudX.The unusual operation is the latest example of how drones, also known as unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), are quietly becoming an extra pair of hands and eyes in Nepal's disaster response.From ferrying food and medicines to cut-off communities, searching for survivors in inaccessible areas and even airlifting bodies from locations too dangerous for rescuers to reach, drones in Nepal are rapidly shedding their image as mere tools for photography and mapping and emerging as an unlikely lifeline during disasters.In Devighat-3, one of the worst-hit areas, an AI-enabled drone recently flew over stranded villagers, its loudspeaker asking them a series of simple questions: Do you have water? Food? Medicine?Villagers were asked to raise their hands in response."Based on the villagers' response, we make an assessment for what they require and send the delivery through drones," Milan Pandey, director of Airlift Technology and a drone pilot, was quoted as saying by the Post report.The drone also asked people to provide a phone number or address, which could be written on a placard or even in the mud, allowing operators to identify their location and requirements.The system has particular value in a disaster like the recent floods, where roads and bridges have been washed away and communities separated by swollen rivers can no longer reach one another."We supplied at least 1.5 tonnes of emergency supplies, including food, to the affected areas in three days," Pandey said.In another operation, a drone was flown inside the tunnel of the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, where scores of workers are believed to have been trapped following the floods, the report said."We reached platform 1 of the project and saw the tunnel filled with water and rocks. It's risky and challenging to get inside," said drone operator Adarsha Bhusal.The drone found no signs of life inside the tunnel, he said.Around 900 workers have been reported missing at various hydropower projects along the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi rivers, according to the Independent Power Producers' Association of Nepal.The country's drone ecosystem began taking shape after the 2015 earthquake, when international agencies brought the technology for damage assessment and recovery operations. Much of that capability is now being developed and operated by Nepali companies and young drone enthusiasts.Nepal's growing expertise is also beginning to find applications outside the country. Its private sector has provided drone-based services in Bhutan for multi-hazard risk assessment, according to the World Bank.There are, however, limits. Payload capacity, range and weather conditions can restrict their use.But where roads disappear, rivers become impassable or terrain is simply too dangerous for humans, operators say the impact of a relatively small aircraft can be disproportionate to its size.It's the cheapest mode of transporting supplies compared to choppers, operators say."For a country repeatedly exposed to earthquakes, floods, landslides and mountain hazards, the rise of locally developed drone technology could mark a significant shift in how Nepal responds to disasters - putting eyes, cargo and rescue capability into places where human access is simply too dangerous," Pandey said.Airlift Technology, which assembles drones in Kathmandu using imported components, says the next step is enabling the technology to be used more widely."We just need an appropriate policy to promote such a life-saving machine," Pandey said.

full_text:

BBC



NUWAKOT DISTRICT, Nepal- Thousands of people remain missing after a catastrophic flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border a week ago, as rescuers scramble to reach anyone who may be alive even as they turn to recovery.

At least 1,114 people have died in Nepal and nearly 4,000 more are missing, according to Nepal's disaster agency. On the Tibetan side, the death toll stands at 16, and more than 500 people are unaccounted for, Chinese state media reports.

The UN's humanitarian agency has said the response is entering a new phase, with authorities intensifying relief and recovery operations.

In Nepal, efforts continue to rescue workers, potentially in the hundreds, believed to be trapped in hydroelectric station tunnels.

A massive flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through a Himalayan valley last Wednesday, wiping out villages.

Nearly 12,000 people have since been rescued, according to Nepal's disaster management agency.

But thousands more, including hundreds of foreign nationals - from India, the UK, Australia, the US, Malaysia, and more - are still missing. A week on, fears are growing that the death toll will only rise.

Chinese state media has not reported any survivors on the Tibetan side of the border, but the search continues. Beijing, which annexed Tibet in the 1950s, tightly controls the region. All information comes from state media and foreign journalists cannot travel there without permission.

Rescuers using heavy machinery, working around the clock, have been able to re-open the route to the Gyirong border crossing between Nepal and Tibet and clear the road of debris, which will accelerate the search for the missing, Chinese state media said.

Rescue operations continue in challenging conditions, and experts from China and India are helping build temporary bridges to reach remote areas. Drones are being deployed over hard-to reach areas to scan for survivors.

title: Glacier collapse at 8 . 37am , alert at 9 . 15 : Why Nepal sent disaster warning 38 minutes late
full_text:
Nepal floods exposed gaps in disaster monitoring and early-warning systems

Why alert was sent late

Blind spot beyond Nepal’s borders

Nepal’s warning system came under scrutiny after a glacier collapse triggered devastating flash floods in Rasuwa on August 26, with authorities issuing a disaster alert 38 minutes after the ice-rock avalanche. The deadly floods have killed thousands and several remain missing.The collapse struck the Lhende valley near the Nepal-Tibet border at 8.37am, sending a rapid surge of water, debris and boulders downstream. Communities were caught off guard, with survivors relying largely on instinct and help from neighbours to escape, according to a report in the Kathmandu Post.Scientists said predicting the specific glacier collapse was difficult and the steep terrain gave authorities little time to respond. However, the disaster exposed a wider weakness: Nepal’s warning systems are largely built around individual hazards even as Himalayan disasters increasingly involve cascading and cross-border risks.“There is no such thing as an early warning system in Nepal. Simply having sensors does not mean it’s a system; it has to be much more comprehensive,” the report quoted Anil Pokhrel, former chief executive of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority saying.He said an effective system needs risk assessment, real-time observation, communication mechanisms and emergency preparedness. “If the Chinese sensors detect something upstream, a series of sirens should automatically go off all at once. Text messages should go off with a loud buzzer even if it is on silent mode,” he added.Nepal’s department of mines and geology recorded seismic activity when the glacier collapsed, but did not issue an alert because the signal did not match the pattern of an earthquake.“Our records showed a 4.4 magnitude. But the frequency of the seismic activity did not match that of an earthquake, which is the department’s monitoring mandate, so we did not alert the public like we usually do,” the Post quoted Lok Vijay Adhikari, chief of the National Earthquake Monitoring and Research Center saying.A second opportunity to detect the danger came when water levels began rising in the Bhotekoshi. But at 8.50am, the flash flood swept away the river gauge at the Syabrubesi hydrological station. The gauge was designed to monitor gradual rises in river levels and was not equipped to detect such a fast-moving flood.At 9am, Rasuwa’s district administration informed the department of hydrology and meteorology (DHM). Communications towers had already been destroyed, forcing local officials and residents to rely on door-to-door warnings.“We informed DHM at nine. We could not do much in Rasuwa because the flood had destroyed the [communications] towers, yet local authorities informed communities, and people went from door to door warning each other,” the report quoted Shanti Mahat, spokesperson of NDRRMA, saying.“But for people downstream we used every means to inform them—through text alerts, caller tune, media broadcasts, and police miking,” she added.At 9.15 am, 38 minutes after the avalanche, alerts reached people in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan, urging them to move to higher ground. Tamang’s phone, however, showed that he received the warning at 9:42 am.The Rasuwa disaster also highlighted gaps in cross-border monitoring. The Lhende Khola originates in Tibet and flows towards Nepal, feeding into the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers.Nepal has flood forecasting and data-sharing arrangements with India, but there is no comparable operational early-warning protocol with China despite a 2019 commitment by the two countries to cooperate on climate change and environmental issues.“There is no protocol. The practice that we have right now is that we cooperate with the ministry of foreign affairs to share information,” said Prakash Pokhrel, geologist at NDRRMA.“Whenever a foreign country is involved, we have to go through the ministry.”Monitoring the remote northern reaches also remains difficult. Officials said the terrain is extremely challenging and real-time monitoring stations are difficult to establish.DHM information officer Dinkar Kayastha said it was impossible to monitor every vulnerable area with available resources, particularly given Nepal’s mountainous terrain.Nepal monitors major high-risk glacial lakes, while ICIMOD has identified 21 potentially dangerous glacier lakes among 2,070 lakes across the Gandaki, Koshi and Karnali basins.ICIMOD warned in March that glaciers in the Hindu Kush Himalaya were losing ice at twice the rate recorded since 2000. Yet many glaciers remain largely unmonitored.The disaster also exposed the vulnerability created by development in the Himalayan river valleys. Thirteen hydropower plants in Rasuwa and Nuwakot were damaged, disconnecting around 431 MW of capacity from Nepal’s national grid.

title: Families perform cremation of victims a week after devastating flash floods in Nepal
full_text:
Kathmandu [Nepal], September 2 (ANI): Families performed the cremation of the victims on Wednesday, a week after the devastating flash floods hit Nepal.

The families used 'kush', a sacred grass, to make the effigy.

Additionally, the Nepal Police and rescue team carried the bodies from Dhunche for burial beside a river on the outskirts of Kathmandu, as some bodies could not be identified.

Earlier on Tuesday, mass burial began in the capital, Kathmandu, as well, after the morgue ran out of space after one week of the devastating flood in Nepal.

Security forces donned in Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) carried the body bags and buried them in the Gorkarna forest area on the outskirts of Kathmandu.

Amid the rainfall, the security personnel walking through the muddy forest carried the bodies and buried them with markers on top. The big bags contained the tags through which the bodies would be later exhumed and handed over to families after establishing the identities.

DNA of the buried bodies has already been kept for cross-matching with the family. As the bodies of the victims swept away by the Bhotekoshi flood are being dumped downstream, hospitals are struggling to find places to store and identify them.

The Himalayan Nation only has a capacity of storing about 350 bodies in the morgues nationwide, which has led to a shortage of space to store the bodies until the family identifies and claims them.

The remains of the victims swept by flood from Rasuwa and Nuwakot are being recovered in different parts of the nation.

The district of Chitwan, a major low lying areas has collected the highest number, 321 bodies. The morgues there have already been filled with the bodies of the victims swept downstream, which has prompted authorities to set up temporary facilities.

Authorities are managing the bodies under the Unidentified and Unclaimed Bodies Management Guidelines, 2021, under which a committee headed by the district police chief is responsible for managing the remains.

With morgues running out of space, the government has engaged in managing unidentified bodies by amending the Unidentified and Unclaimed Body Management Guidelines, 2021.

Meanwhile, a 19-member Indian forensic team began analysing DNA samples alongside forensic experts to assist in identifying people affected by the recent flash floods in Nepal, the Indian Embassy stated.

The team commenced the analysis at the Nepal Police Central Forensic Science Laboratory and the National Forensic Science Laboratory in the Khumaltar area of Kathmandu Valley.

The Indian experts are working with their counterparts to speed up the processing of DNA samples collected from flood-affected areas and help establish the identities of victims and missing persons, according to the Embassy.

'The deployment of the Indian forensic team is part of ongoing efforts to support Nepal in the aftermath of the recent flash floods, which caused significant loss of life and left several people unaccounted for,' the Embassy said.

Nepal Police said 1,068 bodies had been recovered by Tuesday evening, of which 400 had only partial remains, complicating the identification process.

With the death toll continuing to rise following last week's deadly floods, authorities have collected DNA samples from several unclaimed bodies to support identification efforts in the future.

This comes as the death toll from floods in Nepal has risen to 1,127, according to the Nepal Police, on Wednesday.

As per the Nepal Police, a total of 45 bodies have been recovered from Rasuwa, 155 from Nuwakot, 59 from Dhading, 348 from Chitwan, 66 from Gorkha, 38 from Tanahun, 217 from Nawalparasi East and 190 from Nawalparasi West.

Nepal Prime Minister Balen Shah has said that the rescue of people remains the top priority. He further added that a total of 11,993 people have been rescued so far, while 3,916 people are still missing. (ANI)

full_text:
By SHRISTI KAFLE and SHEIKH SAALIQ

KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Tourists previously reported missing in Nepal have made contact with authorities, officials said Wednesday, as families of locals still unaccounted for after last week’s catastrophic floods held symbolic funerals for their loved ones.

Nepal’s Foreign Ministry said 324 foreign nationals have been rescued, while another 590 from 39 countries remain missing following the Aug. 26 floods. At least 1,204 people have been killed and more than 4,200 are missing, according to the country’s disaster management agency.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Wednesday that the number of Australians missing in the disaster had fallen from 43 to 38 after five were confirmed safe overnight.

“Amidst all of this tragedy, we are seeing some positive news. Today, another five Australians have been confirmed safe,” Albanese told reporters in Palau, where he is attending a regional summit.

“We hope, of course, for positive news further, and we’re doing everything we can to work with authorities,” Albanese added.

On Thursday, the Australian government said it would send a team of drone operators to Nepal within days to assist search and rescue efforts.

Sunil Sharma, a spokesperson for the Nepal Tourism Board, said at least five other tourists who were previously reported missing had contacted authorities by email or telephone in recent days.

It is thought the disaster happened when a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream. The surge entered rivers flowing through Tibet and Nepal, causing them to rise rapidly. Floodwaters swept away homes, buildings, roads and bridges, carrying mud and rocks downstream.
