Nepal police personnel prepare the bodies of flash flood victims for a mass burial in Kathmandu, Nepal, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha)

A man, right, comforts a woman after he performed rituals during symbolic last rites for his family members who remain missing and are presumed dead following flash floods in Kathmandu, Nepal, Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/Dar Yasin)

People whose relatives remain missing following flash floods perform symbolic funeral rites on the banks of the swollen Trishuli River in Nepal’s Nuwakot district, Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/Rajesh Kumar Singh) Show Caption 1 of 4 People whose relatives remain missing and are presumed dead following flash floods perform symbolic last rites on the banks of the swollen Trishuli River in Nepal’s Nuwakot district, Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/Rajesh Kumar Singh) Expand

Families hold symbolic funerals

Some families in Nuwakot, one of Nepal’s worst-affected districts, have held symbolic funerals for relatives still missing, hoping to free their souls after they were presumed dead.

In Hindu tradition, cremation is an important final rite, and for some families, performing the ceremony even without the bodies of their loved ones provides a sense of spiritual release.

Mukunda Rijal said his cousins and their daughters had not been found, prompting the family to perform a symbolic funeral for them.

Along the banks of the Trishuli River, a priest placed straw effigies representing the missing family members and covered them with small piles of wood before setting them alight. The symbolic funeral pyres were surrounded by offerings to Hindu deities as relatives gathered to perform the final rites.

Authorities in Nepal have also been burying recovered bodies in temporary graves until they can be identified. They are preserving DNA samples, photographing distinguishing facial features and recording other identifying details to help match the remains with missing people and eventually return them to their families.

China builds access road for rescue crews

On the Chinese side, rescue crews completed a makeshift road to the disaster site at Gyirong Port on the Nepal border, state broadcaster CCTV reported on Wednesday.

Crews have been clearing access for heavy machinery to be used in the search at the border crossing complex, which was washed away by the floods. The road leading to the crossing was destroyed and buried under water, mud and rocks.

At least 21 people have been killed and 541 remain missing in China, according to the Chinese state news agency Xinhua.

Survivors find shelter in Kathmandu

Some flood survivors are fleeing the devastation to seek shelter in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu.

Around 400 survivors, mostly from the town of Timure, about 110 kilometers (65 miles) west of Kathmandu, have been staying at the Yellow Gumba monastery. The shelter is being organized by locals and relatives, with relief supplies donated by individuals and charity organizations.

Riya Tamang, 21, who fled with her 10-month-old baby as the floodwaters approached, is among those taking shelter at the monastery. She lost her grandparents in the disaster.

“I was the last one to leave the house. It was so difficult to escape,” she said.

Her husband, who works as a cook in Gyirong town on the Chinese side of the border, also survived, and the couple now stays in touch through video calls.

Associated Press journalists Yasin Dar in Nuwakot, Nepal, Rod McGuirk in Melbourne, Kanis Leung in Hong Kong and Huizhong Wu in Bangkok contributed to this report.

title: Families perform cremation of victims a week after devastating flash floods in Nepal
full_text:
Kathmandu [Nepal], September 2 (ANI): Families performed the cremation of the victims on Wednesday, a week after the devastating flash floods hit Nepal.

The families used 'kush', a sacred grass, to make the effigy.

Additionally, the Nepal Police and rescue team carried the bodies from Dhunche for burial beside a river on the outskirts of Kathmandu, as some bodies could not be identified.

Earlier on Tuesday, mass burial began in the capital, Kathmandu, as well, after the morgue ran out of space after one week of the devastating flood in Nepal.

Security forces donned in Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) carried the body bags and buried them in the Gorkarna forest area on the outskirts of Kathmandu.

Amid the rainfall, the security personnel walking through the muddy forest carried the bodies and buried them with markers on top. The big bags contained the tags through which the bodies would be later exhumed and handed over to families after establishing the identities.

DNA of the buried bodies has already been kept for cross-matching with the family. As the bodies of the victims swept away by the Bhotekoshi flood are being dumped downstream, hospitals are struggling to find places to store and identify them.

The Himalayan Nation only has a capacity of storing about 350 bodies in the morgues nationwide, which has led to a shortage of space to store the bodies until the family identifies and claims them.

The remains of the victims swept by flood from Rasuwa and Nuwakot are being recovered in different parts of the nation.

The district of Chitwan, a major low lying areas has collected the highest number, 321 bodies. The morgues there have already been filled with the bodies of the victims swept downstream, which has prompted authorities to set up temporary facilities.

Authorities are managing the bodies under the Unidentified and Unclaimed Bodies Management Guidelines, 2021, under which a committee headed by the district police chief is responsible for managing the remains.

With morgues running out of space, the government has engaged in managing unidentified bodies by amending the Unidentified and Unclaimed Body Management Guidelines, 2021.

Meanwhile, a 19-member Indian forensic team began analysing DNA samples alongside forensic experts to assist in identifying people affected by the recent flash floods in Nepal, the Indian Embassy stated.

The team commenced the analysis at the Nepal Police Central Forensic Science Laboratory and the National Forensic Science Laboratory in the Khumaltar area of Kathmandu Valley.

The Indian experts are working with their counterparts to speed up the processing of DNA samples collected from flood-affected areas and help establish the identities of victims and missing persons, according to the Embassy.

'The deployment of the Indian forensic team is part of ongoing efforts to support Nepal in the aftermath of the recent flash floods, which caused significant loss of life and left several people unaccounted for,' the Embassy said.

Nepal Police said 1,068 bodies had been recovered by Tuesday evening, of which 400 had only partial remains, complicating the identification process.

With the death toll continuing to rise following last week's deadly floods, authorities have collected DNA samples from several unclaimed bodies to support identification efforts in the future.

This comes as the death toll from floods in Nepal has risen to 1,127, according to the Nepal Police, on Wednesday.

As per the Nepal Police, a total of 45 bodies have been recovered from Rasuwa, 155 from Nuwakot, 59 from Dhading, 348 from Chitwan, 66 from Gorkha, 38 from Tanahun, 217 from Nawalparasi East and 190 from Nawalparasi West.

Nepal Prime Minister Balen Shah has said that the rescue of people remains the top priority. He further added that a total of 11,993 people have been rescued so far, while 3,916 people are still missing. (ANI)

title: Waterloo region , Guelph residents worry for loved ones missing after flash floods in Nepal
full_text:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's been almost exactly a week since Gireesh Raina from Guelph went missing.

He was on a trek, crossing the border from Tibet, heading to Kathmandu when flash floods ripped through Nepal last Wednesday, killing at least 1,114 people and leaving thousands more people like him missing.

Raina was with a group of about 80 people on a trek from Tibet to Kathmandu when the flood first hit. Including Raina, there are 12 Canadians on that trek.

Their trip was a sacred pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet and it was organized by the Isha Foundation in North America, a non-profit spirituality group.

The missing man's wife, Rama Raina, strongly believes her husband is still on the Chinese side of the border.

She says she hasn't heard from him since he reached that checkpoint and she's hoping rescuers will hear her plea to go check for survivors there.

"This is my firm belief that they are stranded there waiting for some help, but so far nothing is going on," she said, urging the Chinese government to share more information about ongoing rescue efforts.

A satellite image shows the valleys near the Nepal-China border on August 26, 2026, after the devastating floods. (Planet Labs/Reuters)

She's also asking the Canadian government to do more.

"I don't think there is much help from the Canadian government yet. I don't know why they're waiting, what they're waiting for. I don't understand. I just need the information through that side of the border what's happening," she said.

"The more time is passing, it's getting more worse."

Gireesh Raina's family has been circulating this digital poster in hopes that it will help authorities find him. He was last seen at the Nepal-Tibet border just minutes before flash floods crashed through the area. (Gautam Raina)

Global Affairs Canada said in a media update on Thursday it was aware of about 30 missing Canadian citizens and permanent residents in Nepal and Tibet.

"Our consular officials are working urgently to establish contact with them and confirm their safety. They are also reaching out to travel agencies, local authorities and likeminded countries to gather additional information," the government agency said, adding it is deploying five consular officials to Kathmandu to support Canadians and co-ordinate with local officials and partners and will provide further resources as needed.

'We've lost everything'

Ganesh Adhikari is the owner of Momo Day — Himalayan Street Food in Cambridge. He has close friends who were living where the flash floods happened.

He said it's been days since he's heard from them and fears the worst.

"Everything is damaged like house, whatever was left around the area for the second flood," he told CBC News, adding that there are about 40 families he is connected to in that area of Nepal.

"They are still missing ... they have little child ... We are hoping they [are] still alive."

Adhikari says he's been sending money in an effort to try and help people in Nepal. He's encouraging more people to donate directly through the Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund, an online fundraising page set up by the Nepali government.

"We've lost everything," Adhikari said. "Half of Nepal is almost is gone right now."

Prakash Gurung from Kitchener has also been sending money through the fundraiser. His family was not close to where the flooding happened, but Gurung was born and raised in Nepal.

He says watching videos of the devastation in his home country "ripped through his heart."

"I couldn't believe it, I thought that was some kind of AI video," he said.

"There is so many things happened before in Nepal, but those kind of floods, that was the first time I seen that happening and I was literally crying inside because even though I don't have relatives and my friends there, it's the country I was born. So it feels very personal to me."

WATCH | Nepal flood survivors return to ruined homes: 'Nothing left': Nepal flood survivors return to ruined homes | Duration 2:30 A devastating flash flood in Nepal killed more than 900 people, with thousands more missing. Now, residents of neighbourhoods swallowed by mud are returning to see what they can salvage. CBC’s Briar Stewart follows a Nepalese couple as they return to their home to face the damage.

Gurung said he feels speechless, unsure what to say and how to react to the devastation in Nepal. He said his family has been praying for the lives lost in Nepal.

"I've been praying for those people to get this strength because if I was in their place, I would not be able to handle all that," he said.

"My children, they are very young and then I see those family who lost some of their family members, their children, their parents."

Assistance from Mennonite Central Committee

Some Canadian charities are stepping up to help with disaster relief, including the Mennonite Central Committee (MCC), which has a main office in Kitchener.

The organization is working with local partners in Nepal including Sahayogi Hatharuko Samuha and the National Mental Health Self-Help Organization to provide emergency relief.

MCC says it is providing survivors with food, water purification tablets, hygiene and dignity kits, bedding, clothes and psychosocial support in the affected districts.

In the first days after the flood, the organization says it also helped search and rescue operations by providing five generators in areas without power.

"It was heartbreaking to witness the scale of devastation caused by the floods,” says Durga Sunchiuri, MCC Nepal program director said in a press release.

"I have never seen such extensive destruction before. Many affected families are struggling without electricity and basic necessities in temporary holding areas, facing significant uncertainty about their housing and livelihoods."

title: China embassy accuses a senior Argentine official of spreading  rumours  about the Nepal flood MercoPress
full_text:
China's embassy accuses a senior Argentine official of spreading “rumours” about the Nepal flood

2nd Wednesday, September 2026 - 21:22 UTC Full article

Juan Pablo Carreira, digital communication director at Argentina's presidency, blamed a Chinese state company for the Nepal disaster

China's embassy in Buenos Aires has accused an official in Javier Milei's government of spreading “malicious rumours” and seeking to “stain the international image” of the Asian country, after he attributed to a Chinese state company responsibility for the flood that devastated the border corridor between Nepal and Tibet on August 26.

The disaster began when a mass of ice and rock broke away from a glacier front on the northern slopes of Langtang Lirung, in Nepali territory, and fell some 1,200 metres to the valley floor. The material temporarily blocked the Lhende Khola river, forming a lake that later burst through, generating a surge of water and mud that swept away the Gyirong border crossing and descended along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. The United States Geological Survey initially recorded the signal as an earthquake and later reclassified it as the trace of the glacier collapse. The current toll stands at at least 1,050 dead and 3,916 missing in Nepal, and 16 dead and 546 missing on the Chinese side. Among those unaccounted for are more than 900 workers at hydropower plants in central Nepal.

Juan Pablo Carreira, national director of digital communication at the Argentine presidency, wrote on August 30 from his personal account on X that a Chinese state company was building a hydroelectric installation beside a glacier on the border and that failures in state organisation of industrial activity had caused the collapse. He linked the episode to other disasters he attributed to communist governments and concluded by asserting that communism kills.

Records of the episode note that attribution of the disaster to Chinese infrastructure circulated on social media during the first hours and was ruled out by subsequent satellite imagery and scientific analysis, which identified the glacier collapse on the Nepali side as the immediate source.

“A certain Argentine official, driven by biased ideological prejudice, is maliciously spreading rumours,” the Chinese mission said, calling for an end to speculation and urging him to “stop politicising or instrumentalising natural disasters”.

Declaración de Portavoz de la Embajada China en Argentina pic.twitter.com/hwciHJIXCo — Embajada de China en Argentina (@ChinaEmbArg) September 1, 2026

Presidential spokesman Adrián Ravier said the government answers only for the content of its official accounts and that “there is no official that we know of who has made any statement on the matter”. Opposition deputies have requested that Carreira be summoned to Congress.

The episode comes as Buenos Aires negotiates with Beijing. China is Argentina's second trading partner after Brazil; the currency swap between the two central banks was renewed at the start of the month, and Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno has confirmed preparations for a trip to China with the economy minister and the presidency's general secretary, with no date set.

title: Devastating Floods Hit Nepal as Climate Change Bites
full_text:
Some 45 miles north, high in the Himalayas along the Nepal-Tibet border, a large section of a glacier had collapsed, sending a torrent of water, sediments, and boulders and swallowing downstream settlements. It took the flood barely 30 minutes to reach Tamang’s village in Nuwakot district, hitting with the terrible speed of a tsunami.

KATHMANDU—The rains had briefly quelled, and beneath a bright mid-morning sky, 43-year-old Subash Tamang was working along the banks of the monsoon-swollen Trishuli River with his family. They were extracting sand, as they had done before, when the river suddenly rose to consume them.

KATHMANDU—The rains had briefly quelled, and beneath a bright mid-morning sky, 43-year-old Subash Tamang was working along the banks of the monsoon-swollen Trishuli River with his family. They were extracting sand, as they had done before, when the river suddenly rose to consume them.

Some 45 miles north, high in the Himalayas along the Nepal-Tibet border, a large section of a glacier had collapsed, sending a torrent of water, sediments, and boulders and swallowing downstream settlements. It took the flood barely 30 minutes to reach Tamang’s village in Nuwakot district, hitting with the terrible speed of a tsunami.

Tamang survived by holding on to a patch of weed. But it swept away his wife, his two brothers and their wives, and his elder sister. The body of one of his brothers has been retrieved, while the five other family members remain missing. Tamang was ferried to Kathmandu for treatment two days later.

“I’ve lost everything,” he said from a hospital bed. “We didn’t receive any warning and weren’t expecting the water to rise that high. One moment I was hanging by the weeds, and the next moment when I looked, none of my family members were there. I now have a hole in my leg and my heart.”

A crowd of people standing on a muddy slope watching rescuers, with a fallen concrete pole in the midground and a rescue worker in a yellow helmet and bright orange vest in the foreground.

The Aug. 26 flood has obliterated parts of three districts—Rasuwa, Dhading, and Nuwakot—in north and central Nepal, but the shock has reverberated throughout the country. The death toll from the flood has climbed to more than 1,000, with nearly 4,000 people still missing, of which nearly 600 are foreign nationals, many of them pilgrims to Tibet’s Mount Kailash, revered by both Hindus and Buddhists.

As quickly as disaster hit, such cataclysmic events have been decades in the making. Carbon emissions have steadily warmed the Himalayas and destabilized its glaciers. A February study shows that the temperatures in Nepal’s glacier collapse area have increased 4.7 degrees Fahrenheit since 1940, twice the average global warming rate.

Low-income countries in the Hindu Kush—which stretches roughly 2,100 miles across eight countries, including Nepal—are paying a grim price for a climate crisis they did little to create. Floods and landslides have become routine and largely normalized despite significant loss of life and economic damage, but a disaster on this scale poses harder questions.

“The ecosystem and landscapes have evolved over geological time, but carbon emissions are changing them so quickly that they’re adapting on a human-dominated time scale,” Simon Cook, a geoscientist and senior lecturer at Scotland’s University of Dundee, told Foreign Policy.

High-angle landscape view showing severe soil erosion, steep mudbanks, and a wide river flowing through a mountain valley near a small settlement. Image 4: Back view of a person carrying a young child on their shoulder while standing in a crowd of people looking at photos posted on a closed shop shutter. Image 5: An elderly woman covered in mud sitting in the metal bucket of an excavator, being assisted by two men, one wearing an orange life jacket and another in a blue uniform. Image 6: A damaged concrete bridge ending abruptly over a wide, muddy riverbed, with a motorcyclist parked near the broken edge and onlookers standing along the sides. Image 7: Close-up of two women crying and embracing each other on a street, with one covering her face with her hand and wearing a black face mask. Image 8: Two people viewed from behind standing on a rocky riverbank, looking out over a wide, turbulent river under a dark sky with sun rays breaking through clouds.

Almost a week after the event, scientists, including three Foreign Policy spoke with, have determined what caused the Aug. 26 disaster: a rock-ice avalanche. The glacial collapse and landslide occurred on the northern face of the Langtang Lirung peak—the 99th highest peak in the world—on the Nepali side bordering Tibet at around 8:37 a.m. Satellite images show that a 2,000-foot-wide mass of rock and ice fell from an elevation of 17,000 feet to around 4,000 feet in the valley below.

Basanta Raj Adhikari, director at the Centre for Disaster Studies at Kathmandu’s Institute of Engineering, told Foreign Policy that his estimates show it took about nine minutes for the water and debris from the landslide to reach the Rasuwa border checkpoint, about 12.5 miles from the site of the glacier collapse. That is where waves—potentially as high as 1,500 feet in some places—crashed into the border buildings, hotels, and houses in Gyirong Port on the Chinese side and Rasuwa, crushing people running for their lives—all captured in unsettling CCTV footage.

“The rock is holding the ice, and when it fell both the rock and ice mass broke off, triggering a rock-ice avalanche,” Adhikari said. “Its mass could be over 300 million cubic meters—the size of nearly 120,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools—from our estimate. The energy it created is more than the atom bomb that fell in Hiroshima.”

The thud was so immense that it created a 5.2 magnitude tremor—which the U.S. Geological Survey initially believed to be a 4.4 magnitude earthquake—with the debris blocking the Lhende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi river, flowing through villages such as Timure and Syabrubesi, before merging into the Trishuli river system. When it burst, an enormous volume of water was released, roaring past the trading posts and villages, which Adhikari said could have been flowing at about 100 miles per hour downstream.

Cook said the potential energy stored in the substantial block of ice gets converted into kinetic energy when it falls, with “all that material being pulverized and broken into smaller pieces of ice slush and water.”

“There were possibly dead and decaying glaciers, too, downstream, which could have been pulverized into the flowing mix of ice, rock, boulders, and so on,” he said. “Some sort of snowmelt or water within the glaciers we didn’t see—it’s common for glaciers to contain pockets of water—could also have resulted in the water flow. Also, the narrow constriction created a funneling effect, resulting in huge waves enveloping buildings.”

An elderly woman covered in mud sitting in the metal bucket of an excavator, being assisted by two men, one wearing an orange life jacket and another in a blue uniform.

By the time the ferocious waves reached downstream districts, they had turned into a muddy slush, swallowing person after person and house after house.

Bhakta Bhandari from Devighat in Nuwakot—one of the worst-hit communities—was working on his farm that morning when a neighbor sounded the alarm. He had just started running when the waves violently tossed him into the air before he landed in neck-deep muddy water, injuring his back. I visited him at a Kathmandu hospital, while his wife lay in a bed beside him with severe arm and neck wounds. One of his relatives, he suspects, is missing, with another one dead.

“In all my lifetime, I’ve never seen anything like this,” he told Foreign Policy. “We didn’t even imagine the flood would be this intense. We thought it would be like the previous year. But it was like a tsunami, just like in other countries.”

A damaged concrete bridge ending abruptly over a wide, muddy riverbed, with a motorcyclist parked near the broken edge and onlookers standing along the sides.

Studies have shown links between climate change and extreme weather events, with a Carbon Brief analysis from March showing that 71 percent of 504 such episodes globally were “found to be made more likely or more severe by human-caused climate change.”

Nepal has also been at the forefront of such events, with erratic and intense monsoon rains triggering flash floods and landslides almost every year. Last year, an outburst of a supraglacial lake on the Purugu Glacier in Tibet caused widespread devastation in the same area as last week’s disaster. In 2024, the Kathmandu Valley suffered one of the country’s most severe urban floodings ever, and the 2021 flooding of Melamchi River inundated the Melamchi Bazaar.

Other mountain countries are facing similar disasters. From the 2023 glacial lake outburst flood in Sikkim, India, to the 2025 rock-ice avalanche that flattened the Swiss village of Blatten, thousands of people have been killed in such disasters, with economic losses mounting in the billions of dollars just over the past few years.

Miriam Jackson, a research scientist at Norway’s hydrology department who has worked extensively in Nepal and Bhutan, told Foreign Policy that the recent incident in Nepal has similarities to the 2021 Chamoli disaster in India’s Uttarakhand state, where a hanging glacier broke off, releasing energy approximately equal to 15 times the bomb dropped on Hiroshima. She added that the powerful 2015 earthquake also destabilized mountain slopes across Nepal, increasing the risk of landslides and rockfalls.

“Some 25 years ago, you barely heard about glaciers detaching, but there have [been] a few similar incidents in the past two decades,” Jackson said. “Before they were unusual, and now we’re seeing more and more of them—perhaps we’re becoming better at attributing them through satellite images and advanced technology. But these events are huge, and they come suddenly and are hard to predict.”

Back view of a person carrying a young child on their shoulder while standing in a crowd of people looking at photos posted on a closed shop shutter.

On the ground, thousands of people are still waiting to hear if their relatives or friends survived.

Outside Kathmandu’s Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, a steady stream of people stops by every day. Their desperate eyes scan the wall where photos of the dead bodies, many of them muddy and naked, are plastered.

Dev Bahadur Rana has been visiting one hospital after another, hoping to trace his nephew, Dil Bahadur Magar, a police officer stationed in Rasuwa. Another man, Risan Tamang, looked away from the photos and called family with no answers. Two of his in-laws, both truck drivers, are missing.

“Once the videos of the floods surfaced, we have been calling, but the phone is now switched off,” Risan said. “We haven’t been able to eat. Their mother and wives have fainted multiple times.”

Close-up of two women crying and embracing each other on a street, with one covering her face with her hand and wearing a black face mask.

Nearby, Rabin Lama, who was checking updates on his phone, said that his niece, nephew, and brother-in-law are missing, along with 25 others from his village of Gatlang in Rasuwa.

“I’m sending photos because not everyone can come to Kathmandu, so we want to send them to others with missing family members and relatives for identification,” he said.

A few miles away at the National Trauma Center, people gathered at a temporary information booth set up by the Nepal Police, where Devi Sapkota came looking for his cousin Laxman’s whereabouts. Laxman worked for a Chinese road construction firm on the Syabrubesi-Rasuwagadhi road stretch along the border. The family does not even know the company’s name.

“He had gone on leave three days before the flood and was coming home on Thursday (the day after the disaster),” Sapkota said. “He was going to Timure on Wednesday and taking a bus for Sindhuli. He has been out of contact since then. His wife and 5-year-old son are waiting.”

Families of more than 600 people who are trapped inside the tunnels of as many as 11 hydropower stations are also waiting. They are angry and urging the government to expedite the search for people who may be buried in remote areas near the Chinese border. Nepal Army personnel have been seen navigating waist-deep muddy slush inside the tunnels, while India and Chinese tunnel rescue workers have also joined the search since Saturday. But many are already questioning the government’s initial reluctance to accept foreign help before accepting “specialized” support only on the third day.

Two people viewed from behind standing on a rocky riverbank, looking out over a wide, turbulent river under a dark sky with sun rays breaking through clouds.

Nepal ranks sixth globally among countries most affected by climate change, according to development organization Germanwatch’s 2026 Climate Risk Index. As the intensity of such extreme weather events rises, the country is inadequately prepared to face them.

Adhikari, the disaster risk reduction expert, said that Nepal has a disaster strategy, but it’s highly focused on rescue and response, calling for more investment in preparedness and risk assessment, including mapping, monitoring, and early-warning systems.

“There should be risk-sensitive landscape planning that would identify suitable areas for settlements and infrastructure construction, as well as identify risk areas, which Nepal hasn’t done yet,” he said.

Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said during a press conference Saturday that the country is “one of the major victims of climate change and its impacts,” despite its negligible contribution to carbon emissions responsible for global warming. Amid growing calls for transboundary collaborations on an early-warning system, he said Nepal and China have been “actively working” to establish such mechanisms.

“Since this disaster, we are in very close coordination, cooperation, and communication with the Chinese authority, and they have been very forthcoming with sharing information and data,” Khanal added.

But climate activists and policy analysts say that narratives around disasters should go beyond devastation to address climate justice.

Sneha Pandey, a climate diplomacy and policy analyst at Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute, told Foreign Policy that the cost incurred by emissions from the richest nations must not overburden poor countries and communities on the front lines. She added that the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage—a global climate finance mechanism—financing “must be scaled up substantially to meet the scale of climate-imposed disasters.”

“At COP31, pressure must be built at the high level to mobilize more finance for loss and damage and adaptation and resilience-building, and to reduce global emissions in line with the Paris Agreement,” Pandey said, referring to the 2026 U.N. Climate Change Conference being held in Turkey later this year. “Nepal must continue to push for dedicated negotiations space for mountain-related concerns so that cryospheric risks are more firmly anchored in the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change process.”

Nepal has fallen, risen, and rebuilt only to be shaken again over the past decades. The end of the decade-long Maoist insurgency in 2006 brought a push for new development, which was shattered by the devastating 2015 earthquake. And as Nepal rebuilt again, the 2025 Gen Z uprising shook the country, leaving behind widespread arson, destruction, and economic losses. But just as a young government took office in March, the floods have now washed away hopes of a fresh start for many. And once again, those with the least are likely to pay the highest price.

Survivors like Bhandari and Subash Tamang, who relied on marginal and climate-sensitive industries like agriculture and sand extraction, respectively, survived the floods, but they feel living with the uncertainty that comes next could be worse.

“We don’t know what sort of help we’ll get from the government, and we don’t know if we are going to be displaced from our home,” Bhandari said. “We’ve lost everything. We only have a pair of clothes now. Everything is gone.”

“After being discharged, I have nowhere else to go,” Tamang added. “I don’t know what to do.”

title: Nepal Holds Symbolic Funerals as Flood Death Toll Rises to 1 , 204
full_text:
At Pashupatinath temple in Kathmandu, families gathered Wednesday to perform a ritual that Nepali Hindu tradition reserves for those whose bodies cannot be recovered. They cremated effigies woven from kush grass — surrogate bodies representing the souls of the missing — and performed the rites of death for people they cannot confirm are dead. One week after a glacier collapsed on the Nepal-Tibet border and sent a wall of ice, rock and mud through Himalayan valleys, this is what grief looks like when there is no body to bring home.

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority confirmed Wednesday that the death toll from the August 26 disaster has risen to at least 1,252 on the Nepali side alone, with the combined toll across Nepal and China surpassing 1,270. Some 4,216 people remain missing across both countries, while nearly 12,000 have been rescued. The United Nations has described the event as Nepal's worst natural catastrophe since the April 2015 earthquake, which killed approximately 9,000 people. The NDRRMA called it "not just a flood — a Himalayan climate disaster that came without warning."

The kush grass effigies — dressed, garlanded and carried to the river steps — served as proxies for a goodbye that the flood had denied thousands of Nepali families. Among those mourned Wednesday was Bishi Pandey, 48, whose body remains missing; his relatives wept through the smoke at Pashupatinath as the effigy burned in his place. The ceremonies continued through the morning as helicopters carried more bodies from Rasuwa district to Kathmandu, and morgues already past capacity struggled to hold what the river kept returning.

The most consequential development from Wednesday's operations was the conclusion of search work at the Rasuwagadhi hydropower facility in Rasuwa district — the last of eleven sites where active searches had been under way. An army team accompanied by engineers and a drone unit entered the 111-megawatt facility's tunnel system, advanced to its innermost section and flew a drone through the full interior. The prime minister's secretariat confirmed no one was found inside. Approximately 897 workers across all eleven projects remain out of contact, with roughly 500 believed to have been inside tunnel systems when the surge struck. At the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project alone, at least 576 people are missing, with approximately 300 believed trapped inside the tunnel. Rescue crews have used controlled explosives to clear boulders while simultaneously pumping water from the shafts. Vertical drilling — boring down from the mountain's summit to pierce the top of the powerhouse — remains under examination where frontal access stays blocked. The tunnel at Trishuli 3A runs more than four kilometers; Indian and Chinese tunnel specialists continue working alongside Nepali army engineers at the most critical remaining sites.

Six days after the disaster, survival conditions inside sealed shafts are increasingly in doubt. The head of the Independent Power Producers' Association said publicly that some workers may have suffocated. One survivor estimated roughly 1,000 people had been working across nearby projects the morning the flood struck, with only about 100 making it out. Another described gripping ceiling rungs for six hours as water rose in the darkness, passing a tin sheet between colleagues as the group inched toward the exit. By the time they emerged, the flood had claimed their clothing. His brother-in-law remained among the missing — his pregnant wife waiting at home. What began as a rescue operation is, at most sites, now being managed as a recovery mission in all but official terminology.

In Chitwan district, nearly 200 kilometers downstream from the disaster's origin, mass burials continued in the Devghat forest area of Bharatpur Metropolitan City. Hundreds of graves were prepared along trails that until recently served as morning walking paths. Before each burial, DNA samples, photographs and fingerprints were collected, and precise location coordinates were recorded so remains could be matched and exhumed if families came forward. A forensic team from India is assisting in the identification process. In Chitwan alone, 233 bodies had been recovered from riverbanks in the initial days, with only four identified before mass burial preparations began. Nepal's foreign minister said refrigerated storage for decomposed remains was urgently needed and had been formally requested from foreign governments without confirmed commitment.

Across the disaster zone, survivors are improvising in conditions that relief workers describe as among the most logistically complex they have encountered. At Devighat in Nuwakot district, hundreds of displaced residents gathered at a temporary relief camp Wednesday to receive utility supplies — the modest inventory of tarpaulins, rice sacks and clothing laid out on blue sheets in an open field representing, for many, everything they now own. Elsewhere in Nuwakot, flood survivors grip a makeshift cable above the swollen Trishuli river as Nepali soldiers and residents pull them hand over hand to the opposite bank — a zip line strung between the ruins of what was once a bridge. In Trishuli Center, the turquoise house that locals have taken to calling the "miracle house" stands almost intact amid a landscape of gray sludge, the only structure in its immediate surroundings that the flood left whole. The family inside survived as the water destroyed everything around them.

The China-Nepal border crossing at Gyirong — the primary land route between the two countries, handling roughly a third of bilateral trade — was destroyed entirely in the initial surge. Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported Wednesday that the road to the border has been largely reopened after excavators carved a new route along the riverbank. Chinese rescue teams continue searching for survivors on the Tibetan side, where at least 16 people have died and 546 remain missing. The avalanche of ice and rock reached the Gyirong Port complex within six to seven minutes of the initial collapse — catching pilgrims, traders and hydropower workers simultaneously in their most exposed positions along the valley. The August 26 collapse struck at the peak of the pilgrimage season on the Kailash Mansarovar route, which draws tens of thousands of travelers through Rasuwa district and across the Gyirong crossing each year.

Among the missing are approximately 583 foreign nationals on the Nepali side alone. Australia confirmed Wednesday that five previously listed nationals have been found safe, reducing its missing count from 43 to 38. Approximately 80 Americans, 53 Ukrainians, 51 Malaysians, 33 British nationals and 32 Canadians remain unaccounted for. Three American families have described searching publicly for parents on a Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage who have not made contact since the morning of August 26. Malaysia's prime minister pledged a rescue team and $1 million in aid. Singapore dispatched a police rescue team alongside humanitarian supplies. The United Nations estimates 65,000 people require urgent emergency water, sanitation and hygiene support. More than 22,000 children have been identified as requiring protection services. Nepal has deployed approximately 30,000 security personnel across relief operations, and the UNDP estimates the disaster generated more than 2.4 million tons of debris across five affected districts — Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan.

A rapid hazard assessment by an international scientific consortium raised serious questions about whether the disaster could have been anticipated — and whether workers could have been evacuated in time. Analysis of pre-event satellite imagery revealed visible signs of instability in the days before the collapse, including brown meltwater discharge and cracks forming in surrounding bedrock. Researchers noted that water within the affected glacier appeared to accelerate measurably before the final collapse. The findings call for improved early warning systems and cross-border data sharing between Nepal and China, as well as risk protocols extending beyond the immediate perimeter of infrastructure project boundaries. That the same river corridor had flooded catastrophically just fourteen months earlier, killing nine people, makes the absence of enhanced monitoring especially difficult to defend in retrospect.

The glacier responsible sits within a system that has been deteriorating for decades. The Langtang Valley has lost more than 40 percent of its glacier volume since 1815, with the pace of loss accelerating sharply in recent years. The high-mountain zone above 4,000 meters is warming significantly faster than the global average. Permafrost that once bound rock, ice and glacial mass together for millennia is weakening, increasing the likelihood of sudden, catastrophic detachments. Nepal's Prime Minister stated publicly there is no doubt climate change contributed to the disaster. In a region where hydropower investment has expanded rapidly over the past two decades precisely because meltwater resources appeared abundant and predictable, the August 26 collapse now tests the foundational assumptions of that development model. China's Ministry of Water Resources has warned that glaciers surrounding the impact crater may still be unstable, and a barrier lake of approximately 14,000 square meters upstream remains under active monitoring. With Nepal's monsoon season continuing through September, compounding risk to already-saturated riverbanks remains a live concern.

At Pashupatinath, the smoke from the kush grass pyres drifted over the Bagmati river as more families arrived through the afternoon — each carrying an effigy for someone the flood had taken without leaving a body behind.

U.S. citizens seeking emergency consular assistance may contact the State Department's 24-hour hotline at 1-888-407-4747 (from abroad: +1 202-501-4444).

title: Family searches for Bartlett woman missing in Nepal flood
full_text:
Family members of a Bartlett woman who went missing in last week’s massive flood in Nepal have been in Kathmandu since Monday hoping to find her and bring her home safe.

Poonam Thakkar, 42, embarked Aug. 20 on a holy pilgrimage to Mount Kailash near Nepal’s border with Tibet. She was following in the footsteps of her oldest sister, Bhumika, who made the journey a year ago.

Now Bhumika and two cousins have traveled to Nepal to retrace the path Poonam was on when she vanished during the Aug. 26 flood, middle sister Gunjan said Wednesday.

“They intend to visit that impacted area because we believe she’s still there,” Gunjan said.

Their hope is strong, she added, because people have been found alive throughout the week since the flood — blamed on the collapse of a glacier in the Himalayas — despite the official death toll exceeding 1,100 as of Wednesday. Nearly 4,000 others remain missing.

A relative talks on his mobile phone while looking at photographs of missing persons in the aftermath of flash floods, at the Tribhuvan University Teaching hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal, on Aug. 31, 2026. (Manan Vatsyayana/Getty-AFP)

Buddhist monks and Nepali children take part in a vigil to pay tribute to flash flood victims at Swayambhunath Stupa on Aug. 31, 2026, in Kathmandu, Nepal. The floods, caused by a glacier collapse on Langtang Lirung on Aug. 26, have killed at least 900 people and left nearly 4,000 missing in Nepal, with dozens more dead or missing in neighboring Tibet, authorities have said. (Ezra Acayan/Getty)

Om Bahadur sits on the ledge of his damaged house a week after the devastating flash floods at Baireni in Nepal's Dhading district on Sept. 2, 2026. Devastating floods on the China-Nepal border killed at least 1,114 people in Nepal and 3,916 were missing, the disaster authority said on Sept. 2, a week after the disaster. (Manan Vatsyayana/Getty-AFP)

Residents pull a newly installed zipline to help people move across the Trishuli River in the aftermath of flash floods at Bidur in Nepal's Nuwakot district on Sept. 2, 2026. (Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP) Show Caption 1 of 4 A relative talks on his mobile phone while looking at photographs of missing persons in the aftermath of flash floods, at the Tribhuvan University Teaching hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal, on Aug. 31, 2026. (Manan Vatsyayana/Getty-AFP) Expand

Poonam left Chicago on Aug. 20 for an organized tour to the Tibet border that was to begin Aug. 23. Family members last spoke to her by phone the day before the flood.

“It was all casual, and she was just sharing how excited she was to be starting the pilgrimage,” Gunjan said. “She was enjoying every minute of it.”

Poonam has dual citizenship in the U.S. and Canada, having worked in Canada before joining her sisters and immediate family in Bartlett 7½ years ago, Gunjan said. Extended family also lives in Chicago.

Poonam is a senior manager for one of the big four consulting firms and colleagues have reached out to the family with support, Gunjan said.

Bhumika had wanted to leave for Nepal the day after the flood, but authorities weren’t encouraging travelers that quickly. By the time the three family members left, securing a flight to Nepal was relatively easy.

For now, they are unable to travel beyond Kathmandu, but the family has been in touch with authorities — including from the U.S. and Canadian embassies — whose answers have been compassionate but standard, Gunjan said.

They’ve also met with others seeking loved ones who are missing. They have formed groups that meet each morning to divide up their shared tasks for the day and then collaborate over their findings, according to Gunjan.

While the part of the country they’re hoping to reach continues to be plagued by rain, mudslides and power issues, Kathmandu has been a relatively safe base to operate from, Gunjan said.

While the search for information — and Poonam herself — goes on, Gunjan asks those reading about her sister to hold positive thoughts and wishes for her safe return.

title: Church in Nepal helping flood victims find hope , apostolic administrator says
full_text:
Although a small minority in Nepal, the Catholic Church through Caritas is providing what aid it can to help to those affected by the major flooding.

Father Silas Bogati, apostolic administrator of the apostolic vicariate of Nepal, said the Catholic Church, a small minority of about 10,000 faithful in the Asian nation, is committed to aiding those affected by the recent major flooding.

According to authorities, the number of dead from last week's flood exceeds 1,000, while more than 4,000 people remain missing across both countries, CNN reported.

"By being there, providing relief now and, later, contributing to reconstruction, we give hope. Our presence among those who are suffering will give them hope," the priest said in an interview with the pontifical foundation Aid to the Church in Need (ACN).

Bogati explained that in Nepal, "the Catholic Church has 13 parishes and 10,000 Catholics, but it has always worked for the Nepali population irrespective of their religion, and we will continue to do so as they suffer in this hour of need."

Caritas Nepal has set up community kitchens and dispatched food supplies for 300 affected families to last for 15 days. Given the forecast of additional rainfall and the fact that many people are still sleeping outdoors, the organization said there is a need for tarpaulins, blankets, and sleeping mats.

After noting that "no Catholic churches or chapels have been destroyed," the Nepalese priest recalled that "the Holy Father, Pope Leo, was the first to pray and to show his sympathy and closeness to the victims of these flash floods. In the same way, we are receiving prayers and support from the Catholic Church around the world."

Leo XIV has encouraged prayers for those affected and for rescue teams, and has urged the international community to provide aid in a spirit of solidarity.

Bogati described the affected area of Rasuwa, located on Nepal's border with Tibet. He said an important trade route with Tibet runs through the region, as well as the city of Syabrubesi, "one of the main departure points for tourists traveling toward the Langtang Valley."

One of this concerns is that "members of one of the Catholic communities [who] go down to Syabrubesi to work … may have been swept away by the waters. We do not have any figures yet."

"All these hotels and settlements were swept away. There has been a high death toll in this area, and the river continued downstream, wreaking havoc across five districts. The flood has caused enormous devastation, as a huge mass of water surged downstream, destroying everything in its path. Some communities are still cut off, and search and rescue operations are proving difficult," he recounted.

The apostolic administrator asked for prayers for all the victims and those affected by the tragedy, and expressed gratitude for ACN's closeness and solidarity.

This story was first published by ACI Prensa, the Spanish-language sister service of EWTN News. It has been translated and adapted by EWTN News English.

title: Sewa International united states Releases $100 , 000 for Nepal Flash Flood Relief
full_text:

Volunteers conduct rescue operations, distribute emergency supplies and assist affected families across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts

Sewa International USA has released $100,000 for emergency flood relief in Nepal, as its volunteers work on the ground to rescue stranded people and deliver urgent humanitarian assistance to communities across the severely affected districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

Following the August 26, 2026, catastrophic glacier collapse, avalanche and landslide, thousands are still missing, as floodwaters caused extensive destruction to homes, roads, bridges, hydropower facilities, water systems and communication networks, leaving numerous communities isolated and urgently requiring food, clean drinking water, shelter, medical assistance and other essential supplies.

Several Sewa International USA volunteers who were near the Nepal-Tibet border when the disaster struck were also reported missing, adding to the organization’s concern as search-and-rescue efforts continued throughout the affected region.

According to Sewa International, its volunteers and local relief teams immediately mobilized to assist affected families. Rescue teams have been working to evacuate stranded residents, while volunteers are distributing food, water and emergency relief materials in flood-ravaged communities, the organization said.

“Sewa has started a fundraiser, ‘Nepal Flash Flood Relief,’ and raised more than $134,000 in the last few days,” said Srikanth Gundavarapu, President of Sewa International.

“Flash floods have devastated parts of Nepal, killing hundreds and sweeping away many devotees gathered for the Kailash Yatra. It is heart-wrenching to see the suffering and grief of people,” Gundavarapu added.

Sewa International established a missing-person helpdesk through its Nepal Flood Relief program in a bid to help families connect with those missing. People who have lost contact with a family member, friend, pilgrim or volunteer can submit the individual’s information. Those who have located or rescued a missing person may also report the details so that families can be notified.

The initiative is particularly important because damaged communication networks and transportation infrastructure have made it extremely difficult for families to obtain reliable information about loved ones traveling through or living in the affected areas.

Sewa International USA has launched the “Nepal Flash Flood Relief” fundraiser to strengthen rescue operations and provide emergency assistance to affected communities.

As the emergency response continues, Sewa International appealed to individuals, community organizations, religious institutions, businesses and corporate partners to contribute generously and help provide immediate relief to families facing enormous hardship and uncertainty. Contributions will help support the distribution of food, clean water, clothing, temporary shelter, medical supplies and other urgently needed relief materials.

Sewa’s response is expected to continue beyond the immediate rescue phase. Once conditions stabilize, the organization says it may also assist with rehabilitation and rebuilding initiatives to help families restore their homes, livelihoods and essential community infrastructure.

Sewa International USA is a 501(c)(3) Hindu faith-based humanitarian nonprofit organization specializing in disaster relief and rehabilitation, education, family services and community development. Founded in 2003, the organization has chapters throughout the United States and is part of an international service movement active in multiple countries.

title: Nepal sent disaster alert 38 minutes after the glacier collapse . It wasnt enough
full_text:
Nima Dorje Tamang was in Hakubesi, a hamlet south of Syafrubesi in Rasuwa, when the flood struck. Before Tamang could prepare, he heard a thunderous roar and saw the flood gushing toward him, its waves taller than him.

Tamang and his family ran uphill for their lives but the waves caught him and a rock struck his leg, fracturing it. Swept into the river, he managed to grab a tree near the bank and clung to it for what felt like two hours until his father and his brother came to rescue him. For the next 24 hours, he said he slipped in and out of consciousness before a helicopter brought him to Kathmandu.

At the orthopedic inpatient ward of Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, Tamang told the doctors, “Even the air makes it hurt,” when they pressed his left foot. It was still swollen after the surgery. But from his hospital bed, Tamang worried about his family back home. “We lost our uncle, aunt, sister, and brother-in-law,” he said. “And everyone says there will be a massive flood again.”

Like Tamang, communities and authorities were caught off guard when the glacier collapsed at 8:37am on August 26. Scientists say the likelihood of predicting this particular type of disaster was minimal, and the resulting flash flood surged so rapidly through the steep mountain terrain that there was little time to warn communities downstream. But the disaster exposed a deeper problem: Nepal’s warning systems remain largely designed around individual hazards, while disasters in the Hindu Kush Himalaya are becoming increasingly complex, cascading and transboundary.

Image Nima Dorje Tamang receiving treatment at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital. Photo: The Kathmandu Post



“There is no such thing as an early warning system in Nepal. Simply having sensors does not mean it’s a system; it has to be much more comprehensive,” said Anil Pokhrel, former chief executive of National Disaster Risk Reduction & Management Authority (NDRRMA), stressing the word “system.” For it to be a system, it needed to have a proper assessment of who and what is at risk, he said, then an observation system to anticipate hazards in real time, a comprehensive communications plan for timely alerts, and preparedness for emergencies.

“If the Chinese sensors detect something upstream, a series of sirens should automatically go off all at once. Text messages should go off with a loud buzzer even if it is on silent mode,” he added.

Over the last decade, Pokhrel said Nepal had invested a lot on the observation side, installing sensors. Without multiple sets of sensors monitoring different hazards across different locations, as we saw with Rasuwa floods, it is inadequate to save lives.

When the massive glacial collapse hit the Lhende valley, near the Nepal-Tibet border, Nepal’s Department of Mines and Geology recorded seismic activity. “Our records showed a 4.4 magnitude. But the frequency of the seismic activity did not match that of an earthquake, which is the department’s monitoring mandate, so we did not alert the public like we usually do,” said Lok Vijay Adhikari, chief of National Earthquake Monitoring and Research Center in the Department of Mines and Geology. The US Geological Survey also initially recorded the event at magnitude 4.4, but later revised its assessment, attributing the seismic activity to the glacial collapse.

Image A drone view shows damaged buildings and houses covered in mud next to the Likhu River following deadly flash floods and mudslides, in Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 30, 2026. Photo: Reuters

In the minutes that followed, rising water levels in Bhotekoshi in Rasuwa could potentially have provided another opportunity to alert the public. It was the same Lhende Khola, a transboundary high-altitude river that originates in Gyirong County in Tibet and flows toward the Nepal border, feeding into Bhotekoshi as well as Trishuli downstream. But at 8:50am, the flash flood swept away the gauge in the Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa, at the Syabrubesi hydrological station. Designed to detect gradual rises in the rivers, the gauges were ill-equipped to detect the high-speed flood.

Who knows what to do with the warnings

Twenty-three minutes later, the District Administrative Officer in Rasuwa informed the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology (DHM) about the flash flood. “We informed DHM at nine. We could not do much in Rasuwa because the flood had destroyed the [communications] towers, yet local authorities informed communities, and people went from door to door warning each other,” said Shanti Mahat, spokesperson of NDRRMA.

“But for people downstream we used every means to inform them—through text alerts, caller tune, media broadcasts, and police miking,” she added.

Within 15 minutes of receiving the information, at 9:15am — 38 minutes after the ice-rock avalanche — people in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Chitwan got text alerts that advised them to immediately move to safe, higher ground as water levels in the Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa had crossed the danger threshold. It also listed hotlines for rescue assistance.

Such alerts are critical in a crisis. Over 95 percent of Nepali adults have mobile phones with data, and it is an effective method even if language and literacy levels may hinder access.

Early warning mechanisms can also be basic, where people are vigilant, spot a danger, inform on time, and those at risk know how to act.

Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers & People recalled an incident from the 2021 glacier collapse in Chamoli of Uttarakhand in India, part of the Hindu Kush Himalayan region. “A woman who was on top of a hill saw the flood [in Rishi Ganga] ravaging from a distance and immediately informed her husband, who was working at the hydropower project downstream,” Thakkar said. Her husband initially did not believe her because he could not see the flood. When he finally caught sight of it, he alerted his colleagues, and a group of them ran uphill and survived.

He juxtaposed that with having information about a risk and not knowing how to act on it, referring to the tour guide Ziha Yitie and other mountaineers in Tibet who videographed the slab of glacier falling off of Langtang Lirung Peak. But they did not immediately understand what they were seeing and realized the magnitude of the disaster only after descending down.

Where does accountability lie?

Ultimately, the responsibility for timely warning lies with the state. Nepal already has a bilateral flood-forecasting mechanism with India where the two countries exchange rainfall and river level data. But Nepal is mainly the provider of information, as most of the monitoring stations are in Nepal’s upstream rivers. On the other hand, despite agreements between the two presidents—Xi Jinping and Bidya Devi Bhandari—in 2019, committing to promote cooperation in different fields, including addressing climate change and protecting the environment, seven years on, the countries still do not have even a rudimentary early warning plan.

“There is no protocol. The practice that we have right now is that we cooperate with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to share information,” said Prakash Pokhrel, Geologist at NDRRMA. “Whenever a foreign country is involved, we have to go through the ministry.”

The danger of not having a mandatory protocol, former NDRRMA chief executive Anil Pokhrel warned, is that, “It comes down to the subjective judgement of individuals in authority who may or may not choose to inform.”

After last year’s catastrophic supraglacial flood in the same Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa, Nepal’s monitoring of that area remained limited. The northern side of Nepal’s mountain range, however, happened to be in a “blind spot” that no one, including Nepal, China, and international geologists, was monitoring.

Asked if the area was a low priority for Nepal, government officials suggested it was easier said than done.

“The terrain above the settlement in Timure is extremely remote and difficult to access,” said Mahat. “While we have monitoring stations at the Bhotekoshi river, setting up stations that provide real-time data farther out has been very challenging. Even now we’re struggling to get images using drones.”

Dinkar Kayastha, information officer at the DHM, says that looking at the resources at their disposal, it is impossible to monitor everything, especially when 20 to 25 percent of Nepal is mountains.

Pointing to the Thame flood of 2024 in the Everest region, Kayastha said, “We saw that even such small glacier lakes, that were not considered threatening, can become devastating.”

As of now, according to him, Nepal has monitored major “high-risk” glacial lakes including Imja Tsho in the Khumbu, Everest region, and Tsho Rolpa in Rolwaling valley of Dolakha.

After last year’s flood in Bhotekoshi, Pokhrel, the geologist at NDRRMA, said they were monitoring potentially dangerous glacial lakes every day using satellite images to identify the risk of glacial lake outburst floods. International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has identified 21 potentially dangerous glacier lakes in Nepal across Gandaki, Koshi, and Karnali river basins and mapped 2070 lakes. Their numbers and their size are not absolute; ICIMOD’s research found that as temperatures rise, both the number and size of the lakes are increasing in Nepal.

Earlier this year in March 2026, ICIMOD also warned that glaciers in the Hindu Kush Himalaya were melting at double the rate since 2000. They warned that catastrophic floods and water uncertainty were testament to the fact that it was a critical decade for the cryosphere, where retreats in certain parts could be irreversible. Yet, out of the 38 glaciers ICIMOD monitored, only seven met the global benchmark, and many in the region remained largely unmonitored.

But Prakash Pokhrel said the same satellite images are far less useful for anticipating a glacier collapse. “Many places look stable. We can’t know from the images how fractures have developed or if weathering has occurred,” he said.

When “Clean & Green” development deepens risks

For Thakkar, the responsibility is also on the investors of the 13 hydropower plants in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts that were damaged by the floods, disconnecting roughly 431MW, a tenth of its total power, from the national grid.

The Asian Development Bank, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, and International Finance Corporation were among the major financiers of the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, while China’s state-owned Exim Bank funded the Upper Trishuli 3A project. The projects also included financing from British International Investment, Korea Development Bank, and Exim Bank of Korea, as well as the Netherlands FMO, OPEC Fund and Canadian Climate Fund.

The Asian Development Bank’s panel of independent experts overseeing the Upper Trishuli-1 project had recommended strengthening the warning system and emergency plan, coordinating alerts with hydropower projects upstream and downstream, and putting evacuation protocols in place for dangerous floods.

“But they don’t do it. It’s complete callousness. There is no accountability in South Asian countries,” said Thakkar. “They [funders] know nobody is going to be held accountable so they just get away with it.”

Thakkar said that hydropower projects can aggravate disaster risks by creating additional vulnerabilities in already fragile Himalayan landscapes through deforestation, tunnelling, blasting, excavation and muck dumping. Dams can also worsen downstream flooding, while reservoirs accumulate silt that can create additional risks. When multiple hydropower projects are built in a cascade, he said, these impacts accumulate and multiply.

Climate change is adding another layer of risk through more intense rainfall, warmer winters, melting glaciers and thawing permafrost.

“Our dishonest EIAs, lack of accountability in governance and non-implementation of basic monitoring, forecasting and implementable disaster management plans is worsening the disaster impacts in river valleys with multiple hydropower projects,” said Thakkar. “By not doing independent post-disaster impact assessments, we have shut the doors for learning any lessons for the future.”

Nepal’s Trishuli river basin alone, which originates in Rasuwa, has 36 hydropower projects in various stages of construction and planning. In Tamang’s village in Hakubesi, he said about eighty percent of the population worked at the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower plant, and the rest of them were children or the elderly.

“We have no choice but to go to Kathmandu or to the Dhunche [headquarters of Rasuwa] for work. But with the hydropower people stayed back. Now all of them are trapped in it, the hydropower is gone, we have nothing,” he said. The government’s latest data shows 639 people remained trapped in Upper Trishuli-1 and Trishuli 3A.

What next?

For Dr Saswata Sanyal, who is a disaster risk reduction specialist at ICIMOD, people need to understand the changing realities of living in the Hindu Kush region, where the risks we were familiar with yesterday are no longer the same today.

The Rasuwa flood was a testament to the complex interactions of hazards. “Something triggered an ice avalanche that led to flash floods, debris, sediments and boulders,” he said. Relief efforts since the disaster have also been affected by monsoon rains and flood alerts.

“The risks can be further exacerbated by earthquakes or climate change, so we need to understand the complex nature of hazards in the mountains,” he added.

Flood sensors, even if some of them were washed away in the flash floods in the Trishuli river in Galchchi, continued to be critical in monitoring the drastic increase in water levels and warning people. Sanyal suggested that it’s imperative for Nepal to increase those sensors upstream, not just in its own territory, but other countries in the Hindu Kush region should collaborate to do the same.

Pokhrel, the former chief executive of NDRRMA, added that Nepal needs to set up multiple sensors in diverse locations. Even for floods, he suggested, it’s not enough to install sensors in the bridges, and recommended setting them up on top of hills that can detect seismic waves or the rumble of boulders and floods to alert people using sirens.

Sanyal says people need to comprehend the scale of the Hindu Kush region.

“It has around 54,000 glaciers and more than 2000 glacier lakes, and permafrost covering an even larger area,” he said. While it is not possible to track every inch of the region, he suggested prioritizing the monitoring of areas with settlements downstream, with the countries not only sharing data but also working closely with each other.
