title: Bihar rivers swell after Nepal floods , Diara residents flee with cattle , children as water enters homes
full_text:
Patna (Bihar) [India], September 3 (ANI): Water levels in several rivers in Bihar, including the Ganga, Kosi and Gandak, have risen rapidly following flash floods in Nepal, forcing residents of low-lying Diara areas to evacuate their homes and move to safer locations.

Residents of Nakta Diara and other riverine areas said floodwaters have entered their homes, roads have been submerged, and livestock are struggling for food and shelter. They also alleged that relief materials and essential facilities have not reached them.

Affected residents have also alleged that relief camps lack adequate arrangements, with shortages of food, drinking water and fodder for livestock forcing families to make their own arrangements to meet basic needs.

With the flood situation worsening, affected residents have urged the administration to intensify relief and rescue operations and ensure timely supply of food, drinking water, fodder and other essential items for both people and livestock.

A local resident from the affected area said the Ganga water level was continuing to rise and had crossed the danger mark.

'The water level continues to rise. It has crossed the danger mark, and water has inundated everything. Water has also entered our homes. We are crossing over by boats. I appeal to the government to arrange fodder for the animals and food and drinking water for the people as soon as possible,' the resident told ANI.

The resident said families had been forced to leave their homes two to three days ago and alleged that no relief supplies had reached them.

'Nothing has arrived yet. No relief supplies have reached us so far,' he said.

Another resident, Nirala Kumar, said the situation in Nakta Diara was 'very bad' as water had entered houses and people were facing shortages of food and drinking water.

'Water has entered all the houses. There is a severe shortage of food supplies. People have no food to eat or water to drink, and all walking paths and roads are blocked,' Kumar said.

He said more than half the residents had already left their homes and urged the government to arrange food, water and facilities for livestock.

'The government should arrange food and water for us and make arrangements for the cattle. They should set up community kitchens or arrange food relief,' he said.

Kumar said residents face the same hardship every year during the floods and sought relief arrangements for the three months when the area remains affected.

Another resident, Umesh Kumar Yadav, said families were fleeing with their cattle and children as floodwaters entered their homes.

'Yes, that's why we are fleeing with our cattle and our children. We are bringing all our cattle along,' Yadav said.

He alleged that residents of Diara areas were not receiving adequate government support.

'We get nothing. Only the market town people get relief. People from Diara receive nothing,' he alleged.

Yadav said residents were being forced to arrange food and fodder for their livestock with their own money.

'We will feed them with our own money,' he said, adding that the damage across the panchayat was extensive.

Meanwhile, a local shopkeeper at a cremation ground said the rising Ganga water level was making it increasingly difficult to conduct last rites.

'The water level of the Ganga is continuously rising. If it rises by another foot or so, it will reach the road, and cremations will have to be done on the road itself,' shopkeeper Santosh Kumar told ANI.

He urged the administration to take measures to prevent soil erosion and place sandbags along the riverbank.

BJP MLA from Digha, Sanjeev Chaurasia, said the administration was monitoring the situation and taking steps to provide shelter and fodder to affected residents and livestock.

'We are continuously conducting ground inspections along the Ganga and monitoring the water levels. You can see how rapidly the water level of the Ganga has surged. Consequently, a large number of cattle are arriving from the Nakta Diara panchayat area,' Chaurasia said.

He said the Circle Officer had been called and temporary shelters and fodder arrangements were being made.

'Tents and temporary shelters have been erected immediately, and more are being set up. Fodder arrangements for the cattle are also being made here,' the MLA said.

Chaurasia said he had coordinated with the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and would visit Nakta Diara and Bind Toli to assess the situation.

'In coordination with the administration, all necessary flood relief facilities provided by the government will certainly be delivered. There will be no shortage of relief; everyone will receive aid,' he said.

Appealing to residents to remain assured, Chaurasia said the government was taking measures to provide shelter, fodder and food through community kitchens.

'The government is taking swift, proactive measures on all fronts. We are ensuring that no one faces hardships-whether it is arranging fodder for livestock, setting up shelter homes for flood victims, or running community relief kitchens,' he said.

He said Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary had reviewed the situation following the deluge in Nepal and asserted that the state government was prepared to deal with the flood situation.

The situation in Bihar comes amid devastating floods in neighbouring Nepal. According to an official update by Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), the death toll from the flash floods has reached 1,204.

The crisis began after a catastrophic flash flood struck the Tibet-Nepal border on August 26, sending a powerful surge of water, sediment and boulders through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems and causing widespread destruction.

As water levels continue to rise in Bihar, residents of vulnerable riverine areas have sought immediate relief, including food, drinking water, shelter and fodder for livestock. (ANI)

title: Why should the Nepal floods not be surprising ?
full_text:
By Dr. Portia B. Conrad

Kathmandu [Nepal], September3 (ANI): The latest incident of flash floods in Nepal has drawn the attention of the world towards the geologically fragile Himalayan region, which has been warming rapidly, experiencing glacier retreat, snowmelt and degradation of permafrost, which can remove the cement covering on the mountain slopes. In the 26 August 2026 incident, the evidence available so far points to a glacier/rock collapse and massive debris avalanche, rather than an ordinary monsoon flood. The glacier/rock mass destabilisation led to an ice-rock avalanche which in turn caused a temporary blockage/surge in the Bhote Koshi river. With the enormous debris flowing along the Bhote Koshi/Trishuli river, there was large-scale destruction in the lower reaches. The avalanche, which occurred in the high Himalaya near the Nepal-Tibet frontier, travelled downwards at the rate of 50 metres per second.

Nepal is today sitting on a "geological precipice". The Himalayas are among the youngest and most tectonically active major mountain systems on Earth. Nepal sits directly on the collision zone between the Indian and Eurasian plates which produces four overlapping vulnerabilities - Active tectonics, very steep topography, monsoon rainfall and rapidly changing glaciers. Active tectonics is a constant feature based on the push northward by the Indian plate beneath Eurasia, thus producing earthquakes, fractured rocks, fault zones, extremely steep slopes and frequent landslides and rockfalls. The 2015 earthquake in Nepal demonstrated the interaction dramatically.

Research following the 2015 earthquake found that earthquake-triggered landslides were the principal mechanism damaging hydropower infrastructure, and estimated that about 25% of existing, constructed and planned Himalayan hydropower projects had high probabilities of moderate-to-severe earthquake damage. This brings into question the viability of various projects, including hydro projects being undertaken in the region with the help of Chinese companies. The Rasuwa border region is marked by the presence of large number of Chinese construction companies which are involved in numerous projects turning the green belt into a maze of white rock and cement feature, without any consideration for the surrounding flora and fauna and the geological damage these can cause.

Moreover, the extremely steep topography in the region has led to enormous elevation differences over very short horizontal distances. A river can descend thousands of metres through a narrow valley, and once a large volume of water, ice and rock enters such a valley, it becomes an extremely efficient natural chute. There are several river pathways in the region, that pass through very high mountain walls that are virtually hugging each other. Any glacial outburst in the region can thus lead to a massive rush of mud, ice and stones causing severe destruction to nature and any physical features on the way.

The heavy monsoon rainfall further saturates already-fractured slopes and weakens the soil at certain locations thereby enhancing the threat level of landslides and downward flow of water, rocks and soil. Therefore, Nepal's landslides identify a combination of steep slopes, geological weakness, intense rainfall, river erosion and land-use changes as major drivers.

The rapidly changing glaciers is the new and increasingly important variable. Glaciers are retreating and the high-altitude environment is becoming less stable. Nepal has thousands of glacial lakes, some of which have the potential to produce catastrophic Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOF). A tracking of the incidents of glacial outbursts and flash floods in the region indicates that the August 26 incident should not be a surprise. On the contrary, more such instances could be anticipated in the coming times.

A look at the number of such incidents that have taken place indicates that their frequency has gone up several folds in recent times as climate change and heating of the high mountains increasingly become a regular feature. There have actually been more than 100 documented flood-related events in Nepal since 1954, according to a reconstruction of Nepal's flood history published recently. These include GLOFs, cloudbursts, landslides and major river floods.

Geologists have warned about the vulnerability of the Rasuwa/Bhote Koshi access since the 2025 floods in the region. They had accordingly suggested that enough preparations need to be made to deal with any such eventualities. The region has also seen large-scale construction by Chinese companies. As one drives towards the Rasuwa crossing on the Nepali side, one can see a change in the landscape from the lush green forest and pine trees to a wide patch of rocks and quarries with heavy construction equipment spread across. Most of these construction projects are undertaken by Chinese companies who operate freely in the area using Chinese heavy vehicles without registration plates. The local offices of these Chinese companies are clearly marked on the rock walls alongside the road and one can see Chinese engineers and senior company officials moving about in their facilities 5 to 10 kms inside Nepal.

While construction of bridges, roads , tunnels and hydro projects is a necessity, at the same time construction of any kind in these areas leads to cutting mountain slopes, removing vegetation, blasting rock, excavating tunnels, dumping spoil, altering drainage and narrowing river corridors besides creating large concrete structures in the valleys. Research on Nepal has found that construction related cut slopes account for a substantial proportion of landslides, and that poorly planned roads can dramatically increase landslide risk.

China has been constructing several projects in Tibet which would cause significant change in the geological matrix of the Tibetan plateau. Some of the projects which are along the Nepal-China border in the high Himalayas, which could cause serious damage to nature and the geological features are :

--Girong-Rasuwagadi corridor - on the Chinese side, the project involves logistics and highway infrastructure, while on the Nepal side the project is marked by the Syaphrubeshi-Rasiwagadi highway and Timure border facilities;

--Zhangmu-Tatopani project - the traditional China- Nepal highway project connecting Kathmandu to Tatopani and includes port facilities;

-- Korala-Mustang project - border infrastructure along Lomangthang/Burang which aims to open western Nepal to Tibet;

-- Burang - Hilsa road and border facilities - This involves Burang border facilities on the Chinese side and Hilsa-Simikot road and Hilsa bridge on the Nepal side. The project aims to open western Nepal to Tibet;

--Kerung/Rasuwa- Kathmandu project - involves construction of highway and logistic network connecting Nepal with Tibet and involves significant tunnelling, such as the Tokha-Chhahre tunnel;

--Kamathanka project - a network of road structure on the Tibetan side which will form the Kimathanka-Khandbari/Koshi corridor aiming to connect Eastern Nepal with Tibet

-- Power connectivity - Several power connectivity projects being considered including the Ratmate-Rasuwagadhi-Kerung 400-kv transmission proposal;

-- Railway - Shigatse-Gyirong railway project under development - Nature's challenges being confronted and hence moving slow.

-- Gyirong - Kathmandu railway project - this is a proposed China- Nepal cross border railway with the aim of having a direct Tibet-Kathmandu connection;

Besides the above projects, which have a direct cross border connect between Tibet and Nepal and involve mass scale construction work causing serious ecological damages in the high Himalayas, China is also undertaking several projects along the Tibetan lower plateau which would have an impact on the mountain ranges with a ripple effect on Nepal over a period of time. Some of these projects are : Yarling tsangpo/Medog hydropower, Sichuan- Tibet railway project, Xinjiang - Tibet Railway project, G 219 Western highway, G 318 and associated Himalayan tunnels, Medog-Zayu connectivity, Yadong/Sikkim connectivity and the Chinese border settlements along Arunachal Pradesh, Bhutan and Sikkim.

All of these projects require cutting into mountains, blasting, removing vegetation, dumping excavation rock, alerting natural drainage, constructing bridges and retaining structures, drilling through unstable geological formations etc. A major landslide high above in the mountains can cause landslides and river blockage. This in turn will cause temporary lake formations at very high altitudes, which when breached can cause flash floods. China's massive railway and highway projects have increasingly caused serious damage to nature in the mountains, especially due to the long kilometres of tunnelling which cause intersecting geological faults, change ground water movement, destabilise rock masses, drain or redirect underground water and weaken slopes above tunnel portals.

On the Tibet-Nepal axis, the scale and importance of the Gyirong (Tibet) - Rasuwagadhi (Nepal) corridor is the most consequential, and its scale of importance became particularly obvious during the August 2026 disaster as the flood devastated the Gyirong/Rasuwagadhi corridor and temporarily cut the principal China-Nepal land connection. The Gyirong-Rasuwagadhi corridor is particularly ecologically sensitive, not because the road automatically causes floods or glacier collapses, but because construction takes place in an exceptionally steep, seismically active and hydrologically unstable Himalayan environment.

There is already a strong warning from Nepal's Langtang National Park management plan that the Syaphrubesi-Rasuwagadhi road passes along the Bhote Koshi within the park, and the plan specifically identifies risks of habitat fragmentation and impacts during construction. Animal conservationists mention of rare animals such as the red panda, Himalayan black bear, snow leopard, Assamese macaque and other forest and high altitude species being endangered as a result of these projects.

One of the major potential ecological interventions by China in Tibet is the Yarlung Tsangpo mega project. China has already started the construction process in the great bend of the Yarlung Tsangpo in Medog. The site is marked by an extraordinarily deep gorge, enormous elevation gradient, active tectonic environment, very steep slopes, glaciers and unstable rocks and having exceptionally heavy rainfall in the region. The geological concerns are particularly serious as the area is seismically active. While climate change is bound to destabilise high altitude rock and ice and increase the potential for floods, landslides and avalanches, construction of tunnels, roads, dams, hydro projects, settlements only act as risk multipliers.

Another important issue is that of hydropower projects which are potentially more consequential than the roads. Nepal is undergoing an enormous hydropower build-out. Chinese capital as well as Nepali investment are involved. The problem is that hydropower development as well as construction of roads and tunnels naturally tends to take away the crucial space meant for nature in its own surroundings, and further narrows down the path of water flow making the impact piercing and damaging. Infrastructures in narrow valleys, steep slopes and along major rivers are indeed geological fault zones. That is almost the perfect combination for cascading disaster.

While these projects would have to be implemented looking at the larger issue of energy generation and potential for Nepal to emerge as a major energy producer and supplier, there is need for a combined effort by the international community to assess the prevailing challenges that the Himalayas face. This would require mandatory cumulative environmental-impact assessments for entire river basins, geological assessment before road/tunnel construction, much stricter controls on mountain - slope cutting, comprehensive glacier and permafrost monitoring. There should also be real-time GLOF warning systems in place and cross border sharing of satellite, hydrological and seismic information.

There is also need to ensure that there is no major infrastructure in identified avalanche/debris - flow corridors and independent safety audits of existing hydropower projects should be carried out. Nepal should take the lead in assessing the projects in a cumulative manner to examine their viability at a particular location given the fragile play of nature. The Kathmandu based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) could be involved in setting up an advanced Himalayan disaster-warning mechanism, while India can work closely with Nepal in this sphere considering India lies downstream from all these Himalayan rivers and would inevitably get affected by the ecological disasters that occur in these mountains.

The world cannot let Nepal deal with these challenges alone and this has been brought out clearly by the Prime Minister of Nepal Balendra Shah, who declared on 2 September 2026 that "climate change is the world's shared responsibility, and that Nepal must forcefully campaign for climate justice and international financial compensation rather than simple post-disaster aid". During his address to the House of Representatives, he linked the recent catastrophic flash floods in Rasuwa directly to warming climate, framing it as a warning for the entire Himalayan region and global civilisation. title: Two Australians found alive in Nepal flood disaster
full_text:
Two Australians have been found safe as officials work around the clock to locate those missing. Photo: AP PHOTO

Survivors of the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster face an uphill battle in contacting loved ones, an aid worker says, as workers were pulled alive from a hydropower tunnel.

It comes after Australian authorities on Friday confirmed two citizens had made contact overnight, bringing the number of missing Australians to 36.

As the search for the remaining survivors continues, Australian Red Cross head of migration Nicole Batch said infrastructure damage was posing a major challenge.

The missing Australians are among more than 5000 people unaccounted for after the deadly floods. (EPA PHOTO)

Interruptions to mobile networks, intermittent power and collapsed bridges and roads meant fewer opportunities to make contact, added to a surge in demand.

"The collapse of bridges, the poor road access - all of these elements will be making it difficult for people to travel quickly," Ms Batch said.

"The scale of the disaster and the number of people that are trying to make contact - that is one challenge in itself."

Ms Batch, who specialises in locating missing people following disasters, said reaching loved ones was almost always the first thing survivors tried to do.

But many likely lost their phones during the floods or else were limited in their ability to use them due to power or mobile network blackouts.

State-owned provider Nepal Telecom announced on Thursday services had been fully restored to disaster-hit regions, after being progressively brought back online.

But it followed days of coverage challenges and ongoing capacity strain, added to more immediate infrastructure roadblocks.

It comes as rescue efforts continue for the hundreds of workers feared trapped in underground power stations damaged or obscured by the floods.

Melbourne-based engineer and geologist Arnold Dix, who is advising Nepalese authorities on the rescues, said there was no test case for their work.

"It's like solving a puzzle you can't see."

He is advising on the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, where rescuers reportedly pulled two workers alive from a tunnel on Friday, nine days after the floods began.

Melbourne-based engineer Arnold Dix is advising Nepalese authorities on the rescues. (James Ross/AAP PHOTOS)

The rescues have been reported on local television news channels and by Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane on Facebook, AP reported.

Speaking hours before the reports surfaced, Mr Dix told AAP he had received word members of the Nepali army had heard voices inside the tunnel.

"When you're exhausted, sometimes your mind plays trick on you ... but once rescuers hear there might be someone alive ... this spurs you on," he said.

More than 1200 people have died and 5000 are missing since a glacier collapse brought flash flooding to towns and valleys along the border region.

The federal government has sent 19 officials and disaster response specialists to the region, with another 23 to be deployed within days.

Penny Wong says the government is holding on to hope, despite grave concerns for those missing. (Michael Errey/AAP PHOTOS)

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spoke with his Nepalese counterpart on Friday, offering Australia's deepest condolences. "The loss of life and destruction is devastating, and we will keep doing everything we can to find the Australians still unaccounted for," he wrote on X.

On Thursday, Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirmed local authorities would conduct searches in areas where many Australians were believed to have been staying.

Rescue teams from the Nepali army were expected to search those target areas identified by Australia on foot, with helicopter and drone support.

DFAT is working with local authorities to establish the whereabouts and welfare of affected Australians and to contact next of kin where appropriate.

Disaster response specialists will use drone technology in the search for missing Australians. (HANDOUT/Fire Rescue NSW)

Aid supplies aboard a Royal Australian Air Force plane arrived in Kathmandu on Wednesday.

More than 1400 hygiene kits, 2200 solar lights and phone chargers were among the items.

Australians have donated more than $4 million to the Emergency Action Alliance to support recovery efforts.

The federal government will provide a further $3 million to match public donations, bringing the ongoing humanitarian support package to a total of $11 million.

Australian Associated Press

title: Omaha Nepalese community feels impact of deadly floods
full_text:
OMAHA, Neb. (WOWT) - More than 1,200 people are confirmed dead and more than 4,000 remain missing following floods near the Nepal-China border, according to the United Nations.

Members of Omaha’s Nepalese community are hoping for good news about family and friends still unaccounted for.

Community leaders wait for updates

Yadu Sapkota, president of the Nebraska Nepalese Society, said the wait for information continues more than a week after the floods hit.

“Today is the ninth day, still family members are waiting, maybe. They hope that they will be back,” Sapkota said.

Sapkota is waiting for an update on a childhood friend and his middle school teacher. No one has heard from them since the floods.

Flooding described as sudden

The U.S. Geological Society said the speed of the water combined with 30-foot waves washed out towns within minutes.

Subash Baniya, healthcare coordinator with the Nebraska Nepalese Society, said the flooding caught people off guard.

“That wasn’t something that people were anticipating or like anything like that, because it happened out of nowhere,” Baniya said.

UNL student reflects on nearby hometown

Sandeep Sharma, a Ph.D. student at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and president of the Nepalese Student Association at UNL, was born in Nuwakot, nine miles from the flood site.

“You really can’t not look at all of those, like, videos or not feel for the families that have had their family members missing or look at their stories and see how difficult it is,” Sharma said.

Society organizes relief efforts

The Nebraska Nepalese Society has created GoFundMe pages, reposted flyers for missing people and spread awareness about Nepal this week.

“I think one of the biggest things that we have seen in a crisis like this is how different communities and people from all over the world have really come together to help people in need of this crisis,” Sharma said.

“It has been a really humbling experience for all of us because there are different communities, different people really trying their best in order to help and support these victims and the families impacted,” Sharma said.

title: Nepal Flood Toll Tops 1 , 270 as Symbolic Funerals Begin ; No Tunnel Survivors
full_text:
At Pashupatinath temple in Kathmandu, families gathered Wednesday to perform a ritual that Nepali Hindu tradition reserves for those whose bodies cannot be recovered. They cremated effigies woven from kush grass — surrogate bodies representing the souls of the missing — and performed the rites of death for people they cannot confirm are dead. One week after a glacier collapsed on the Nepal-Tibet border and sent a wall of ice, rock and mud through Himalayan valleys, this is what grief looks like when there is no body to bring home.

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority confirmed Wednesday that the death toll from the August 26 disaster has risen to at least 1,252 on the Nepali side alone, with the combined toll across Nepal and China surpassing 1,270. Some 4,216 people remain missing across both countries, while nearly 12,000 have been rescued. The United Nations has described the event as Nepal's worst natural catastrophe since the April 2015 earthquake, which killed approximately 9,000 people. The NDRRMA called it "not just a flood — a Himalayan climate disaster that came without warning."

The kush grass effigies — dressed, garlanded and carried to the river steps — served as proxies for a goodbye that the flood had denied thousands of Nepali families. Among those mourned Wednesday was Bishi Pandey, 48, whose body remains missing; his relatives wept through the smoke at Pashupatinath as the effigy burned in his place. The ceremonies continued through the morning as helicopters carried more bodies from Rasuwa district to Kathmandu, and morgues already past capacity struggled to hold what the river kept returning.

The most consequential development from Wednesday's operations was the conclusion of search work at the Rasuwagadhi hydropower facility in Rasuwa district — the last of eleven sites where active searches had been under way. An army team accompanied by engineers and a drone unit entered the 111-megawatt facility's tunnel system, advanced to its innermost section and flew a drone through the full interior. The prime minister's secretariat confirmed no one was found inside. Approximately 897 workers across all eleven projects remain out of contact, with roughly 500 believed to have been inside tunnel systems when the surge struck. At the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project alone, at least 576 people are missing, with approximately 300 believed trapped inside the tunnel. Rescue crews have used controlled explosives to clear boulders while simultaneously pumping water from the shafts. Vertical drilling — boring down from the mountain's summit to pierce the top of the powerhouse — remains under examination where frontal access stays blocked. The tunnel at Trishuli 3A runs more than four kilometers; Indian and Chinese tunnel specialists continue working alongside Nepali army engineers at the most critical remaining sites.

Six days after the disaster, survival conditions inside sealed shafts are increasingly in doubt. The head of the Independent Power Producers' Association said publicly that some workers may have suffocated. One survivor estimated roughly 1,000 people had been working across nearby projects the morning the flood struck, with only about 100 making it out. Another described gripping ceiling rungs for six hours as water rose in the darkness, passing a tin sheet between colleagues as the group inched toward the exit. By the time they emerged, the flood had claimed their clothing. His brother-in-law remained among the missing — his pregnant wife waiting at home. What began as a rescue operation is, at most sites, now being managed as a recovery mission in all but official terminology.

In Chitwan district, nearly 200 kilometers downstream from the disaster's origin, mass burials continued in the Devghat forest area of Bharatpur Metropolitan City. Hundreds of graves were prepared along trails that until recently served as morning walking paths. Before each burial, DNA samples, photographs and fingerprints were collected, and precise location coordinates were recorded so remains could be matched and exhumed if families came forward. A forensic team from India is assisting in the identification process. In Chitwan alone, 233 bodies had been recovered from riverbanks in the initial days, with only four identified before mass burial preparations began. Nepal's foreign minister said refrigerated storage for decomposed remains was urgently needed and had been formally requested from foreign governments without confirmed commitment.

Across the disaster zone, survivors are improvising in conditions that relief workers describe as among the most logistically complex they have encountered. At Devighat in Nuwakot district, hundreds of displaced residents gathered at a temporary relief camp Wednesday to receive utility supplies — the modest inventory of tarpaulins, rice sacks and clothing laid out on blue sheets in an open field representing, for many, everything they now own. Elsewhere in Nuwakot, flood survivors grip a makeshift cable above the swollen Trishuli river as Nepali soldiers and residents pull them hand over hand to the opposite bank — a zip line strung between the ruins of what was once a bridge. In Trishuli Center, the turquoise house that locals have taken to calling the "miracle house" stands almost intact amid a landscape of gray sludge, the only structure in its immediate surroundings that the flood left whole. The family inside survived as the water destroyed everything around them.

The China-Nepal border crossing at Gyirong — the primary land route between the two countries, handling roughly a third of bilateral trade — was destroyed entirely in the initial surge. Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported Wednesday that the road to the border has been largely reopened after excavators carved a new route along the riverbank. Chinese rescue teams continue searching for survivors on the Tibetan side, where at least 16 people have died and 546 remain missing. The avalanche of ice and rock reached the Gyirong Port complex within six to seven minutes of the initial collapse — catching pilgrims, traders and hydropower workers simultaneously in their most exposed positions along the valley. The August 26 collapse struck at the peak of the pilgrimage season on the Kailash Mansarovar route, which draws tens of thousands of travelers through Rasuwa district and across the Gyirong crossing each year.

Among the missing are approximately 583 foreign nationals on the Nepali side alone. Australia confirmed Wednesday that five previously listed nationals have been found safe, reducing its missing count from 43 to 38. Approximately 80 Americans, 53 Ukrainians, 51 Malaysians, 33 British nationals and 32 Canadians remain unaccounted for. Three American families have described searching publicly for parents on a Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage who have not made contact since the morning of August 26. Malaysia's prime minister pledged a rescue team and $1 million in aid. Singapore dispatched a police rescue team alongside humanitarian supplies. The United Nations estimates 65,000 people require urgent emergency water, sanitation and hygiene support. More than 22,000 children have been identified as requiring protection services. Nepal has deployed approximately 30,000 security personnel across relief operations, and the UNDP estimates the disaster generated more than 2.4 million tons of debris across five affected districts — Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan.

A rapid hazard assessment by an international scientific consortium raised serious questions about whether the disaster could have been anticipated — and whether workers could have been evacuated in time. Analysis of pre-event satellite imagery revealed visible signs of instability in the days before the collapse, including brown meltwater discharge and cracks forming in surrounding bedrock. Researchers noted that water within the affected glacier appeared to accelerate measurably before the final collapse. The findings call for improved early warning systems and cross-border data sharing between Nepal and China, as well as risk protocols extending beyond the immediate perimeter of infrastructure project boundaries. That the same river corridor had flooded catastrophically just fourteen months earlier, killing nine people, makes the absence of enhanced monitoring especially difficult to defend in retrospect.

The glacier responsible sits within a system that has been deteriorating for decades. The Langtang Valley has lost more than 40 percent of its glacier volume since 1815, with the pace of loss accelerating sharply in recent years. The high-mountain zone above 4,000 meters is warming significantly faster than the global average. Permafrost that once bound rock, ice and glacial mass together for millennia is weakening, increasing the likelihood of sudden, catastrophic detachments. Nepal's Prime Minister stated publicly there is no doubt climate change contributed to the disaster. In a region where hydropower investment has expanded rapidly over the past two decades precisely because meltwater resources appeared abundant and predictable, the August 26 collapse now tests the foundational assumptions of that development model. China's Ministry of Water Resources has warned that glaciers surrounding the impact crater may still be unstable, and a barrier lake of approximately 14,000 square meters upstream remains under active monitoring. With Nepal's monsoon season continuing through September, compounding risk to already-saturated riverbanks remains a live concern.

At Pashupatinath, the smoke from the kush grass pyres drifted over the Bagmati river as more families arrived through the afternoon — each carrying an effigy for someone the flood had taken without leaving a body behind.

title: Two Australians found alive in Nepal flood disaster
full_text:
Two more Australians have been found safe in the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster, but grave concerns remain for the 36 still missing.

The two Australians, who had been uncontactable, have confirmed they are safe and do not require consular assistance.

It brings the number of Australians found since the catastrophic floods began on August 26 to seven, after five were confirmed safe on Wednesday.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the update would bring relief to their families, but the federal government remains concerned for those still missing.

“That would be a huge relief to the loved ones of these two Australians who have been located,” Dr Chalmers said on ABC News Breakfast on Friday.

“But we still have very serious concerns for the 36 Australians that we haven’t been able to locate yet.”

More than 1200 people have died since a glacier collapse near Nepal’s border with Tibet triggered devastating floods across towns and valleys.

The three dozen Australians still missing are among more than 5000 people unaccounted for, according to the latest count from Nepali authorities.

The federal government has sent 19 officials and disaster response specialists to the region, with another 23 to be deployed within days.

On Thursday, Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirmed local authorities would conduct searches in areas where many Australians were believed to have been staying.

Rescue teams from the Nepali army were expected to search those target areas identified by Australia on foot, with helicopter and drone support.

“I can indicate that after our inquiries that Nepali authorities have advised us that searches are being conducted in the locations identified by Australia, including (The Kailash Hotel) and the Royal Himalaya Hotel amongst others,” Senator Wong told reporters.

Australian drone operators and incident management specialists would be sent to the region along as part of a broader on-the-ground support team.

The 15-person Australian Disaster Assistance Response Team will use advanced drone technology for real-time imagery and geospatial information and mapping of affected regions, where transport routes and critical infrastructure remain severely damaged.

The technology has AI capabilities that can help find victims, along with thermal imaging to identify trapped victims through heat sources.

DFAT is working with local authorities to establish the whereabouts and welfare of affected Australians and to contact next of kin where appropriate.

Nepali authorities will also be given telecommunication data to help narrow the last known location of missing Australians.

“We continue to work around the clock to ascertain as much information as we can and provide it to the families of missing Australians,” Senator Wong said.

“We all hold on to hope, and we’ve got to hold on to hope.”

Aid supplies aboard a Royal Australian Air Force plane arrived in Kathmandu on Wednesday.

More than 1400 hygiene kits, 2200 solar lights and phone chargers were among the items.

Australians have donated more than $4 million to the Emergency Action Alliance to support recovery efforts.

The federal government will provide a further $3 million to match public donations, bringing the ongoing humanitarian support package to a total of $11 million.

title: India to provide DNA profiling to identify Nepal flood victims
full_text:
New Delhi: To facilitate the identification of mortal remains of Nepal flood victims, the Centre will make available the services of central and state-level forensic labs for DNA profiling of their first-degree biological relatives in India, the MEA said on Thursday, September 3.

First-degree biological relatives residing in India, i.e. father, mother, son, daughter or sibling, may have their biological samples collected and DNA profiles prepared at Central Forensic Science Laboratories (CFSLs); State Forensic Science Laboratories (SFSLs); laboratories of the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU); and NABL-accredited laboratories having DNA profiling capability, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said in a statement.

The death toll from last week’s flash floods in Nepal has risen to at least 1,259 after rescue workers recovered more bodies from affected areas, according to Nepalese authorities.

While emergency teams have rescued more than 12,000 people, roughly 5,000 remain missing as search and rescue operations continue.

Also Read Death toll rises to 1,252 in Nepal amid threats of fresh floods

In a press statement on Tuesday, the Embassy of India in Kathmandu outlined the information available regarding the procedures for identification of mortal remains of the August 26 flash flood victims, the MEA said.

The MEA also shared a list of government forensic science laboratories having DNA profiling facilities.

“As advised by the Nepal Police, Autosomal STR DNA profiling may be undertaken for the purpose of identification, subject to the technical requirements communicated by the Nepali authorities. The helpline number in this regard is: +977 9841 6160 95,” it said.

Once prepared, the DNA profiles, along with the preliminary information required by the Nepali authorities, may be sent by email — dnacodis@nepalpolice.gov.np — for comparison with DNA profiles obtained from unidentified mortal remains, the statement said.

For facilitation and coordination by the Embassy of India, Kathmandu, a copy of the DNA profile may also be sent to eoikathmandufloodsupport@gmail.com, it said.

The flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal, leaving a trail of destruction.

title: Nepal floods : In Nepal , hope gives way to grief with few counting on miracles

Dawa Yangji Tamang is mourning the loss of her son, her daughter-in-law and her grandchildren in the Tibetan flood.

In the village of Thulo Bharkhu, families mourn the loved ones lost, even as relatives of the Australians missing after the floods continue their desperate search.

Thulo Bharkhu, Nepal: It is the first day of Buddhist mourning in the heartbroken village of Thulo Bharkhu, and a grandmother is weeping by two photos she has fixed to her dresser. They show Santu Tamang, the only one of her six children to attend university, dressed sharply in a blazer, smiling beside his wife, Pasang. In the other frame, Yanin, 3, is sitting rugged up against the cold, his little sister, Bhechen, cosied between his legs. On paper, they are missing, but Dawa Yangji Tamang, 66, knows they are dead. Too many days have passed now. Nepalese rescuers sifting the river banks and obliterated villages along the Trishuli River are finding body parts, not survivors. So Dawa lights candles under photos from the family’s recent holiday to the capital, Kathmandu, and cries. “I have lost my will to live,” she says. Dawa Yangji Tamang says she has lost the will to live after the deaths of her family members. Kate Geraghty Thulo Bharkhu village, built onto a mountainside in Nepal’s stunning Himalayas, lost 22 sons and daughters on Wednesday last week when a glacial collapse near the border with Tibet sent an inland tidal wave tearing down the Trishuli River.

The Ghewa ceremony being carried out for bus driver Karma Waleya Tamang, who is believed to have died while ferrying passengers back from the Tibet border. Kate Geraghty Residents of Thulo Bharkhu, a hamlet that lost 22 people in the floods, pray for their deceased loved ones even as the search continues to recover their bodies. Kate Geraghty The dead had been working out of town along the river corridor, providing for their families. Those families, 12 households in total, are now performing the first of what will be a year-long series of rituals to send their loved ones peacefully to the next life. Ordinarily, the bodies would have been cremated soon after death. Families mourn their own, then go up the street to help other families mourn theirs. No one is talking about miracles. The rituals mark an acceptance, and they are accepting together. They serve calorific cups of a local tea made with salt, wildflower and yak butter. In Tamang culture, when people eat at funeral rituals, called Ghewa, they are also eating for the dead. The families, ever warm, insist everyone, including this masthead, eats and drinks their fill. Dawa’s son Santu, an engineer, was the pride of the family. For a time, he had even worked in Japan. When a job came up at the Rasuwagadhi hydro plant, one of many stations harnessing Nepal’s snow-fed rivers, he moved his family there. Santu’s relatives believe he died at work. Pasang and the children would have been taken at home.

Advertisement

Dawa was on a video call with the kids only the day before. They were chirping “amma”, she says – the Nepali word for grandmother. With luck, she will get their bodies. Nepal has called for international help with processing DNA and testing. For now, marked body bags are being buried in mass graves in Chitwan district. Some are going in ambulances and police buses. Anyone caught within a dozen vehicles behind will know because of the smell. Hundreds of bodies and parts have washed all the way into India. The ones recovered in Nepal are coming out of ruins or being picked out of the muddy banks. It’s possible thousands are buried under the freshly laid quicksand. Nepalese police carry bodies to a helicopter for a flight to Chitwan, where hundreds of disaster victims are being buried. Kate Geraghty A woman among destroyed buildings in Betrawoti, which was severely affected by the Nepal flash flood that has killed more than 1000 people. Thousands are still missing. Kate Geraghty The market town of Betrawoti has been swallowed up by a deluge of mud. Many of its buildings have been destroyed. Kate Geraghty Only at river level can you appreciate the volume of water the people were up against. Steep mountainsides at the narrow passes are sheared clean of any vegetation 50 metres above the present river level.

Advertisement

It will grow back. Bridges will be rebuilt, eventually. But the damage to villages such as Thulo Bharkhu will last. The pain extends beyond borders and ocean, linking this small, unknown village with a profound grief being felt on many shores. At the most recent count, 36 Australians are feared dead. Mendo Lapachi, who lost her brother and two sisters-in-law, speaks about her family and the flood as she prepares to hold the Ghewa ceremony. Kate Geraghty Destroyed buildings in Betrawoti. Kate Geraghty Chogyal Dorje Lama is holding a Ghewa for his wife, Pratima, his brother Thile and sister-in-law Chenku. All three were killed in Syabrubesi, about a kilometre away on the banks of the Trishuli. Chogyal’s wife, the deputy mayor, managed one final call to her husband as the river bore down. “She was saying, ‘My mother, my mother, mother,’” he says. It is the Nepalese equivalent of “my god”. Chogyal says it sounded like she was running. “Then the voice was gone,” he says. “That voice is still coming to my head. How can I forget?” He gazes mournfully at Pratima’s framed portrait resting low on a coffee table, recalling the community work she did for children and the elderly, how she was made to run for deputy mayor by insistent locals.

The couple were just about to try for a family. “Now, I am alone. So how to live?” Chogyal asks. Chogyal Dorje Lama sits near photos of his wife, Pratima Tamang, who was a nurse and deputy mayor of the local council. She was in an office building in Syabrubesi when the floods hit. Kate Geraghty Syabrubesi is best known as the starting point of the Langtang Valley trek. It is also a stopover for Hindu pilgrims on their way north to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash. Chogyal’s brother owned one of Syabrubesi’s hotels, the Royal Himalaya, and was probably inside with Chenku and guests as it was swept away about 9am. The hotel was fully booked with 70 to 80 people the night before the flood, Chogyal believes. At least four of the guests were Australians. Sydney’s Sreedharan Iyer, 53, his wife, Lakshmi, 49, and the couple’s two sons, Rishab, 23, and Rudhra, 20, were travelling as part of a group of 15 Australian pilgrims, most of whom stayed the night before the tragedy at the Hotel Kailash, close to the border. That hotel, too, was swept away. The pilgrims are part of a wider group of Australians caught up in the tragedy.

title: I am very happy : Wife rejoices after husband rescued alive from flood - hit hydropower project in Nepal

Kathmandu, Sep 4 (IANS) Laxmi Kumari Sah, wife of Sanjaya Sah, who was rescued from the tunnel of Nepal’s flood-hit Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project, is over the moon after her husband was rescued alive on Friday morning.

Sah was one of two people rescued by a joint team of the Nepal Army and Armed Police Force from deep inside the tunnel, which was damaged by last week’s deadly floods.

Sanjaya Sah, 30, a foreman employed at the project, hails from the southern district of Saptari. Along with him, Kabir Maharjan, 45, a supervisor in the Hydropower Automation section of the project, was also rescued alive.

“I am very happy about the rescue of my husband, and it has brought happiness to all my family members,” Laxmi told IANS in a brief conversation.

“I was at home when I heard about his rescue at around 8:30 a.m. It has brought immense joy to our family.”

She said she was heading to Kathmandu to meet her husband following his rescue. She said the last 10 days were very painful for her and her family.

Earlier, the Nepali Army said the two men were rescued following sustained efforts to reach those believed to be trapped inside the tunnel, which was affected by the deadly floods last week. The disaster has so far claimed 1,259 lives, while 5,053 people remained out of contact as of Thursday evening, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

“After 10 days of darkness, life has seen the light again. Two people have been rescued alive from inside the hydropower project tunnel at Trishuli-3A,” the Nepali Army said earlier in a social media post. “The rescue operation is underway.”

The successful rescue of the two men alive has revived hope that others believed to be trapped inside tunnels at several flood-affected hydropower projects could also be rescued alive.

The Independent Power Producers’ Association, an association of private-sector power developers, said on Thursday evening that as many as 945 people working in 11 hydropower projects affected by the floods remained out of contact.

To facilitate the identification of mortal remains of Nepal flood victims, the Centre will make available the services of central and state-level forensic labs for DNA profiling of their first-degree biological relatives in India, the MEA has said.

First-degree biological relatives residing in India — father, mother, son, daughter or sibling — may have their biological samples collected and DNA profiles prepared at Central Forensic Science Laboratories (CFSLs); State Forensic Science Laboratories (SFSLs); laboratories of the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU); and NABL-accredited laboratories having DNA profiling capability, the ministry said in a statement.

The death toll from last week's flash floods in Nepal has risen to at least 1,259 after rescue workers recovered more bodies from affected areas, according to Nepalese authorities.

While emergency teams have rescued more than 12,000 people, roughly 5,000 remain missing as search and rescue operations continue.

The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) also shared a list of government forensic science laboratories having DNA profiling facilities.

"As advised by the Nepal Police, Autosomal STR DNA profiling may be undertaken for the purpose of identification, subject to the technical requirements communicated by the Nepali authorities. The helpline number in this regard is: +977 9841 6160 95," it said.

title: Over 5 , 600 people still missing after Nepal flood , as death toll passes 1 , 200
full_text:
One week has passed since a catastrophic flood struck several communities in northern Nepal and part of Tibet, China. The confirmed death toll has risen to 1,280, while more than 5,600 people remain missing on both sides of the border. According to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), 1,252 bodies have been recovered. More than 2.5 million people who live downstream have been affected.

The disaster was not simply “natural,” but the product of the capitalist system, which has rendered Nepal’s masses defenseless against the consequences of climate change.

Soldiers rescue a worker from a tunnel at the Trishuli-3A hydropower project in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. [AP Photo/Nepal Army]

Thousands have been rescued, but many still listed as missing are presumed dead, trapped under rubble, swept into rivers, or buried beneath landslides. In the worst-hit parts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Chitwan, entire families have been erased; in some villages, only a handful of survivors remain.

With decomposition advancing in the humid monsoon heat and the risk of waterborne disease rising, authorities have resorted to mass burials. Some families have also held symbolic funerals for loved ones whose remains may never be found.

Burying her husband, Dolma Newar Tamang said, “We had to do this to set his soul free, so that he is at peace and happy wherever he is,” the Straits Times reported on September 2.

Homes, livestock, seed stocks, and tools were washed away in minutes. This material devastation is compounded by psychological trauma.

Thousands of survivors escaped the initial surge by scrambling up the steep valley sides into the surrounding mountains. Helicopter drops of rice, lentils, and tarpaulins have reached some locations, but the scale of need far outstrips what has been delivered. Medicine, clean water, and blankets are critically short, with night temperatures dropping and monsoon rains continuing; exposure and illness are mounting threats.

At present, rescue operations are focused on the ruins of hydropower projects, where hundreds of workers are trapped. For more than a week, rescue teams have been drilling, cutting, and pumping to reach these spaces, but progress is slow and dangerous, with the risk of secondary collapses and renewed surges. Every hour that passes reduces the chances of finding anyone alive.

The disaster has laid bare the bankruptcy of Nepal’s early warning system (EWS). An article published in the Kathmandu Post on September 2 said although Nepal invested in sensors and SMS alert infrastructure over the past decade, the system collapsed when it was most needed. Automated gauging stations in upper Bhote Koshi stopped functioning at 8:40 a.m. on August 26, just as the flood crossed the border from Tibet. The first SMS warnings to downstream communities were sent only after the surge was already racing through Rasuwa.

By the time the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology posted a public update that the upstream blockage had not fully drained, five hours had elapsed, and the worst destruction was already done.

A robust, multi-hazard EWS covering glacial lake outbursts, landslide-dammed lakes, and trans-boundary floods is entirely feasible with existing technology. But it requires sustained investment, cross-border data sharing, and a state that prioritizes the lives of workers and peasants over debt servicing and elite enrichment.

The Post cited research by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), which has identified 21 potentially dangerous glacial lakes in Nepal across the Gandaki, Koshi, and Karnali river basins, and mapped 2,070 glacial lakes in total. As temperatures rise, both the number and size of glacial lakes are increasing.

Nepal has endured repeated flood disasters. According to the Ministry of Home Affairs’ Nepal Disaster Report 2024, “A total of 9,886 small and large weather- and climate-related disaster incidents killed 1,173 people and incurred a total economic loss of NPR 6 billion [around $US40 million] between January 2020 and September 2022.” Yet the ruling class in Nepal has treated disaster preparedness with lethargy, not as a life-and-death imperative.

The hypocrisy of the imperialist powers is stark. The United States, Britain, the European Union, and Australia have pledged a combined total of around $16 million in aid for Nepal—a pittance compared to the billions they expend weekly on wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

Washington allocates trillions of dollars annually to its military machine and has spent more than $100 billion on its war against Iran—nearly 28,000 times the pittance it has pledged for Nepal’s flood victims.

The same technological arsenal deployed for destruction—satellite imagery, drone swarms, thermal sensors, AI-driven surveillance systems, and rapid-deployment engineering units—could within hours locate survivors trapped under rubble, map real-time landslide risks, and deliver food and medicine to villages cut off by floods. The US military can mobilize carrier strike groups, F-35 squadrons, and precision-guided missiles for war with Iran within hours. NATO floods Ukraine with artillery shells, reconnaissance drones, and real-time battlefield intelligence daily.

Yet for Nepal, the US has not dispatched a single rescue worker, a single field hospital, or a single heavy-lift helicopter dedicated to evacuation. For imperialism, the lives of Nepali workers and peasants are expendable.

As the World Socialist Web Site (WSWS) explained, the flash floods are a direct consequence of global warming, for which the major industrial powers bear primary responsibility. The United States, China, India, Russia and Japan account for nearly 60 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions. Nepal contributes less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet it stands on the front lines of climate catastrophe.

Nepal’s Prime Minister Balen Shah and his right-wing Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP)-led government are already facing criticism over both the failed early warning system and the disorganized and grossly inadequate rescue and relief efforts.

A statement released on Tuesday signed by 35 members of non-government organisations, including Amnesty International and a former Nepali Human Rights commissioner, declared that “the federal government has not been able to demonstrate [a] coordinated and responsible role in the search, rescue and relief distribution.” It said the “centralization of the process has meant that collected relief materials have not seen distribution in the initial days when the need was the greatest.”

The greatest fear of the ruling elite is that the flooding disaster will lead to a resurgence of mass opposition from below. The RSP rose to power following Nepal’s explosive “Gen Z” protests in September 2025. In the past year it has continued to impose the worsening economic crisis on working people, who have fallen deeper into poverty.

The catastrophe in Nepal demonstrates the incapacity of the ruling classes to address even the most basic requirements of the masses. A socialist movement of the working class, in alliance with the peasantry and poor, must be built to break the shackles of imperialism and build a society where technology serves human need rather than profit. Halting the destruction of the environment is inseparable from the fight against the capitalist system that is destroying it.

Devighat, were directly affected, while assessments at five others are ​ongoing, he said.Data ​from the Nepal Insurance Authority show the regulator has so far received 583 flood-related claims ⁠worth 25.87 billion Nepalese rupees ($171.13 million) as of August 31.Chakraborty said these ​figures largely reflect insured exposure rather than final claims, which will only be clear ​once detailed surveys are completed.Claims could rise further if repairs delay project commissioning, as some policies compensate developers for lost revenue resulting from postponed commercial operations, he said.Nepal's non-life insurance market is small by global standards. The country's 14 non-life insurers generated premiums of about 5.3 billion Nepali rupees ($35.06 million) during July-August, regulatory data showed, compared with 314 billion Indian rupees ($3.3 billion) written by Indian insurers during a similar period.The market is supported by domestic reinsurers Nepal ‌Re and Himalayan Re, alongside international players including India's GIC Re and Germany's Hannover Re.The floods could have lasting implications for insurance coverage of Himalayan infrastructure, four industry ​executives said.The Himalayan ​region faces severe risks from earthquakes ⁠and any future glacial floods, a senior U.N. official told Reuters this week."The recent mountain floods in South Asia may lead insurers to further review hydropower and infrastructure risks, particularly in highly exposed locations," said Benjamin Ng, power ​leader for Asia at Aon, an international insurance broker.Insurers may increasingly impose exclusions, lower sub-limits and narrow coverage, resulting in higher premiums and more selective underwriting, Ng said.Other recent Himalayan catastrophes include the 2023 glacial lake outburst flood in India's Sikkim and the flash flood in the northern Indian state of Uttrakhand in 2021.The latest floods could reshape industry views on risk accumulation and glacial lake outburst flood exposure, said Sanjay Mokashi, chief underwriting officer at Indian state-owned reinsurer GIC Re.

title: Clip shows mare rescue in Venezuela in 2024 , not in Nepal flood
full_text:
The devastating Himalayan glacial floods in Nepal and Tibet in August 2026 caused widespread destruction and mounting death tolls, but a video showing a mare being pulled out of a mudslide is not from the recent disaster. The footage actually depicts a rescue that took place in Venezuela in November 2024.

"A flood in Nepal accompanied by a landslide trapped a horse, but it miraculously survived and was rescued!" reads a Threads post in traditional Chinese shared on August 30.

The post includes a video showing an animal trapped in mud, with several people clearing dirt using tools before the animal is pulled out with heavy machinery.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The video was shared in Chinese on X with similar claims. It has also spread in English and Spanish across social media.

Screenshot of the false Threads post taken on September 3, 2026, with a red X added by AFP

At least 1,280 people have been killed and more than 5,500 missing after a gigantic wave of freezing water, rocks and debris wiped out entire settlements and carved a path of destruction across Nepal ( archived link).

Search and rescue teams are still carrying out operations despite difficult conditions and unstable terrain.

While there have been reports of animals pulled to safety after the deadly floods, the circulating video has no connection to the disaster (archived here and here).

Advertisement Advertisement

A reverse image search using keyframes from the clip led to a news report by UK outlet The Mirror on December 3, 2024 that published pictures showing the same scene ( archived link).

According to the report, the mare in the photos was trapped by a landslide-made hole in the city of La Grita, located in the northwestern state of Táchira, Venezuela, before firefighters pulled it to safety.

It also included several pictures credited to "@bomberosjaureguilagrita". A keyword search on Instagram found the account, run by the La Grita fire department, that published the pictures used by the report on November 17, 2024, along with other photos and a video showing the rescue ( archived link).

Screenshot comparison of the false Threads post (L) and the Instagram post published by the local fire department in La Grita on November 17, 2024

Other outlets -- including the UK-based What's The Jam website and El Diario -- also published visuals showing the rescue at the time (archived here and here).

The mare survived without major injuries.

AFP Fact Check has previously debunked other misinformation about the Tibet-Nepal flash flood.

title: India offers DNA profiling services for Nepal flood victim kin
full_text:
India is providing crucial forensic support by making central and state-level DNA profiling services available for first-degree relatives in India to help identify victims of the devastating Nepal flash floods.

IMAGE: A view of a home damaged and surrounded by thick mud and debris following flash floods, in Nuwakot, Nepal, September 2, 2026 . Photograph: ANI Video Grab

Key Points India is offering DNA profiling services through central and state forensic labs to identify Nepal flood victims.

First-degree biological relatives in India can submit samples for DNA profiling at designated laboratories.

The initiative aims to assist Nepal in identifying the missing after flash floods caused over 1,259 deaths and left 5,000 missing.

DNA profiles will be sent to Nepali authorities for comparison with unidentified mortal remains.

The embassy of India in Kathmandu is coordinating the facilitation of this identification process.

To facilitate the identification of mortal remains of Nepal flood victims, the Centre will make available the services of central and state-level forensic labs for DNA profiling of their first-degree biological relatives in India, the MEA has said.

First-degree biological relatives residing in India -- father, mother, son, daughter or sibling -- may have their biological samples collected and DNA profiles prepared at Central Forensic Science Laboratories (CFSLs); State Forensic Science Laboratories (SFSLs); laboratories of the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU); and NABL-accredited laboratories having DNA profiling capability, the ministry said in a statement.

India's Support for Victim Identification

The death toll from last week's flash floods in Nepal has risen to at least 1,259 after rescue workers recovered more bodies from affected areas, according to Nepalese authorities.

While emergency teams have rescued more than 12,000 people, roughly 5,000 remain missing as search and rescue operations continue.

In a press statement on Tuesday, the embassy of India in Kathmandu outlined the information available regarding the procedures for identification of mortal remains of the August 26 flash flood victims, the MEA said.

In this backdrop, and as an additional measure to facilitate the ongoing identification process, the Union ministry of home affairs has decided to make available the services of CFSLs, SFSLs and NFSU laboratories in India for "DNA profiling of first-degree biological relatives of persons who remain missing following the flash flood in Nepal", it said.

DNA Profiling Process and Coordination

The ministry of external affairs (MEA) also shared a list of government forensic science laboratories having DNA profiling facilities.

"As advised by the Nepal Police, Autosomal STR DNA profiling may be undertaken for the purpose of identification, subject to the technical requirements communicated by the Nepali authorities. The helpline number in this regard is: +977 9841 6160 95," it said.

Once prepared, the DNA profiles, along with the preliminary information required by the Nepali authorities, may be sent by email -- dnacodis@nepalpolice.gov.np -- for comparison with DNA profiles obtained from unidentified mortal remains, the statement said.

For facilitation and coordination by the embassy of India, Kathmandu, a copy of the DNA profile may also be sent to eoikathmandufloodsupport@gmail.com, it said.

The flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal, leaving a trail of destruction.

title: Nepal announces relief package for flood - hit businesses , plans settlement relocation
full_text:
Nepal's government has announced a special relief package for businesses hit by the devastating Bhotekoshi floods, offering concessions, loan restructuring and cheaper credit, as authorities began work on relocating settlements destroyed by the disaster.

The measures came as the government stepped up recovery efforts following the devastating floods, which swept away homes, roads and bridges in Nepal on August 26, leaving hundreds dead and thousands missing, with several settlements along the Trishuli riverbanks destroyed.

The Nepal Cabinet on Thursday described the business-related measures as the first phase of its recovery package, The Kathmandu Post newspaper reported.

Businesses whose commercial vehicles, transport equipment, plants, machinery, tools or other equipment were destroyed beyond repair or swept away will be allowed to import replacements without paying customs duties, the report said.

The concession will also apply to goods on which customs duties had already been paid but which were destroyed before reaching their destination. Replacement goods will have to be imported through any customs office within six months, it said.

Provincial and local governments will also be asked to provide temporary concessions on property and business taxes, building permit fees and other local charges for affected businesses and properties, the report added.

The government has directed Nepal Rastra Bank, the country's central bank, to facilitate restructuring or rescheduling of loans taken by flood-affected borrowers, it said.

The Insurance Authority has separately been asked to speed up claims by allowing insurers to deploy surveyors through simplified procedures. Insurers will be required to provide advance payments of up to 50 per cent of estimated losses based on preliminary assessments.

The relief measures come as authorities prepare a longer-term plan for communities whose homes and settlements were swept away.

The August 26 flood destroyed around 15 settlements across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, The Kathmandu Post reported.

The National Planning Commission (NPC) has begun work on a master plan to rebuild infrastructure, develop safer settlements and address longer-term development needs.

NPC vice-chair Gunakar Bhatta said the commission was also preparing a post-disaster needs assessment, which will examine damage and losses across infrastructure, productive sectors, services, the environment and the wider economy.

A preliminary assessment by Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) found that around 1.6 million people across 15 local units were directly affected, while 8,317 houses were destroyed, the report said.

The Ministry of Infrastructure Development will first focus on restoring roads and bridges connecting the affected areas before planning new settlements.

Ministry Secretary Gopal Prasad Sigdel said the long-term plan would be to relocate people away from flood-risk areas.

“The long-term plan will be to establish settlements in areas outside the flood-risk zones,” he was quoted as saying by The Kathmandu Post.

Authorities are mapping settlements that are no longer habitable while continuing rescue, relief and temporary shelter operations.

Around 3,948 people rescued by the government were staying at holding centres in Nuwakot, Rasuwa, Dhading and Kathmandu, the report said.

NDRRMA chief executive Dharmaraj Upreti said teams were identifying safer locations for displaced communities.

“People cannot return to settlements that have been swept away by the flood. The government has formed teams to identify safer locations and is working on a plan to relocate them,” he was quoted as saying by The Kathmandu Post.

Officials are considering moving some communities to other districts or finding safer vacant land within the affected districts.

The government has previous experience of relocating disaster-hit communities, including after the 1993 floods and the 2015 earthquake.

Experts have also urged authorities to consider livelihoods, social ties and future disaster risks while choosing new locations, the report said.

“There is a serious risk of major disasters in the Himalayan region from Taplejung to Darchula in the coming years,” former prime minister Baburam Bhattarai was quoted as saying by The Kathmandu Post.

“Safer areas should be identified nearby, such as small valleys in the mountains and higher ground in the hills, where at-risk settlements can be relocated,” Bhattarai said.

Meanwhile, Nepal's government has also announced support for personnel engaged in the rescue effort.

Government spokesperson and Education Minister Sasmit Pokharel said the Cabinet decided on Thursday to provide risk allowances and meal expenses to security personnel and government employees deployed for search and rescue operations following the Bhotekoshi flooding, Onlinekhabar news portal reported.

Those injured during the operations will receive free medical treatment, while families of personnel who die during rescue operations will receive NRs 1 million in relief, according to the report.

Published on September 4, 2026

title: Nvidia CEO donates $10 million for Nepal flood victims
full_text:
Nvidia CEO donates $10 million for Nepal flood victims

Kathmandu: Jensen Huang, Chief Executive Officer of US technology company Nvidia, has donated $10 million to Nepal’s Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund to support people affected by the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River basin in Rasuwa district, Nepal’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said.

In a video message, Wagle thanked Huang, Nvidia’s founder and CEO, for the contribution, which he said had helped push total donations to the Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund above NPR 10 billion ($66 million).

“On behalf of the government of Nepal, I’d like to express my sincere gratitude to Mr. Jensen Huang for donating $10 million to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund in aid of flood victims,” Wagle said in the video message. “I hope this sizable contribution, notable by any philanthropic standard, will inspire many others to also contribute to this noble cause.”

The death toll from the devastating Rasuwa floods has reached 1,259, while 5,053 people remain missing by Thursday evening, according to the latest situation report released by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

Since the deadly floods occurred last week, Nepal has been receiving various forms of assistance from several countries and agencies.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a social media post on Thursday evening that neighboring India had been providing all necessary forms of assistance from the first day in various phases.

“So far, India has provided 74 tonnes of relief and rescue materials in five phases. It has also been deploying expert teams to the affected areas for rescue operations,” he said.

China has provided Nepal with NPR 300 million and 50 tonnes of relief materials. In addition, the Government of Nepal has requested China to provide 30 Bailey bridges for the affected areas.

According to the Prime Minister, Pakistan is providing 86 tonnes of relief materials. Sri Lanka has pledged $1 million in assistance. Bangladesh is also preparing to send relief materials.

The United States has pledged $500,000 in assistance. Australia has pledged $1 million in cash assistance and is also preparing to send a team, including experts and drone operators, to Nepal soon.

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has already provided 83 tonnes of essential relief materials and pledged up to $10 million in assistance. Qatar has also provided 40 tonnes of relief materials, according to the Prime Minister.

The United Kingdom (UK) has announced 5 million pounds sterling in assistance. Similarly, the European Union’s Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (ECHO) has announced 2 million euro, Switzerland $1 million, Denmark 3.5 million Danish kroner, Germany $2 million, Ireland 500,000 euro, the Czech Republic 2.5 million Czech koruna, and Norway 12.7 million Norwegian kroner in assistance.

France has provided emergency relief materials for 200 households in the affected areas. Luxembourg and Latvia have also provided relief materials.

In addition, the World Bank has pledged $167 million in concessional loans, while the Asian Development Bank (ADB) has pledged $5 million in budgetary support (grant) and $150,000 in technical assistance.

title: India has sent 95 tonnes of relief material , 54 personnel to flood - hit Nepal : MEA
full_text:
New Delhi, Sep 4 (IANS) Continuing with its humanitarian assistance to Nepal, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) on Friday said that India has so far sent around 95 tonnes of relief material on seven aircraft, along with 54 personnel to support rescue and relief efforts following the devastating flash floods in the Himalayan nation.

Addressing a bi-weekly press briefing in New Delhi on Friday, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India would continue to extend assistance based on the requirements communicated by the Nepalese government, with plans to send additional forensic kits, Bailey bridges and other requested materials in the coming days.

"We will continue to provide assistance as per the requirements of the Nepal government. In the coming days, we plan to send more forensic kits, Bailey bridges and other materials that are requested by the Nepal government. Yesterday, we had two Indian aircraft flying to Kathmandu along with 21 tonnes of relief material. Till now, we have supplied around 95 tonnes of relief materials on seven aircraft. In addition to the relief material, we've also sent 54 personnel to support relief and rescue efforts in Nepal. This comprises 30 tunnel rescue experts, 19 forensic experts, and a five-member medical team. Our rescue and forensic teams are deployed on the ground, and they are working closely with the Nepalese authorities," said Jaiswal

Jaiswal further said that 275 Indian nationals are currently unaccounted for, while 1,907 Indian nationals have so far crossed safely into Nepal from China. He added that, according to official sources in China, no Indian travellers are currently stranded in the Tibet Autonomous Region.

We continue to be in close touch with the Nepali government, with the Ministry of Home Affairs here and the concerned state governments in India.
