title: Nepal floods : Indian volunteers take relief to isolated communities
full_text:
For nearly 20 members of a family in Trishuli, one room has become home after devastating floods destroyed homes, cut roads and left several families without basic amenities. A week on, Indian volunteers are travelling up to 10 hours through damaged mountain roads and bridges to take food, bedding and household essentials to such communities, while some areas of Rasuwa remain accessible only by helicopter.

The relief effort is increasingly shifting from accessible flood-hit areas to isolated settlements, where families have lost homes, livestock, belongings and livelihoods, but the terrain and damaged infrastructure make reaching them difficult.

“Almost a week after the floods, some of the more accessible areas are slowly seeing relief reach them, but our biggest concern now is reaching the families who have been most severely affected and remain isolated,” Manohar Naidu, a Khalsa Aid volunteer, told The Hindu from Nepal.

In Trishuli, Tupche and other remote communities, volunteers have found several families living together with little shelter or basic household equipment. Some, they said, have effectively lost everything.

Nepal flash floods: What caused the devastation?

The volunteers also described mass burials being carried out as mortuaries run out of space, with forest land being cleared to accommodate bodies as the death toll rises and many remain unidentified.

“Our immediate support is focused on essential relief such as food, clothing, bedding and basic household requirements. At the same time, we are assessing and documenting what each community will need for longer-term recovery,” Mr. Naidu said.

Reaching the affected communities has become a major logistical challenge. Some journeys from Kathmandu to areas such as Trishuli take nine to 10 hours, with damaged or completely washed-out roads and bridges forcing volunteers to take longer routes. Teams are travelling in trucks carrying supplies, while demand for 4x4 vehicles has surged, making them difficult to arrange and prompting suppliers to raise prices.

The problem is more acute in Rasuwa, where some affected areas have no road connectivity and helicopters are the only practical option. Each trip can cost around $2,000, significantly increasing the cost of delivering relief.

“So the challenge is not simply having relief material available. The biggest challenge is getting that aid to the families who need it most,” Mr. Naidu said.

The organisation is procuring supplies locally, but demand is outstripping availability for mattresses, solar lights and other household items.

“People need much more than food. They are asking how they are going to rebuild their lives,” Mr. Naidu said.

The next phase will require shelter, clean water and sanitation and getting children back into education, followed by restoring livelihoods and rebuilding homes, roads, bridges and community infrastructure.

Khalsa Aid had earlier proposed adopting inaccessible villages for longer-term support. The proposal is being assessed on the extent of damage, families affected, livelihood losses and infrastructure needs, with the aim of concentrating resources in severely affected communities rather than spreading assistance thinly.

The organisation is also considering temporary holding centres with mattresses, portable washroom facilities and cooking arrangements for families living together without basic amenities.

Ten Indian volunteers are currently involved in logistics, assessments, packing and distribution. Many have prior disaster-response experience, including during the recent Assam floods, but Nepal has posed added challenges of mountainous terrain, long journeys and limited electricity and internet connectivity.

The organisation has also sought official permission to clear debris in local areas to restore connectivity and ease access to affected communities.

title: Nepal - China Flood Death Toll Rises to 1 , 280 ; Over 5 , 200 Still Missing
full_text:
TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - The death toll from devastating flash floods along the Nepal-China border has risen to 1,280, while more than 5,600 people remain missing as search and rescue operations enter their second week.

As reported by Anadolu, Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority reported 1,259 deaths and 5,083 people still missing as of Thursday, September 3. The missing include 583 foreign nationals.

More than 21,400 security personnel have been deployed to affected areas as authorities continue searching for victims and delivering emergency assistance.

With many missing people presumed dead, some families in Nepal have begun holding symbolic funeral ceremonies for relatives whose bodies have not been recovered.

Families Hold Funerals for Missing Relatives

In Rasuwa, one of the areas hardest hit by the floods, families have created symbolic funeral effigies using kaas-kush, a type of sacred grass, to perform rituals intended to help release the souls of missing relatives.

The ceremonies were held as families increasingly lost hope of recovering the bodies of loved ones swept away by the floods, The Kathmandu Post reported.

On Wednesday, September 2, dozens of the effigies were cremated in a mass funeral ceremony at Pashupati Aryaghat, a cremation site on the banks of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu.

The rituals reflect the growing humanitarian and emotional toll of the disaster, with many families still unable to locate relatives more than a week after the floods.

In Chitwan, another badly affected district, authorities have cremated unidentified bodies after collecting DNA samples in an effort to preserve the possibility of future identification.

The scale of the disaster has made identifying and storing bodies increasingly difficult. In some districts, floodwaters swept away homes as well as family members, leaving survivors without suitable places to conduct funeral rites.

Families who have lost their homes and traveled to Kathmandu in search of shelter have also struggled to find adequate public facilities for traditional funeral ceremonies.

Search and Rescue Operations Continue

Meanwhile, military and police personnel continue search and rescue operations across flood-hit areas.

Their efforts have been hampered by damaged or severed roads, power outages and disruptions to communication networks. Rescue teams are also working to deliver humanitarian supplies and maintain sanitation at temporary shelters to reduce the risk of infectious diseases.

Anadolu also report that in neighboring China, authorities reported 21 deaths and 541 people missing, including 261 foreign nationals.

Together, the reported figures from Nepal and China bring the death toll to 1,280 and the number of missing people to 5,624.

The flash floods struck the Nepal-China border on August 26 after a glacier at an elevation of about 5,200 meters broke away from Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal.

The collapse triggered a massive flow of ice, rocks and debris that swept through valleys along the border.

The resulting flash floods and mudslides devastated Nepal's Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts before reaching the Kathmandu Valley. On the Chinese side, debris also buried the Gyirong border crossing in the southwestern part of the Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet.

Search teams remain deployed as authorities race to locate survivors, recover victims and provide assistance to communities whose homes and infrastructure were swept away by the disaster.

title: Nepalese Experts , Victims Contemplate the Future After the Flood
full_text:
Subash Tamang, rescued from the Bhotekoshi flood, is under treatment at Kathmandu Trauma Center; three of his family members are still missing. Credit: Sunita Neupane/IPS

KATHMANDU, September 4 (IPS) - That day, Subash Tamang was mining sand along the banks of the Trishuli River near the Trishuli Hydropower Project, working alongside his wife, brother, sister-in-law, and two other family members. Suddenly, he noticed water gushing down from above the hydropower site. His first thought was that the dam had burst.

In an instant, everything changed. He and his family dropped everything and ran toward the river, desperate to save their lives. But then he saw something even more terrifying—huge waves of water were surging from the other side too, carrying clouds of dust and thick black mud.

“I couldn’t make sense of what was happening,” he recalls. “It looked like a monster coming at us.”

He was holding his wife’s hand, trying to run toward the hill, when the flood swept him away—carrying him nearly 500 metres downstream. Helplessly, he watched as the same raging waters took his wife, his brother, his sister-in-law, and three other family members right before his eyes.

“I was holding her hand, and then the flood pulled her away,” he recalls.

His leg was broken in the disaster. An army helicopter later rescued him and brought him to Kathmandu, where he is now receiving treatment at the Trauma Center.

“Our village has been reduced to ruins,” he says. “I don’t know where to go after this.”

Dr Rijan Bhakta Kayastha, a professor at Kathmandu University, says the August 26 disaster started when a massive chunk of glacier and surrounding rock gave way at altitudes of about 5,200 to 1,200 metres above the Lhande River in Tibet, just across the border.

The falling ice and rock turned into a powerful slurry, sending a massive cascade of water, ice, and debris into the Lhande River in Tibet. That surge triggered a devastating flood that raced downstream through the Bhotekoshi River, causing immense destruction.

The death toll from the disaster in Nepal has climbed to 1,114, with 3,996 people still unaccounted for, according to recent government figures. Among the missing are Nepali Hindu pilgrims travelling to the sacred Kailash Mansarovar site in Tibet, as well as tourists from at least 39 countries.

Authorities have recovered bodies swept away by the floods from Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan, Gorkha, Tanahun, Nawalparasi East, and Nawalparasi West districts.

Dr Bijay Jaisi, Director General of the Department of Roads, said initial assessments show flood damage to roads and bridges alone exceeds 30 billion rupees. Around 80 km of roads have been washed away and another 40 km destroyed, while 35 concrete bridges have been damaged and 53 suspension bridges swept away.

The disaster has wreaked havoc on the region’s hydropower infrastructure: the Rasuwagadhi and Chilime projects have been destroyed, and at least 13 other hydropower projects under construction in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts have sustained significant damage. The Rasuwagadhi hydropower project was completely washed away by the flood.

Most Devastating Flood

“This is one of the deadliest disasters in Nepal’s modern history,” said Dharmaraj Upreti, executive director of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. “We have never faced a flood this devastating and widespread before.”

Such floods are not unique to Nepal. In 2015, a similar disaster is believed to have killed around 200 people. More recently, on July 8, 2025, a sudden outburst from a large glacial lake in Tibet sent a surge of water down the Lende River, sweeping away the Maitri Bridge at Rasuwagadhi and killing at least nine people. Just three weeks later, on July 30, the Bhotekoshi flooded again, damaging roads and other infrastructure along the same corridor, according to Binod Parajuli, a senior divisional hydrologist at Nepal’s Flood Forecasting Division.

Arun Bhakta Shrestha, an expert on climate change and Himalayan glaciers, describes it as a “mountain tsunami”.

Kayastha explains that the disaster was first thought to have been triggered by a glacial lake bursting. But satellite images showed something different: a large chunk of glacier on the Nepal side broke off and slid down. Below it lay what experts call a “debris-covered glacier”—a mix of ice and gravel. When that mass collapsed, the ice and its contents began to melt, releasing a surge of water from the glacial lake. Because the terrain below is extremely steep, the mixture raced downhill at high speed, scouring the land next to the river and quickly turning into a devastating flood.

According to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), research over 50 years of monitoring reveals that 89% of recorded years experienced a negative glacier mass balance. Crucially, the rate of glacier ice loss doubled post-2000 compared to the preceding decades.

Between 1990 and 2020, Hindu Kush Himalaya glaciers lost roughly 12% of their total area and 9% of their estimated ice volume, amounting to a cumulative loss of up to 27 metres of ice thickness since 1975.

Arun Bhakta Shrestha explained that rising temperatures are melting the glacier’s surface, allowing meltwater to infiltrate the ice. As this water percolates downward, it enlarges existing cracks and forms new fractures called crevasses.

“Crevasses are multiplying rapidly, and as more water pours into them, they grow both wider and deeper,” Sherstha said. “Meltwater moving through the glacier can reach the bedrock below, undermining large ice masses until they collapse. This is precisely the process we are witnessing now. Rising temperatures are hastening the expansion of these fissures.”

Kayastha said the crevasses on the glacier, which had persisted for several months, may have widened. He added that analysing satellite imagery could have helped minimise the damage, but the images were not reviewed.

Climate Change Reshaping Nepal’s High Mountains

Glaciologist Mohan Bahadur Chand warns that climate change is reshaping Nepal’s high mountains in ways that make new kinds of natural disasters more likely.

In recent years, he said, the landscape has become increasingly unstable. Snow once accumulated gently and settled low on the slopes. But as temperatures rise and glaciers retreat upslope, bare ground is becoming exposed. Sections of rock and ice are now left “hanging” precariously on mountain faces.

“It will fall one day or another,” Chand said. “We will see more such processes in the coming days.”

Three days after the flood, Ekat Bahadur Thapa stood at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu, pinning photographs of his son and nephew to the missing-persons board.

His son, 28-year-old Subindra Thapa, and his nephew, 33-year-old Resham Bahadur Thapa, were driving along the China–Nepal border that day. Thapa said they called to tell him they were ready to transport people from Nepal into China and that they would return home soon.

When news of the flood broke, Thapa tried calling his son, but the call wouldn’t connect. He told himself they must have found shelter on the Chinese side. Still, by evening, there had been no word from either of them. But as three days passed after the flood with no word from them, that hope began to fade.

He rushed from hospital to hospital across Kathmandu, desperately searching for survivors, but they were not there. He went to the rivers where bodies had been recovered, hoping against hope. “When they could not be found there either, he returned to his village with a heavy heart,” said Thapa, 58.

On Wednesday, eight days after they vanished, Thapa performed funeral rites according to Hindu tradition, believing the remains to be theirs.

Tears streamed down his face. “How hard it must have been for them,” he said, his voice breaking. “How many times they must have tried to escape.”

He said, “May their souls rest in peace, wherever they are.”

“The early warning system was delayed because we couldn’t detect the flood in time,” says Binod Parajuli, Senior Hydrologist at the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. “We were only able to act 15 minutes after the flood entered Nepal. By then, damage had already occurred in Rasuwa. When we finally sent out early warning messages to everyone, people assumed it wouldn’t be much worse than previous floods. But the damage ended up being far greater.”

Parajuli continued, “We couldn’t detect the flood early because it began outside our monitoring area. By the time it reached Nepal, we had very little time to respond. Our system sends SMS alerts when it detects rainfall, but this event did not begin with the kind of rain we normally monitor, making it difficult to issue timely warnings.”

He added that this represents a distinct form of cascading, compounding debris flow, and that early-warning systems for such events have not yet been developed.

Kayastha said that last year, when the flood struck, the area was considered highly vulnerable. The Nepal government was also advised to install an early warning system, which would not have been very expensive. The plan included installing two water-level sensors, a monitoring station and cameras in the field so that people could receive flood information more quickly.

“We couldn’t save the people in the upper reaches, but we were able to save those downstream,” says Rajendra Mishra, Secretary at the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment. “This flood taught us that simply sending out a message is not the same as an early warning.”

He said that it was important to understand exactly who and what was at risk. Only then can we build a system that observes hazards in real time, communicates alerts effectively, and prepares communities for emergencies. This flood was a warning: bigger floods could come again.”

“Many people also failed to take the early warning seriously,” said Professor Dr Ranjan Kumar Dahal, an engineering geologist and geohazard expert. “Warnings should be communicated in clear, simple language that everyone can understand.”

Disaster Awareness Should Start Young

He added that disaster awareness should also be included in school curricula from an early age so that people understand the risks and know how to respond. The process of risk communication must be better understood.

Manish Raj Pandey, head of climate change at the National Trust for Nature Conservation, said the region’s topography is a key factor. He said, “Glaciers and the lakes they form, together with low-lying wetlands, are expanding for a range of reasons. In Nepal, this mix of steep terrain, glaciers and glacial lakes increases flood risk. At the same time, rising temperatures driven by climate change are intensifying these hazards.”

“Nepal’s severe flooding is driven largely by high-mountain hazards—especially glacier and rock-ice avalanches—exacerbated by a warming climate that is destabilising ice, permafrost, and slopes across the Himalayas,” said Dr Basantraj Adhikari, director of the Center for Disaster Studies at Tribhuvan University’s Institute of Engineering.

“We can’t stop floods, but we can reduce the damage they cause,” Kayastha said. To do that, he said, glaciers and glacial lakes need round-the-clock monitoring, with dedicated staff appointed to watch them.

He said that the government should also install water-level measurement stations on rivers fed by these glaciers and set up an early-warning system. Field cameras can be placed at these stations to provide real-time data, and they’re not expensive to install.

“Adhikari said that as settlements continue to expand along riverbanks, local, provincial, and federal governments must enforce stricter monitoring. Local authorities, he added, should rigorously implement risk-sensitive land-use planning.

Kayastha elaborated, “Many riverside settlements are not in safe locations; this pattern is evident across Nepal. Going forward, the siting of new settlements must be carefully assessed.”

Nandalal Gharti lies in the intensive care unit at the Trauma Centre with severe injuries. That morning, he was working at the customs yard in Timure when he saw the crowd running. He grabbed his youngest son and fled. As the torrent caught up to them, Nandalal pushed his son away from a collapsing wall, but moments later, the floodwaters swept them both away.

He said he had no idea such a massive flood was coming. The sun had been shining brightly just before the disaster.

Gharti was buried in thick mud for several minutes. Choking in the dark, he believed his end had come. With a final burst of strength, he pulled himself free, only to get pinned between two houses. He broke free a second time and scrambled onto a piece of floating driftwood. From there, he watched the area vanish under mud in seconds. Later, a rescue helicopter spotted him clinging to the wood and lifted him and three others to safety.

“I thought I was going to die. I thought my whole family would die too,” Gharti said

Five people remain missing after the flood, including his 10-year-old daughter, 12-year-old son, and his brother and sister-in-law.

He is receiving treatment at the trauma centre. “After surviving, we have nowhere to go,” he said. “We have lost our family and all our property.”

Nepal-Tibet flood death toll surpasses 900, officials say, more than 4,400 missing

Posted/updated on: September 5, 2026 at 9:20 pm

This graphic shows destruction along the path of a landslide and subsequent flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border. (Felt Maps/ABC News)

LONDON -- The death toll from last week's flash flooding disaster in the Nepal-Tibet border region rose to at least 955 people as of Monday, according to the latest updates from Nepali and Chinese officials, with more than 4,400 people reported missing.

At least 939 bodies had been recovered in Nepal as of Monday, the Nepal National Disaster Management Authority said in a post to X. At least 3,925 people were listed missing, the authority said, marking a significant jump on Sunday's figure.

China's state-run Xinhua News Agency, meanwhile, said that at least 16 people had been confirmed killed on the Tibetan side of the border. Xinhua reported that another 546 people were still missing.

The missing count declined from initial reports on Monday morning local time due to a combination of finding more bodies, rescuing more people and families reporting they had found missing relatives, an official with Nepal's National Disaster Management Authority told ABC News.

At least 85 Americans were still among the missing as of Sunday, State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told ABC News' Martha Raddatz on "This Week." Nine Americans had been evacuated, Pigott said, up from five on Friday.

"Our priority is the safety and security of the American people. As you mentioned, the remoteness of this location makes getting reliable information difficult. But our dedication remains," Pigott added.

"We have activated from the State Department $3.6 million in emergency humanitarian assistance that includes up to three months of emergency food for up to 10,000 flood-affected households," he said.

The flooding occurred in the northern Rasuwa district along the border with Tibet at around 8:40 a.m. local time Wednesday, authorities said. The flooding inundated areas along the Trishuli River, burying buildings and damaging bridges and roadways.

The wall of ice, water and debris that descended from the mountains on the frontier between Nepal and Tibet caused destruction at least 62 miles downriver into Nepal, an ABC News analysis of verified video and satellite images shows.

The flood was reportedly triggered by a landslide about 12 miles northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border post along the frontier, according to Nepali officials.

A 5.2-magnitude landslide was registered in Nepal on Wednesday, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.

The initial location of the glacier was a cliff about 16,000 feet high. The debris avalanche, or landslide, slid down 6,000 feet on the slope, the USGS said.

On Monday, the U.S. Embassy in Kathmandu warned Americans against all travel to the affected region, noting "flood damage, disrupted transportation and communications, search-and-rescue and recovery operations, and the risk of additional flooding and landslides."

The embassy also urged Americans to "exercise increased caution in Nepal due to civil unrest. Some areas have increased risk."

title: Nepal Latest Disaster Signals a Need to Redesign Monitoring and Early Warning Systems
full_text:
This piece was adapted from an earlier Stimson Center Commentary, “A Cascading Disaster on the China–Nepal Border: What to Know About the August 2026 Rasuwa Flood, 72 Hours Later,” and updated to reflect current conditions.



On August 26, 2026, a massive volume of bedrock and glacial ice broke loose 5,200 meters above sea level on the north side of Nepal’s Langtang range, triggering a “rock-ice avalanche” that crashed into the Lhende River on the Nepal-China border fueling the deadliest extreme flow disaster on record in the country. This cascade barreled downstream at an average of ~160 kilometers per hour downstream toward the Nepal-China border. It slammed into and overwhelmed Chinese border facilities at Rasuwagadhi just 7.5 minutes after the mountain gave way, then tore across the border and down the Bhotekoshi/Trishuli River corridor into Nepal, swallowing towns and causing extensive damage over 100 kilometers from its source.

As of 2:00pm ET on September 3rd a total of 1,259 people are confirmed dead and over 5,000 people are still reported missing. These numbers include Nepalis living and working along the river corridor, hundreds of foreign tourists visiting the Langtang region and pilgrims crossing to Mount Kailash, and hundreds of hydropower workers trapped in tunnels. The border town of Timure and the market hub of Syaphrubesi were essentially wiped away; 19 bridges and 40 kilometers of highway are gone, and more than 430 megawatts of hydropower capacity, representing more than 10% of Nepal’s national supply, is offline.

Cropped from Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi Flood: Search, Rescue and Relief Response, Situation Response #3, Issued September 3, 2026. Source: National Disaster Risk Reduction & Management Authority (NDRRMA), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Nepal

The residents of Nepal’s Rasuwa district, which includes a large Tamang population, have lived with disaster risk (e.g. floods, landslides, earthquakes, and avalanches) for centuries and they have adapted to and managed these risks. But the risks are changing fast, and the level of exposure communities face today is unprecedented.

I say this, having spent nearly 14 years conducting research in this river basin (in all of the affected settlements in Rasuwa), having led post-disaster relief activities in many of these towns after the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, and having personally survived a massive glacier avalanche on the other side of the very same mountain, which led to years of research and direct engagement. None of this is abstract to me, and my heart breaks for Rasuwa again.

A Cascade, Not a Rainfall Disaster

This catastrophic event happened on a clear day. Unlike many of Nepal’s recent disasters, it wasn’t triggered by extreme rainfall or an earthquake, and surprisingly, given the volume of water, there wasn’t a lake involved. Post-event analysis points to an unexpected culprit: the sheer force of the rock-ice avalanche that became more flood-like as it gathered water, rock, and sediment and funneled through the Trishuli’s tight canyons, arriving downstream as a fast-moving wall of concrete. This was a single, continuous, cascading extreme flow event.

Figure 1: Map of the impacted areas with timestamps for flood propagation (Source: CLaSH, Accessed September 2, 2026)

Scientists are still working to establish whether climate change played a role in destabilizing the source area, and formal processes of evaluating attribution are now underway. But the frequency of extreme flow events in recent years suggests that climate change is destabilizing the mountain cryosphere across the Himalayan region. Simply put, warming and climatic volatility can impact glaciers, weaken permafrost, and drive rapid or unseasonal changes in snowpack. In Nepal, climate-related risks interact with monsoon dynamics and seismic risk to compound danger in ways that existing monitoring frameworks aren’t built to see.

This event joins a grim and growing list of Himalayan cascading disasters — the 2021 Chamoli flood, the 2021 Melamchi disaster, the 2023 South Lhonak GLOF (Glacial Lake Outburst Flow), and the 2025 Blatten collapse in Switzerland. Notably, a smaller glacial flood struck this exact watershed in July 2025, destroying the same border bridge and killing 19 people — a warning sign that didn’t translate into readiness for what came next.

Of Blind Spots and Needles in Haystacks

It would be wrong to read this as a failure of Nepal’s early warning systems. The source area sits in a genuine gap — a narrow sliver of unpopulated Nepali territory that drains north into China, falling between the scientific attention long focused on the south side of the Langtang range and the Chinese monitoring effort that intensified after last year’s flood. Nepal’s gauge and station networks were built to catch monsoon floods and glacial lake outbursts, not a catastrophic flow that outran any possible alert. But generating alerts for an event like this isn’t just a problem of data scarcity or blind spots, it’s also a problem of speed and scale. The Himalaya has more slopes capable of failing this catastrophically, across more vertical relief, than anywhere else on Earth. Scientists can and have highlighted a variety of high-risk areas and landforms, but finding subtle changes in a timely fashion requires skillfully separating signal from noise as risk changes across the Himalaya.

The overall point is that experts need a signal to effectively direct their tools and attention – and finding these signals can often feel like finding needles in Himalaya haystacks. Of roughly a dozen extreme flow events in the region over the past decade, only one — the 2023 South Lhonak outburst — struck a site already flagged as risky. Every other event originated from somewhere no one was watching, including this one.

Learning from Disasters Like This

Each event offers lessons and insights that allow us to return with greater precision and a new understanding of where similar hazard chains might be stacking up. For example, the 2024 Thame (GLOF) taught researchers that small glacial lakes can grow dangerously fast; last year’s transboundary flood event along the same Lhende River into Rasuwa showed that supraglacial lakes — lakes on top of glaciers — can expand and drain catastrophically. Last week’s event highlights the increasing prevalence of another kind of risk: showing how an ice-rock avalanche can trigger a massive flood-like event and impact communities more than 100 kilometers downstream.

Tools are rapidly developing, but no single instrument will catch everything, so the approach has to be layered — weather stations and river gauges as a foundation, satellite monitoring to track remote terrain, seismic networks to triangulate a failure within seconds, and, critically, local observers such as herders, mountaineers, and fishers who can flag a crack or a filling lake long before a sensor does. Even a few minutes of warning can be the difference between an evacuation and a recovery operation.

What the Stimson Nepal Early Warning Team is Doing

In the wake of this event, on the Stimson Center’s Early Warning for Cascading Disasters in Nepal project team, working in Nepal and Washington, rapidly mobilized to assess the event, gather information, and share expert analysis with Government of Nepal institutions such as the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) and government hydrologists and meteorologists. Using Sentinel-1, Landsat, and Planet Labs imagery, we identified the avalanche’s source, ruled out a supraglacial lake we had assessed last year, and confirmed the landslide-dam mechanism. We also tasked commercial radar/SAR imagery from ICEYE US over the source and blockage sites and delivered pre- and post-event comparisons to NDRRMA and Nepal’s Home Ministry within hours.

After two new lakes formed in the avalanche flowpath — one along the Lhende River, another high in the upper catchment — we worked with the NDRRMA to assess changing conditions, analyze breach scenarios, and provide scientific analysis of the flood pulses that came when the lake began to finally drain on August 30th. Members of our team also contributed to the HIRISK rapid assessment, prepared by an international group of Chinese, Nepali, American, Austrian, Swiss, and Dutch scientists, which was published on August 28.

Lingering Risks and Uncertainties, in Both Nepal and China

Risks remain throughout the region, and heavy rain could still reactivate destabilized slopes or remobilize other landforms within the impacted area. Critically, the monsoon season is not yet over. There are risks that we know of, such as risks from specific glacial lakes in China. But we can’t discount the risks we are not yet aware of from other potential cascading hazards. Monitoring these risks often requires both focused efforts on high-risk areas and triaging between uncertainties.

In this wake of this devastating event, we are already seeing better transboundary coordination between Nepal and China. High-priority information is being shared and new channels of communication opened between Chinese and Nepali authorities — a promising, if overdue, shift. A variety of people have called for greater formal coordination and the establishment of transboundary monitoring networks.

To be clear, no one — not Nepal, not China, not the international scientific community — could have identified the subtle changes and specific risks that triggered this disaster. Forensic analysis is yielding new insights that we can use to search for similar risks in the future, but this event began with a sudden mass movement that turned into an extreme flow far too fast for a true alert to be shared. The hope is that this disaster will catalyze the kind of sustained, cross-border monitoring and cooperation the region has needed for years.

title: 10 - year - old Kushinagar boy offers piggy bank to help Nepal flood victims
full_text:
10-year-old Alfaz at Kushinagar DM office

Lucknow:





For 10-year-old Alfaz Sheikh, the little piggy bank he carried to the Kushinagar district magistrate’s office on Thursday held much more than coins and currency notes. It had a dream — carefully saved over months in one- and two-rupee coins and Rs 10, Rs 50 and Rs 100 denomination currency notes.But images of devastation in Nepal made him rethink what those savings meant.Instead of spending his savings on objects that children of his age crave for, the Class V student decided to give it to people struggling for food, shelter and safety after the disaster in the neighbouring country.A resident of Betia village in Kushinagar, Alfaz, son of businessman Imran Ali Siddiqui, reached the office of district magistrate Mahendra Singh Tanwar with his father and handed over his piggy bank.He also submitted an application requesting the administration to ensure that his savings reach those affected in Nepal.The gesture touched everyone present, particularly Tanwar, who patted the child on the back and praised him for his compassion.Alfaz’s father said the boy had been watching news reports on TV and social media showing houses submerged in water, families getting displaced and people battling for survival in Nepal.“The videos disturbed him deeply. He kept thinking about the people who lost their homes and told me that he wanted to do something to help them. We respected his feelings and supported him,” Imran said.For Alfaz, the decision was simple. He wanted his savings to bring some relief to people facing hardship.“I had saved money for my future needs. But when I came to know about Nepal disaster, I decided to use to it to help people in distress,” Alfaz told TOI.The district magistrate that said the administration deliberately chose not to count the money immediately, as the child’s feelings were more important than the amount.“We respected the child’s feelings and the spirit behind his gesture, so we did not even count the money he brought in his piggy bank. The entire amount will be sent through the appropriate channel so that his contribution reaches Nepal as aid. What matters is not the amount, but the compassion and humanitarian spirit shown by this 10-year-old,” Tanwar told TOI.Asked what he wanted to become when he grew up, Alfaz offered an answer that was as uncomplicated as his gesture: “Whatever I become, I would help people in distress.”

title: Two rescued alive 9 days after Nepal tunnel disaster
full_text:
Rescuers pulled two survivors from a tunnel linked to a hydropower station on Nepal's Trishuli River on Friday, nine days after a wall of ice, rock and mud tore through its valley, killing more than 1,300 people and leaving over 5,600 missing.

Officials and rescue workers say they believe the August 26 collapse of a glacier on the upper reaches of the river trapped at least 900 people in tunnels related to six hydropower projects along the waters.

The two workers pulled from the tunnel at the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station are the first to be rescued from the hydropower projects and have been taken to ⁠an army hospital in the capital Kathmandu, giving search teams a flicker of hope as the possibility of finding other survivors fades. The army said they had ⁠also recovered a body from the site.

Videos released by Nepali authorities showed Kabir Maharjan being hoisted from a hole in the ground as bystanders cheered, then lowered onto a stretcher.

His colleague Sanjay Sah was brought out on a worker's back, his face still caked in mud, before army doctors fitted an oxygen mask and checked his vitals inside a rescue tent.

Sah, a mechanical foreman, later described staying behind ‌in a control room to help others escape after he urged colleagues to flee upon hearing news ​of the disaster.

"I was in the ⁠control room, so my responsibility was to save everyone's lives. When there was such a big accident, it was not right for me ​to run away," he said in a video recording shared by ‌Nepali authorities.

Sah told rescuers he spent time reciting mantras while he was trapped. He said he had been in contact with three or four more people in the tunnel, while others could still be alive deeper in its reaches.

Nepal's army said ​it recovered two bodies from a tunnel at Langtang Hydropower Station, and continued searching.

At least 1,287 people have been killed in Nepal in the floods that swept away houses, streets and schools in towns and villages near the border with China's Tibet, the disaster management authority said on Friday. More than 5,080 are still missing. China has put the death toll in Tibet at 21, with 541 others listed as missing.

The two rescued men are now in intensive care at an army hospital and their vital signs are stable, a source from the facility said.

Mechanical supervisor Maharjan cannot move his hands or legs, but Sah's injuries are not considered critical, according to an aide to the energy minister.

Amir Maharjan, Kabir's brother, ​said he has not received any news officially but has been told to go to the hospital.

Survivor Sanjay Sah is carried by members of a search and rescue team after they rescued alive two people who had been trapped inside a tunnel at the Upper Trishuli-3A Hydropower Project following devastating floods and mudslides that struck the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa, Nepal. — Reuters

"I have been hearing from the news that my brother has been found. ​The entire family ‌is ⁠very happy," Amir said.

A small group of people had managed to escape from another tunnel hours after the disaster struck.

A team of experts in a WhatsApp group was guiding rescue workers in the search at the hydropower projects in what has become a valuable tool alongside helicopters and heavy machinery in the race to find survivors.

More search and rescue ​operations were underway around the Upper Trishuli 3A project, the Nepali army said. Rescue efforts were being led by the army ⁠and police, with assistance ​from experts from India, South Korea and China.

Property, housing and infrastructure worth at least $2.56 billion were lost in last week's catastrophe, Dharma Raj Upreti, chief of Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said on Friday.

Nepal will need to rebuild around 20,000 houses in flood-ravaged areas, Upreti has said, with at least 7,500 of those homes destroyed.

The disaster could result in commercial insurance losses exceeding $132.3 million, with hydropower projects accounting for most claims, according to a top official at one of the country's leading ​insurers. Eleven Nepali hydropower projects lie in the affected region and in many cases, access roads and above-ground infrastructure have been washed away.

At least 583 ​foreign nationals were missing in the floods, Nepal said, many of them pilgrims and trekkers. Australian disaster response specialists left for Nepal to join the search for survivors, as the Australian government expressed "serious concerns" for the welfare of its 36 missing citizens. — Reuters

title: The Ghoulish Race to Turn Nepal Flood Victims Into a  Climate Crisi Talking Point
full_text:
The political talking point ignores tens of millions of years of plate tectonics and its consequences, and completely dismisses well-established mountain-weather dynamics.

From Legal Insurrection

Posted by Leslie Eastman

Reports of the devastation in Nepal following a massive landslide now indicate that the death toll from Wednesday’s devastating flash floods in Nepal and China has risen to 800, with around 3,000 people still missing.

Nepal’s disaster agency said Sunday the death toll had climbed to 788 with 2,502 missing, while Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing on the Chinese side of the border. Poor weather and challenging terrain have hampered aerial rescue operations. In Nuwakot, one of the Nepali districts devastated by the floods, helicopters resumed operations before noon Saturday after poor weather temporarily obstructed their activities. Some helicopters were loaded with boxes and bags of aid, including clothes, instant noodles, crackers and rice. Others returned from the flood-hit areas carrying survivors. …More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far, according to authorities there. Hundreds of the missing are foreigners who were in the area to work, trek or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak on the Tibet side of the border.

Nepal’s deadly Himalayan flash flood this week has predictably produced a familiar ritual: before rescue crews had finished counting bodies, climate cultists and their political acolytes were already racing to slot the disaster into their favorite narrative. Outlets from the New York Times to CNN to Forbes rushed out pieces insisting that “climate change” primed the catastrophe.

Suddenly everyone became an expert on the Himalayan climate.

Climate change is leading to conditions that can destabilize high-mountain rock and ice, which may cause disasters such as the flood along the border between Nepal and Tibet, scientists say, though it might not be the sole trigger https://t.co/qS76HHtT5c pic.twitter.com/QlNuFJ9uWx — Reuters (@Reuters) August 29, 2026

Three clear-eyed voices on X pushed back: Dr. Matthew Wielicki (Director – United States Global Change Research Program), meteorologist Chris Martz, and Jim Steele (ecologist and author of Landscapes & Cycles). They deserve amplification, not the usual media silence.

So, let’s take a deep dive into Himalayan geology and geography with them.

The flooding in Nepal and Tibet is devastating.



Hundreds of people have died in these catastrophic floods and over 2,000 are still missing.



No, President Trump. Climate change is not a hoax. It is causing devastating crises all over the planet. — Sen. Bernie Sanders (@SenSanders) August 28, 2026

What actually happened in Nepal

The disaster began when an enormous chunk of a glacier on Langtang Lirung, high in the Himalayas, sheared off and slammed into the valley below with such force that it registered as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event, according to the US Geological Survey. The ice and rock mass blocked the Lhende Khola river, and when the makeshift dam gave way, it unleashed a wall of water, mud, and boulders the size of cars that buried villages downstream. Even the outlets pushing the climate narrative admit the actual trigger is still “under investigation” and that no formal attribution study has been done.

This newly surfaced video shows the landslide that occurred just a few hours after the main glacier collapse.



The event formed a barrier lake that dammed the Lhende Khola River along the Nepal–Tibet border. pic.twitter.com/U99m3uURaq — Massimo (@Rainmaker1973) August 30, 2026

That inconvenient detail didn’t stop the parade of quotes about “what climate change looks like.” One geologist told CNN, “Whether this particular event can be tied to climate change or not, this is what we expect.” This is not science, but a talking point dressed up as science.

The mountains have been doing this for millions of years.

Meteorologist Chris Martz cut through the noise by noting that landslides and avalanches in Nepal have occurred for tens of millions of years, long before humans existed, let alone burned fossil fuels. As he noted, the V-shaped valleys carved through the region were carved by exactly these landslide-flood events at pre-industrial carbon dioxide levels, a geologic fact that climate cultists conveniently skip.

Long story short, this is BS.



Landslides / avalanches in Nepal have happened for tens of millions of years. In fact, floods associated with landslides are how the V-shaped valleys in the region were carved out millions of years ago at pre-industrial atmospheric carbon dioxide… https://t.co/oud6rlrZqH pic.twitter.com/sRGsVHISIB — Chris Martz (@ChrisMartzWX) August 29, 2026

Geologist Dr. Matthew Wielicki, who has done fieldwork sitting above the Himalaya’s “enormous, deeply incised” river systems in Tibet, made the same point: This landscape is robustly geologically active on its own, independent of anything happening in the atmosphere.

I’ve spent many weeks doing fieldwork in Tibet, sitting above these enormous, deeply incised Himalayan river systems and seeing firsthand just how geologically active this landscape is.



So spare me the climate-change grift every time a natural disaster strikes.



Catastrophic… pic.twitter.com/I08oXu5jmy — Dr. Matthew M. Wielicki (@MatthewWielicki) August 27, 2026

Both men are pointing to something the peer-reviewed record supports. The Himalaya is a young, still-rising mountain range, formed by the Indian plate colliding with Eurasia roughly 40 to 65 million years ago, and it remains one of the most tectonically active zones on Earth.

Research into the region’s landslide history documents “giant rock slope failures” tied to the North Himalayan Fault system going back tens of thousands of years, driven by the constant interplay between tectonic and glacial activity… not modern emissions.

In fact, Wielicki wrote a paper noting that southern Tibet rapidly eroded and exposed rock from about 17–16 million to 12–11 million years ago, probably because tectonic uplift and steep rivers drove intense erosion. Around 10 million years ago, enhanced uplift in the Himalayas (likely driven by crustal thickening and fault-related rock stacking) shifted drainage divides southward and diverted rivers away from southern Tibet. This tectonic restructuring strengthened the Himalayan rain barrier, dried southern Tibet, reduced river power, and largely shut down erosion there even as the mountain belt continued to develop.

In other words, this event is an example of Earth-caused climate change.

Rain, snow, and mountains that manufacture their own weather.

Another detail missing from the climate-panic coverage is that the Himalaya doesn’t just sit there passively, waiting to be affected by global climate. The mountains are so large that they actively create their own extreme weather.

Keep in mind that the Great Himalaya’s average high crest is about 3.8 miles high, with the iconic Mount Everest reaching roughly 5.5 miles.

The sheer height of these peaks forces monsoon moisture upward, and the precipitation released drives erosion and landslides for eons. Add seasonal snowmelt and near-vertical topography, and you have a landscape engineered by nature to periodically fail catastrophically, regardless of the level of carbon dioxide and with or without an added tenth of a degree of global average temperature.

Geothermal heat melts ice from below.

Where there is a collision of 2 tectonic plates, there is a great deal of geothermal heat that arises FROM THE SURFACE, not THE ATMOSPHERE. SUVs are not responsible for this heat. Furthermore, glacial forces themselves can elevate temperature.

The following analysis is from Jim Steele:

However, on Langtang Lirung, at the 5200 meter elevation where the rock-ice block first separated to start the 2026 avalanche, the average summer temperature is still below freezing at -6°C to -8°C (21°F to 17°F). During the warmest summer period, mid-day averages reach 2°C to 6°C (36°F to 43°F) but night temperatures stay near -2°C to -5°C (28°F to 23°F). Furthermore, science suggests air temperatures are not affecting the surface ice. The top few meters of a glacier, rapidly respond to air temperature, sunshine, and seasons. Nonetheless winter cold and summer warmth only penetrate about 10–20 m from the glaciers’ surface. Thus, changes in atmospheric temperature are unlikely to provide “lubricating” melt water in 200-meter thick glaciers. Below the shallow “seasonal layer,” temperature is steady and often close to the local mean annual air temperature, which again averages summer temperature below freezing at -6°C to -8°C (21°F to 17°F). Still studies show the glacier-ground interface is almost always warmer than the ice above it for 3 main reasons: 1) Because ice is such a good insulator, the geothermal heat rising from Earth’s interior accumulates at the glacier’s bottom. 2) frictional heat from ice sliding over rock adds to the temperature. 3) Under thick ice, the melting point is lower due to pressure effects. So even if the surface is –30 °C or colder, the bed of a 2–3 km ice sheet can sit at or very near 0 °C. Global warming is not a factor.

How Grifters Twist Nepal’s Natural Glacier Avalanche to Blame Fossil Fuels.



Avalanches and earthquakes are relatively common in the Himalaya and recently drove Langtang Lirung’s glacier collapses. For example, on the south-facing side of Langtang Lirung, a 7.8 earthquake caused… pic.twitter.com/qrFLpV2WMR — Jim Steele (@JimSteeleSkepti) August 27, 2026

Parting thoughts

The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), the regional scientific body actually based in Kathmandu, remarked that it’s simply “too early to determine what role climate change played in this specific event”. That’s the honest scientific position.

Everything past that point is ghoulish narrative laundering that uses dead villagers as a backdrop for a political talking point and ignores tens of millions of years of plate tectonics and its consequences, and completely dismisses well-established mountain-weather dynamics.

title: University of Rhode Island water expert from Nepal shares insight into recent flood in South Asian nation
full_text:
Newswise — A water scientist at the University of Rhode Island, Soni Pradhanang is balancing the professional and the personal, watching her home country of Nepal make news after the recent glacial collapse and flooding there.

As a hydrologist with expertise in environmental science and water quality, flooding, and hazard communication, the events in her home nation are the subject she has made her career in since she left Nepal in 2001. Pradhanang, in URI’s College of the Environment and Life Sciences, conducts research in runoff, flood, drought, and water quality modeling, and has served as a point of contact in URI’s prior work with Nepal. In 2022, during her Fulbright tenure, she served as an instructor for a hydrological modeling training program in Kathmandu, part of a project on “Modeling Hydrological Response to Changes in Climate and Glacier in a Data-Scarce Glacierized Region in Nepal Himalaya.” The training covered core concepts in hydrology, climate change, and cold-region hydrology, providing early-career professionals with the tools to study these issues. “This tragedy highlights the urgent relevance of this research,” she said.

Raised in Kathmandu, approximately 40 miles aerial distance from the affected area in Rasuwa/Langtang National Park, she shares insight into recent events, while keeping tabs on family members and loved ones there.

“For me, this is not an abstract scientific event,” Pradhanang said. “It is a human tragedy affecting communities, families, livelihoods, and landscapes in my home country.”

What were the contributing factors for the recent events in Nepal and has anything like this happened there before?

Based on the best available satellite imagery, seismic observations, and preliminary field interpretation, the disaster in northern Nepal appears to have begun with a rapid failure of a glacierized mountain slope in Langtang National Park near the Nepal–China border. A very large mass of ice, rock, and debris descended into the valley, likely obstructing the Lhende Khola River temporarily. When that unstable blockage failed or was overtopped, it released a powerful debris-laden flood that traveled downstream through the Lhende and Trishuli river valleys.

It is important to be careful about the cause. The collapse itself generated seismic energy comparable to a magnitude 5.2 event; it should not automatically be described as an earthquake-triggered disaster. Scientists worldwide are still determining the relative roles of steep terrain, fractured bedrock, glacier geometry, meltwater, rainfall or snowmelt conditions, and thawing permafrost. Climate warming is a highly relevant background factor because it causes glacier retreat and can thaw the frozen ground that helps stabilize high-mountain rock and ice. But attributing this particular collapse to one single factor would be premature.

Nepal has experienced destructive glacier- and landslide-related floods before, although every event has its own sequence of triggers. Nepal has recorded 26 glacial lake outburst floods since 1977, including events originating both within Nepal and beyond its borders. The Langtang region also has a history of serious mountain hazards, including earthquake-triggered avalanches in 2015 and recent floods and ice-rock avalanches in nearby valleys. This event is especially notable because it appears to involve a rapid ice-and-rock avalanche and a temporary river-dam failure, rather than a conventional moraine-dammed glacial lake suddenly bursting. A similar devastating event occurred in India in 2021, involving a rock-ice avalanche. More recently, in 2024, a cascading glacial lake outburst flood event in Nepal's Thame Valley, triggered by a rock avalanche and a chain reaction of lake breaches, caused widespread destruction. These past disasters highlight the growing danger.

Is there any technology that could provide a warning for an event like this?

No system can predict the exact moment when every slope or glacier will fail, or when a rock-ice avalanche will occur; that would defeat essentially every operational flood warning system in the world. However, technology can provide critical warning—especially once a collapse, blockage, or sudden rise in river level begins.

A strong system would combine satellite monitoring with ground-based instruments. Satellites can detect changes in glacier extent, new or expanding lakes, ground deformation, slope movement, and post-event flood extent. On the ground, river-stage and rainfall gauges, time-lapse cameras, geophones or seismic sensors, and automated alarms can detect rapidly developing hazards. Warnings then need to be distributed immediately via sirens, cell broadcasts, radio, local responders, and community networks.

The limitation is time. In narrow, steep valleys, a debris flood may reach downstream settlements in minutes. Therefore, the system must be automated, resilient to damage, powered and connected with backups, and linked to practiced evacuation plans. Monitoring alone does not save lives unless people receive, understand, trust, and can act on the warning.

What can be done to lessen impact in events like this in the future?

We cannot eliminate all high-mountain hazards, particularly in a country with steep terrain, active geology, and rapidly changing glaciers. But we can substantially reduce loss of life and damage. While predicting these sudden events is incredibly difficult, especially when no immediate rainfall precedes them to trigger traditional flood warnings, several measures can be taken to mitigate the risks and protect vulnerable communities.

The most important actions are to identify hazardous slopes, glaciers, and glacial lakes; map the downstream pathways that floodwaters and debris would follow; install robust monitoring and warning systems; and ensure that communities, schools, hydropower operators, road agencies, and border facilities know exactly how to respond to an alert.

Risk reduction should include four inter-connected elements:

Regular satellite and field monitoring of glacierized slopes, glacial lakes, landslide-prone areas, and thawing permafrost, if any.

Multi-hazard early-warning systems using river-level sensors, cameras, weather stations, seismic instruments, satellite data, and redundant communications.

Community preparedness: alarms, evacuation routes, safe assembly areas, drills, and warning messages that are understandable and accessible to everyone.

Safer planning and infrastructure. Critical facilities such as bridges, hydropower stations, roads, schools, and settlements should, when alternatives exist, be avoided in the highest-hazard flood corridors. Where exposure already exists, structures and evacuation systems should be designed for rapid-onset debris floods, not only ordinary monsoon flooding.

For selected high-risk glacial lakes, direct interventions can also help—for example, carefully lowering lake levels, reinforcing or modifying unstable moraine dams, and coupling those interventions with locally managed warning systems. Nepal has already implemented lake-lowering and community early-warning measures at Imja Tsho in the Everest region, demonstrating that targeted mitigation is possible.

Was the glacier that triggered the event considered vulnerable and how do researchers assess glaciers?

At this early stage, it is more accurate to say that the glacierized slope was demonstrably hazardous than to imply that the precise failure was fully predictable. Researchers assess vulnerability by examining satellite imagery and aerial data, glacier retreat and surface changes, slope angles, fractures and crevasses, rock and ice volumes, evidence of permafrost thaw, nearby lakes, drainage pathways, and the likely consequences for people and infrastructure downstream.

Researchers assess the vulnerability of glaciers and glacial lakes, using satellite imagery to map their size, evolution, and growth over time. This helps identify which lakes are expanding rapidly and are therefore potentially dangerous.

Pratik Singh Thakuri, a Ph.D. student in my lab also from Nepal, has been actively acquiring and analyzing satellite imagery to better understand both the physical processes that drove this event and the extent of resulting damages. Trained as a water resources engineer, he focuses his research on modeling floods and other extreme hydrologic events. His work provides an important connection between remote-sensing observations of this disaster and the broader effort to understand, model, and reduce flood risks.

Pratik’s comparison of satellite-based images, from Aug. 24 and Aug. 26, 2026, look at the two scenes over the same geographic area, comparing the glaciers, surrounding slopes, avalanche pathways, valley floods, and downstream river corridors. By comparing different time periods, scientists can piece together the development of an event and ascertain whether there were any visual changes in the glacier or adjacent region prior to the event. Although this does not identify the cause of the event, it represents an important starting point for analyzing it.

When possible, teams conduct on-the-ground surveys to study glacial conditions, measure lake depth, assess the stability of moraine dams, and gather data for computer models. Scientists integrate data on lake size, surrounding topography, and downstream population and infrastructure to assess risk. A lake might be deemed "high risk" if a potential outburst could impact a populated area. We use computer models to simulate what would happen if a lake were to breach, predicting the path, speed, and volume of a flood wave.

The key question is not only ‘Could a glacier or lake fail?’ but also ‘Who and what lies in the potential flow path?’

There are other sites of concern in Nepal and across the Hindu Kush Himalaya. A 2020 assessment, by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development / United Nations Development Programme, identified 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes across the Koshi, Gandaki, and Karnali basins spanning Nepal, Tibet, and India—21 in Nepal, 25 in Tibet, and one in India. These inventories are vital but need to be updated because glaciers, lakes, slopes, and downstream exposure are changing rapidly.

Could this kind of an event happen elsewhere and are there other areas that might be vulnerable or at-risk?

Similar cascading hazards can occur wherever steep, glacierized mountains contain unstable ice, thawing permafrost, fractured rock, glacial lakes, and communities or infrastructure in narrow downstream valleys. The Hindu Kush Himalaya is a major concern, but the underlying processes also occur in the Andes, Alaska, western Canada, the European Alps, Iceland, and parts of Central Asia. In a paper I co-authored in 2023, we discussed cascading hazards becoming more prevalent in the central Himalayas and how the need for an integrated modeling framework means more reliable prediction, with early warning systems essential for reducing impacts.

The specific hazard may differ by place. In some valleys, the major concern is a glacial-lake outburst flood; elsewhere, it may be an ice avalanche, a rock-and-ice avalanche, a landslide-dammed lake, a rain-on-snow flood, or a compound event involving several of these processes. Warming does not make every individual collapse directly attributable to climate change, but it is altering the conditions that affect glacier and permafrost stability in many mountain regions.
