title: Nepal flood is over , but the fear remains
full_text:
September 7, 2026

KATHMANDU – Sixteen-year-old Samiksha Dangol was on her way home from school when she saw her father coming towards her.

It was the morning of August 26 at Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in Nuwakot, a district north-west of Kathmandu. Samikshya, a Grade 11 student, had been sent home after the school received warnings that floodwaters were rising.

Her father had come to take her home.

But the two did not get far. A traffic police officer stopped them and warned that the flood was rising and that they should not cross the bridge.

They waited, assuming the rest of the family had already fled.

They had not.

When Samiksha and her father learnt what had happened, both collapsed.

Her older sister, brother and two aunts (father’s sisters) were missing in the flood.

Days later, after staying at a temporary holding centre, Samiksha moved to her maternal relatives’ home. The water has receded, but August 26 keeps returning to her.

She struggles to sleep. Memories of playing with her siblings surface without warning. She cries and feels restless.

“I tell myself to forget it,” she said. “But I keep thinking about my sister and brothers. The things we did together keep playing in my mind.”

The physical effects have been difficult too. Samiksha, who already suffers from migraines, became so unwell that she and her mother had to be taken to hospital. The family had lost so much that even the medicine she normally took was unavailable.

For children like Samiksha, the disaster did not end when the floodwaters fell. Across Nuwakot, Rasuwa and neighbouring districts, children who survived the floods, witnessed destruction or lost relatives are now confronting a less visible aftermath: fear. Some wake in the middle of night. Some become withdrawn. Others panic at sounds that remind them of the disaster.

In Rasuwa, Karsang Tamang’s 21-month-old son becomes frightened whenever he hears a loud noise.

On August 26, Karsang grabbed her sleeping son and ran as floodwaters swept through the area around Timure, Rasuwa. People were screaming and running in panic.

Since then, even the sound of a helicopter can make the toddler cry.

“He had never been like this before,” Karsang said. “Now he gets startled and frightened from time to time. When he panics, it causes me a lot of pain too.”

Karsang is sheltering at Yellow Gumba (Buddhist monastery) in western Kathmandu. She is more worried about her young son than about what she herself endured.

The scale of the impact on children is difficult to measure.

UNICEF estimates that 17,000 children have been affected by the floods in Nepal. Data from Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority show that 6,901 students at 19 schools in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading were affected. Local education offices, municipalities and schools estimate that 622 students in Rasuwa and Nuwakot alone remain unaccounted for following the Bhotekoshi flooding.

The numbers capture the scale of the disaster. They do not capture what it feels like for a child to hear a helicopter and be taken back to the moment they ran for safety, or to close their eyes and see a missing sibling.

Some children were found after spending hours or days trapped by the flood.

A six-year-old girl rescued from Timure on August 28 was among them. An Armed Police Force search team heard what sounded like a child crying and followed the sound. They found her injured and brought her to Kathmandu, where she is receiving treatment at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital.

Her mother, Geeta Magar, said the girl barely spoke during the first days in hospital.

“She would just keep looking at me,” Magar said. Doctors told the family that the child appeared to have forgotten some things after the flood and had also developed pneumonia.

For aid workers who arrived at temporary shelters, the change in the children was immediately visible.

At the holding centre at Chandrajyoti Secondary School in Devighat, Nuwakot, Nepal Scouts volunteer Hritik Magiya saw children who were initially too frightened or withdrawn to participate in even simple activities.

“When we first came here, the children were in a very different state,” he said. “They were very sad and afraid, wondering what to do if another flood came.”

Some had lost parents or other relatives. Others were waiting for family members who had not yet been found.

In the first days, Magiya said, many children would sit apart from the group. Even when volunteers organised games, some refused to join.

“They were quiet and did not participate in any activities,” he said.

That response is not unusual after a disaster, mental health specialists say.

Psychiatrist Dr Amit Jha said children can be particularly vulnerable because they have fewer resources than adults to understand and regulate fear and stress.

After a disaster, children may have difficulty sleeping, experience a racing heartbeat, sweating or rapid breathing. Such symptoms can form part of an acute stress reaction. If they continue for several weeks, they may develop into anxiety or depressive disorders. In some cases, particularly among children who directly experienced the disaster or lost relatives, prolonged trauma can develop into post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

The psychological impact can extend beyond children who were physically caught in the floods.

Children elsewhere may also be affected after repeatedly watching footage of floods and landslides on television or social media, Jha said. Repeated exposure to distressing images and accounts can leave children frightened, anxious or restless even if they were nowhere near the disaster.

For that reason, adults should be careful about what children see and hear, he said, particularly in the immediate aftermath.

The challenge facing Nepal now is to prevent an emergency response from becoming another source of trauma.

For children who have lost parents or guardians, the stakes are especially high.

“There are many children who have lost their father, mother or guardians,” said Geeta KC Darnal, a child protection officer with Sahayatri Nepal. “We cannot fully understand the pain of losing a parent at such a young age. The immediate priority is to help them come out of the trauma.”

Government agencies and aid organisations have begun providing psychological and psychosocial support.

The National Child Rights Council says it is coordinating with volunteers, counsellors, doctors and local authorities working in affected areas. “The council is also collecting information on the number of children killed and affected in the disaster,” Ram Bahadur Chand, an information officer at the council, said.

Bidur Municipality, meanwhile, says medical teams from all three levels of government are providing mental health and psychosocial counselling. Child-focussed organisations have also established services at holding centres.

The municipality is preparing residential arrangements for children who have been separated from their families or otherwise left without adequate care. Two residential schools have been selected to accommodate some of them.

At the holding centre, officials and aid workers have also tried to give children space to play and return, as much as possible, to familiar routines.

That can be more important than it sounds.

Magiya said the children at the Devighat centre gradually became more engaged after volunteers spent time with them, played games, and told stories.

“We gradually involved them in different activities while also feeding them,” he said. “We played games with them on the school grounds, spent time with them and told them stories. We also asked them to sketch and draw with coloured pencils.”

The children who had initially avoided the volunteers eventually began approaching them on their own.

Some now remember the volunteers’ names, play with them and talk to them.

Yet children who lost relatives still become visibly sad from time to time.

The recovery, experts say, will not be measured simply by whether children return to school or leave temporary shelters. Trauma can emerge slowly.

Milan Dharel, a former executive director of the National Child Rights Council, said the effects of disasters can be physical, psychological and socio-economic.

There is another danger: children who lose the protection of their families can become vulnerable to trafficking, child labour, violence and abuse. Dharel warned that even efforts presented as protection can become mechanisms for exploitation.

The risk has become particularly visible on social media, where images and videos of children affected by the floods have circulated.

Offers to take children in or raise them may appear sympathetic, but child protection officials urge caution. Children can also be exploited through fundraising, online content, or institutions claiming to provide shelter, Dharel said.

The government, he said, has two immediate responsibilities: ensuring that search-and-rescue operations remain child-sensitive, and monitoring anyone who assumes responsibility for a child separated from their family.

Authorities have also warned against another form of harm: turning children’s suffering into public content.

The National Child Rights Council and Nepal Police have urged the public and media not to publish photographs, videos, or personal information that could identify children affected by the floods. Such exposure can violate their privacy and dignity and cause lasting harm to their mental health.

For children already carrying memories of homes swept away, relatives disappearing and adults screaming in fear, the recovery may depend on more than rebuilding roads or bridges.

Psychiatrist Jha calls the first response “psychological first aid”.

Children need to feel safe, he said, adding, adults should reassure them that they are protected, rather than repeatedly asking them to recount what happened.

Parents can help where they are present. Where parents have died or remain missing, relatives, communities and the state must take their place.

The most useful response can be remarkably simple: stay with the child, listen and allow them to speak when they are ready, Jha said.

Children should also be helped back into ordinary life as soon as circumstances permit, including a return to school.

The floods have left the country with damaged infrastructure, disrupted communities and families still searching for those who have not returned. But for children such as Samiksha, the disaster continues to affect daily life. She still struggles to sleep and is often reminded of her siblings and the things they did together.

title: Nepal observes day of national mourning in memory of lives lost in devastating floods
full_text: Nepal is observing a day of national mourning on Monday in memory of lives lost in devastating floods which struck on August 26. A Cabinet meeting held on September 3 at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers had decided to observe national mourning in honour of the flood victims. Accordingly, the national flag is being flown at half-mast at government offices across the country, as well as at Nepali embassies and diplomatic missions abroad. The Bhotekoshi flood struck Rasuwa, causing widespread loss of life and extensive damage to homes, roads, bridges, hydropower facilities and other critical infrastructure. The disaster also affected downstream areas along the Trishuli River, including parts of Nuwakot and Dhading, leaving communities displaced and disrupting transport, electricity, water supply and other essential services. Search and rescue operations, relief distribution and infrastructure restoration have continued in the affected areas, with national security agencies, government authorities, local communities and international partners involved in the response. On the eve of the national mourning, Prime Minister Balendra (Balen) Shah issued a public statement acknowledging the ongoing work of Nepals security personnel involved in search, rescue and management operations following flood damage caused by the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. The statement highlighted a recent incident at the Central Jail at Khampa Camp in Bidur-6, Nuwakot, where floodwaters damaged administrative structures and reached lower levels of housing facilities. According to the Prime Minister, 52 personnel from the Nepal Police and the Armed Police Force (APF) transferred all 923 inmates to higher ground within the complex while re-apprehending 50 inmates who attempted to escape through damaged perimeter structures, with several officers sustaining injuries during the process. Despite damage to nearby barracks, loss of road access and disrupted water supplies, security personnel have continued maintaining operations and supplying necessities at the facility. Nationwide, joint operations involving the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and APF have resulted in the rescue of 13,391 individuals via air and ground transport. Current deployments across affected regions include 9,287 personnel from the Nepali Army managing operations in Battar and Dhunche and assembling temporary bridges in Devighat. Similarly, 7,975 Nepal Police officers are handling frontline search operations, body retrieval and canine unit deployments. Moreover, 4,203 APF personnel are operating across 13 response bases, utilising diving units, rope rescue teams and drone surveillance. The Prime Minister also noted that 82 security personnel remain unaccounted for following the floods, including 45 from the Nepali Army, 25 from the Nepal Police and 12 from the APF. Shah expressed appreciation for the continued efforts of the security forces, their families and assisting experts, reaffirming the governments commitment to supporting security personnel deployed in the field. (ANI)

title: Australian tunnel rescuer Arnold Dix says he faces  unprecedented  challenge in flood - hit Nepal
full_text: Australian tunnel rescue expert Arnold Dix, internationally celebrated for his pivotal contribution in extracting forty-one trapped workers from Indias Silkyara tunnel during 2023, has characterised ongoing flood mitigation operations throughout Nepal as a professional challenge unlike any encountered previously in his professional life. Dispatching reports directly from the field in the wake of catastrophic inundations surrounding the Bhote Koshi river, Dix stated early Monday that disaster response squads are steering through a complex, multi-layered emergency. Right now, in Nepal, we are facing something I have never faced before, Dix posted on social media. Not one rescue, but multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties and lives that may still be saved. Recalling insights gained from the Silkyara mission, where a singular, highly intricate subterranean extraction successfully restored forty-one men to their families, Dix underlined that current conditions near the Bhote Koshi require transitioning from a singular concentration towards managing several concurrent crisis zones amidst intense unpredictability. Synthesising Western professional duties with Eastern philosophical frameworks, Dix observed that the magnitude of the calamity demands enduring commitment irrespective of immediate results. Asian traditions offer another powerful idea: dharma, he wrote. The test is not simply whether we succeed. It is whether we continue to do what is right when the path becomes harder, the responsibilities multiply, and the outcome cannot be known. While search and recovery missions proceed across severely impacted segments of the Bhote Koshi corridor, domestic and overseas response units continue traversing perilous terrain to reach isolated populations. Silkyara taught me never to confuse unlikely with impossible, Dix added. Nepal is teaching me something more: when several lives may depend upon us at once, hope must become discipline, compassion must become action, and duty cannot depend upon certainty of success. Specialist response squads and technical personnel maintain continuous operations on-site, contending with persistent water currents and heavy rubble that obstruct routes to devastated settlements. Amid these ongoing rescue operations following the devastating floods, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) reported that an Indian technical team has made encouraging progress in efforts to clear the Chilime tunnel, while an Indian forensic team has processed more than 400 DNA samples. According to the MEA, the Indian technical team continued its manual efforts to clear the tunnel at Chilime and made progress on a makeshift path that would allow access by heavy machinery. The improvised track is now close to one kilometre in length, while the team has also commenced work on creating rope-based access to the tunnel. Meanwhile, the Indian forensic team has been processing more than 400 DNA samples at two laboratories in Kathmandu and has already generated around 70 DNA profiles, as stated by the MEA. In related developments, foreign media journalists seeking to collect news from flood-affected areas along Nepal's Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers will now be required to obtain a Press Accreditation and Journalist Identity Card from Nepal's Department of Information and Broadcasting (DoIB), according to an official notice issued by the Government of Nepal. Concurrently, Nepali authorities have issued an alert along the river basins of the Budhigandaki River following floods in the mountainous region of Gorkha. The alert was prompted by a flood in the Therang River, which flows through Chumanubri Rural Municipality-4 and 2 in the mountainous region of Gorkha district. Officials stated that the flood earlier this morning swept away four houses and a suspension bridge, an incident expected to cause difficulties for tourists trekking in the Manaslu region. According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), the death toll in the Rasuwa flood and related incidents in Nepal has risen to 1,342, following a review of the latest status of search, rescue, and relief operations at the 36th meeting of the Executive Committee for Disaster Risk Reduction and Management and a joint meeting of lead government agencies on Sunday. The latest NDRRMA update issued at 6 pm on September 6 indicated that around 4,996 people remain missing, including approximately 1,967 in Rasuwa and 2,340 in Nuwakot, alongside around 589 foreign nationals. title: Nepal holds a day of mourning after floods kill 1 , 300 – Winnipeg Free Press
full_text:
KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Nepal held a day of mourning Monday to remember those killed in the Aug. 26 floods, with flags lowered at government offices and families concluding mourning rituals.

Monday was the 13th day since the flooding which killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal and Tibet and left some 5,000 missing, including foreigners, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

In predominantly Hindu Nepal, mourning periods last 13 days, during which close family members stay home and relatives visit to pay their respects. Rituals are held on the final day to pray for the souls of the departed.

Buddhist monks offer prayers for the departed soul of the victims of flash flood on the bank of Trishuli river in Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal, Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026. (AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha)

Several people whose relatives remain missing performed symbolic funerals. Cremation is an important final rite in Hindu tradition, and performing the ceremony even without the bodies of their loved ones provided some families a sense of spiritual release.

title: A Stranger in a Regina Park Asks How to Help Flood Victims in Nepal
full_text:
Regina, Saskatchewan, Canada — “Are you Indian or Nepali?”

I was walking through a park in Regina when an elderly woman stopped me with that question.

“I’m Nepali. I’m from Nepal,” I replied.

She had heard about the floods in Nepal and wanted to know what had happened. We sat down, and I told her about the deaths, damaged homes, missing people and the difficulties facing families in the affected areas. I also mentioned reports of Canadian nationals who had been affected or were still missing.

She listened quietly. Then she held my hands.

“How can people donate money to the flood victims without worrying that it will be misused?” she asked.

I told her about the official QR-based relief channel connected with the Nepal government’s disaster-response efforts. I also explained that anyone wishing to help should use verified donation channels and be careful with appeals from people or organizations whose details cannot be confirmed.

I thought that would be the end of our conversation. Instead, she invited me to a daytime community gathering and said she wanted others to hear about what was happening in Nepal.

I agreed to go.

At the gathering, I spoke about the floods and the difficulties facing families in the affected areas. People listened and asked questions. Some said they wanted to contribute to relief efforts. Others said they would share information about the disaster with friends and members of their communities.

The meeting stayed with me.

The woman had no personal connection to the people affected by the floods, as far as I knew. She had never met them. Yet she wanted to help—and she wanted to be sure that her money would reach those who needed it.

The Need for Clear Donation Channels

For people living outside Nepal, finding a reliable way to donate can be difficult. During a disaster, appeals for money appear on social media, in community groups and through different organizations.

Some are genuine. Others are harder to verify.

People who want to help should be able to find out who is collecting the money, where it will go and how it will be used. Official relief funds and established humanitarian organizations are one option. Community groups may also organize their own relief efforts.

The important thing is that donors have enough information to make an informed decision.

This matters not only to Nepalis living abroad but also to people in Canada and elsewhere who want to help Nepal but may not know which organizations or channels they can trust.

Help Is Needed After the Headlines Disappear

The needs created by a flood do not end when rescue operations are over.

Families who have lost their homes, property or sources of income still have to rebuild their lives. Roads, bridges, electricity and other infrastructure may also need to be repaired.

Recovery can take much longer than the emergency response.

That is why support may be needed long after the immediate crisis has passed.

The conversation in that Regina park was a small encounter, but it reminded me that people living far from Nepal are willing to help when they understand what is happening and know how they can contribute.

The woman was a stranger when she first asked whether I was Indian or Nepali.

By the end of our conversation, she was asking what she could do for people affected by the floods in Nepal.

That was the part I found most meaningful.

People are willing to help. They need reliable information and a trustworthy way to do it.

title: Nepal marks national mourning day after deadly flood
full_text:
By Gopal Sharma, Sahana Bajracharya and Ju-min Park

KATHMANDU/BEIJING, Sept 7 (Reuters) – Nepali rescuers searched on Monday for more than 100 hydropower workers feared trapped in tunnels days after four miracle rescues from the wreckage of catastrophic floods that laid waste to towns and villages on the Himalayan border with China.

The rescues have offered a glimmer of hope as Nepal marked the 13th day after the disaster, ​traditionally the final day of mourning in Hindu rites, for the hundreds killed in the floods.

About 121 of a total 900 ‌people missing from the hydroelectric projects could have been trapped in these tunnels, army rescuers said. Others may have been working elsewhere at the power plants but not inside the vast network of tunnels.

Among those whom rescuers were trying to find on Monday were four out of six people missing at the Chilime hydropower project in the hard-hit Rasuwa district who could still be alive, Shri Ram Neupane, a lawmaker involved in rescue efforts, told Reuters.

Authorities had obtained specialised equipment and identified techniques needed for the Chilime operation, Neupane said. Rescuers ‌believe that ​there could be survivors trapped inside tunnels because many have air pockets, as well as spaces and ⁠rooms for people to stay, they said last ⁠week.

In recent days, search teams in Nepal have rescued four people, including a Chinese national who was pulled from a tunnel on Saturday. The others were two hydropower workers rescued from another tunnel on Friday and a Nepali woman pulled out from her buried house on Saturday.

Government offices in the Hindu majority country and at missions abroad would fly the national flag at half-mast to mark the 13th day after death, the ​home ministry said in a statement. The day is considered the final day of mourning by the faithful, who commemorate it with rituals and food offerings.

The disaster was triggered on August 26 when a huge mass of mud and rock, following the collapse of part of a glacier, crashed into ⁠a river along the border between Nepal and China’s Tibet region. The resulting floods ⁠washed away towns and villages and buried roads and highways under mud and debris.

At least 1,380 people have been ​killed by the mudslide and more than 5,500 are missing in Nepal and Tibet.

Nepal has asked the international community for urgent supplies, including high-capacity drones, Bailey ​bridges, DNA testing kits, tunnel rescue suits, and items for epidemic prevention, the foreign ministry said in a statement.

WILL ‌PROMPTLY SHARE INFORMATION, CHINA SAYS

Chinese officials said on Sunday that workers had recovered 12 more bodies as the search continued for hundreds still missing in Tibet. Many among the missing are Indians or people of Indian origin who were in the area in connection with trips to the Lake Mansarovar and Mount Kailash in Tibet, holy Hindu pilgrimage sites.

“The Chinese side will continue to make every effort to conduct search-and-rescue operations and handle post-disaster matters,” foreign ministry spokesperson Mao ⁠Ning said at a press briefing.

China has faced pressure from some families of foreign visitors missing in Tibet, who say they have struggled to obtain information on missing relatives.

Mao said Beijing would promptly release “updated information on the disaster situation and rescue activities.” On Sunday, China for the first time invited journalists ⁠from eight foreign media outlets, including Reuters, to visit ‌the core affected areas.

With search teams still looking for survivors, Nepal’s government has not planned any wider events for ⁠the final day of mourning.

“There are no government programmes organised as the rescue and search operation is ​still going on ‌in the flood-hit areas,” Phanindra Paudel of the National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC) told Reuters.

President Ram Chandra Paudel, ​the ceremonial head ⁠of state, was touring flood-hit areas on Monday and would survey damage caused by the disaster, his aide said.

Security personnel at the district jail in Nuwakot, one of the two worst affected districts, saved 923 prisoners by shifting them to a building in a higher location before flood waters entered their low-lying building on August 26, Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a social media post.

Authorities also captured 50 prisoners who had broken the prison wall and gates as flooding began, and had fled barely 100 metres, Shah said on Monday.

title: Survivor discovered in collapsed home amid flood devastation in Nepal
full_text:
ALIVE. Chandika Kumari Shresth is found by rescuers in her collapsed home in Betrawati village, Nepal on September 5, 2026.

'The four-storey house was swept (away) by the floods and the house was left in the middle of a quicksand. While walking around it, we heard a voice 'save me',' police officer Mahendra Darnal says

BETRAWATI, Nepal – Believing she had perished in Nepal’s deadly floods, the family of Chandika Kumari Shrestha started the ritual of mourning the elderly woman’s death.

Ten days later, rescuers found her alive inside her collapsed home in the devastated Betrawati village, where she had survived in a narrow pocket of air amid water and mud.

Play Video

“The four-storey house was swept (away) by the floods and the house was left in the middle of a quicksand. While walking around it, we heard a voice ‘save me,'” police officer Mahendra Darnal said.

In a rescue operation on Saturday, September 5, lasting 45 minutes, Darnal and his team found Shrestha in a confined space and sent her to an army hospital.

“I was in touch with the family and they had started the 11-day mourning period,” Darnal said.

Play Video

Shrestha was among the hundreds missing in Betrawati, an area among the hardest hit by the floods in Nepal and engulfed with white deposits compacted almost like concrete. Crews continue to recover scores of dead bodies.

The town’s market and most residential buildings, some as tall as four storeys, were almost completely buried under debris left by a torrent that swept through the valley, part of a disaster that killed more than 1,300 people across Nepal. Thousands remain unaccounted for.

Rescue workers wearing hard hats were seen digging with shovels, while some were crawling through the gaps of collapsed buildings periodically blowing whistles to get the attention of anyone trapped and alive.

Five days earlier, 24 bodies were found in a decomposed state in Betrawati’s market area in a building that had contained a small shop, Darnal said.

Looking for signs of life

Eleven days since a glacial collapse triggered the devastating floods, close to 5,000 are still missing.

Hundreds of bodies have been swept onto the banks of rivers far from the ravaged Rasuwa district. In Chitwan, hundreds of miles away, several rounds of mass burials have taken place for unidentified and badly decomposed bodies.

Even as hope is beginning to fade, Nepal authorities continue their effort to look for people stuck in tunnels and under the thick deposits of mud that have hardened over buildings.

Since Friday, they have pulled out three people from the tunnels, including a Chinese citizen by the Trishuli river, where more than 900 are believed to be trapped.

Others like Shrestha have survived in extraordinary conditions, including an 8-year-old boy who was also reunited with his mother. – Rappler.com

title: Nepal Observes Day Of National Mourning In Memory Of Lives Lost In Devastating Floods » IndiaPost NewsPaper
full_text:
KATHMANDU: Nepal is observing a day of national mourning on Monday in memory of lives lost in devastating floods which struck on August 26. A Cabinet meeting held on September 3 at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers had decided to observe national mourning in honour of the flood victims. Accordingly, the national flag is being flown at half-mast at government offices across the country, as well as at Nepali embassies and diplomatic missions abroad.

The Bhotekoshi flood struck Rasuwa, causing widespread loss of life and extensive damage to homes, roads, bridges, hydropower facilities and other critical infrastructure.

The disaster also affected downstream areas along the Trishuli River, including parts of Nuwakot and Dhading, leaving communities displaced and disrupting transport, electricity, water supply and other essential services.

Search and rescue operations, relief distribution and infrastructure restoration have continued in the affected areas, with national security agencies, government authorities, local communities and international partners involved in the response.

On the eve of the national mourning, Prime Minister Balendra (Balen) Shah issued a public statement acknowledging the ongoing work of Nepal’s security personnel involved in search, rescue and management operations following flood damage caused by the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers.

The statement highlighted a recent incident at the Central Jail at Khampa Camp in Bidur-6, Nuwakot, where floodwaters damaged administrative structures and reached lower levels of housing facilities.

According to the Prime Minister, 52 personnel from the Nepal Police and the Armed Police Force (APF) transferred all 923 inmates to higher ground within the complex while re-apprehending 50 inmates who attempted to escape through damaged perimeter structures, with several officers sustaining injuries during the process.

Despite damage to nearby barracks, loss of road access and disrupted water supplies, security personnel have continued maintaining operations and supplying necessities at the facility.

Nationwide, joint operations involving the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and APF have resulted in the rescue of 13,391 individuals via air and ground transport. Current deployments across affected regions include 9,287 personnel from the Nepali Army managing operations in Battar and Dhunche and assembling temporary bridges in Devighat.

Similarly, 7,975 Nepal Police officers are handling frontline search operations, body retrieval and canine unit deployments. Moreover, 4,203 APF personnel are operating across 13 response bases, utilising diving units, rope rescue teams and drone surveillance.

The Prime Minister also noted that 82 security personnel remain unaccounted for following the floods, including 45 from the Nepali Army, 25 from the Nepal Police and 12 from the APF. Shah expressed appreciation for the continued efforts of the security forces, their families and assisting experts, reaffirming the government’s commitment to supporting security personnel deployed in the field. Share Nepal holds day of mourning for more than 1,300 killed in floods on social media

Nepal is holding a national day of mourning to remember more than 1,300 people who died in last month’s catastrophic floods.

Government offices in Nepal and missions abroad are flying the national flag at half-mast on Monday, the 13th day since the floods, the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement.

In the Hindu tradition, it is the final day of the mourning period, during which close family members stay at home and relatives visit to pay their respects. On the final day, rituals are held to pray for those who died.

The government has not planned any wider events for this day of mourning because search teams are still looking for survivors and resources are limited.

“There are no government programmes organised as the rescue and search operation is still going on in the flood-hit areas,” Phanindra Paudel of the National Emergency Operation Center (NEOC) told the Reuters news agency.

A huge wall of mud and rock, triggered by a glacier breaking off, collapsed into a river on the Himalayan border of Nepal and China’s Tibet region on August 26, causing flooding that killed at least 1,380 people and left more than 5,500 missing.

In recent days, search teams in Nepal have rescued four people, including a Chinese national who was pulled from a tunnel at a hydropower site on Saturday. The others rescued were two hydropower workers from another tunnel on Friday, as well as a Nepali woman pulled out from her buried house on Saturday.

President Ram Chandra Paudel, the ceremonial head of state, is touring flood-hit areas on Monday and will survey damage caused by the disaster, his aide said.

In Kathmandu, family members gathered near the offices of the prime minister and key ministries to demand the speeding up of the search for the hundreds of people who were working on hydropower projects and were either swept away by the rushing Bhotekoshi River or buried by the debris.

Sumana Shrestha stood with her family members holding a poster with the photo of her 55-year-old husband, who has not been heard from since the day of the flood.

Her husband, a consulting geologist, was supposed to return home after his shift at the project office for the Trishuli hydropower plant on the day of the flood. The two-and-a-half-storey office was buried by debris.

“We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already,” she said. “The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle.”

Another protester, Mahesh Prasad Shrestha, held a photograph of his brother Niraj Shrestha, a 52-year-old engineer who worked at the same site.

He said authorities sent only a small excavator by helicopter on the sixth or seventh day after the disaster, adding: “They should have ordered big helicopters from places like China or India to fly in equipment.”

Rescue efforts have focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said.

Specialised rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects.

title: Virginia group raises money and awareness for Nepal after catastrophic flooding – WTOP News
full_text:
Eleven days after catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border killed more than 1,300 people and left thousands missing, hundreds of workers are still believed to be trapped in tunnels at hydropower sites buried by mudslides.

Former Haymarket Town Council member Madhu Panthi and the Manassas-based America Nepal Helping Society are asking for support.

“In the world, I’d like to humbly request if there is any equipment that can dig and to open the tunnel … you know more than 5,000 people are missing. And what is the best mechanism to save their life? That’s what we are looking for,” Panthi said.

Related stories

Panthi moved to Northern Virginia from Nepal in 2001 and helped coordinate donations and disaster response efforts after a 7.8 magnitude earthquake killed thousands and damaged more than 1 million homes and buildings in Nepal in 2015.

“That earthquake also did lots of damage. But earthquake, you can remove the debris and you can find the people in there. But this one is, you know, wiping out everything, and now the roads are not there. The bridges are not there. House, school and everything, everything is destroyed and wiped away,” Panthi said

The nonprofit has set an initial goal of raising $100,000 to support emergency shelter, food, water, health services and other relief efforts. As of Sunday, it had raised more than $52,000.

Panthi said the group is working with the Embassy of Nepal in D.C. and the Nepalese government, to help determine where the money is needed most.

According to the organization’s website, all donations are “subject to due diligence and final approval” and that the money “may support Government of Nepal disaster-relief funds identified in the Government’s 26 August appeal and/or other qualified humanitarian recipients.”

“They can donate by credit card. They can send by check. And all money goes 100% to the victims of Nepal: their food, their shelter, their medical, you know, their clothes, their livelihood,” Panthi said.

Panthi, who said one of his closest friends remains among the missing, told WTOP that ANHS is not sending rescue teams to the disaster area, unlike after Nepal’s 2015 earthquake when some of the group’s members went to distribute aid alongside Fairfax County Fire and Rescue personnel deployed with USAID’s Disaster Assistance Response Team.

Instead, the group is focused on raising money and working within Nepal’s “one door policy,” which is intended to streamline relief distribution and prevent aid from being unevenly distributed. “We don’t want to, you know, send somebody and then some area-people are not getting [help], and some area-people have too much,” Panthi said.

Panthi said that’s another reason ANHS is so focused on its financial goal to help Nepal: “Our heart, our brain, our everything is there. Our family are there. What can we do?”

Last week, PKP Tender Hearts Foundation, an area group dedicated to preserving Nepalese culture and serving communities in Nepal, held a candlelight vigil in Fairfax County with the George Mason University’s Nepalese Student Association to raise money and awareness for the flood victims.

People interested in donating to the America Nepal Helping Society’s disaster relief fund can do so through the organization’s website.

title: Monday Starter : Nun leading Caritas Nepal calls for international aid after floods
full_text:
Caritas Nepal, led by Sr. Cecilia Shrestha, extends help to those affected by the recent flash flood. (Courtesy of Caritas Nepal)

With the death toll mounting to more than 1,000 and with more than 4,500 missing, the executive director of Caritas Nepal is warning that the disaster caused by massive flooding in the country on Aug. 26 has not fully played out and will require international support for months to come. "The situation remains extremely alarming, and the number of casualties continues to rise as search and rescue operations are still ongoing," Sr. Cecilia Durga Shrestha, a member of the Sisters of St. Joseph of Cluny and head of Caritas Nepal since 2023, said of Nepal government search, rescue and relief efforts. "Thousands of people have been affected, with many lives lost, people still missing, and significant damage to homes, roads, bridges, livelihoods and other essential infrastructure," Shrestha told GSR, speaking specifically of the flooding that swept through communities in Nuwakot near the Himalayan nation's border with China.

Sr. Cecilia Durga Shrestha, a member of the Sisters of St. Joseph of Cluny, has been serving as executive director of Caritas Nepal since 2023. (Courtesy of Caritas Nepal)

Shrestha said that since the second day of the disaster, Caritas Nepal and its partners have been on the ground accompanying affected communities. "We are providing food and non-food items, essential household utensils, and other emergency supplies," Shrestha said. "We are also supporting people who have lost family members with essential items needed for mourning and funeral rituals, as well as providing medical kits to affected communities in different locations." However, at present, the most urgent needs include temporary shelter, debris clearance, essential household items, temporary learning centers for children, psychosocial counseling, medical assistance and support to restore basic livelihoods and services. Shrestha stressed the need for the international community to continue accompanying affected communities in the coming months. "Financial support would be particularly valuable to enable us to respond to both immediate humanitarian needs and the longer-term recovery and rebuilding of affected families and communities," she said. Nepal has a population of 31 million and is predominantly Hindu, with only about 10,000 Roman Catholics. But Caritas' response, Shrestha said, is to extend a "helping hand to the affected people from the ground," regardless of religious affiliation.

Loyola University honors the late Sr. Jean Schmidt with campus statue Loyola University Chicago has honored one of its icons, the late Sr. Jean Dolores Schmidt — longtime Loyola Ramblers basketball fan, team chaplain and campus fixture — with a statue on the university's Rogers Park campus. The Aug. 21 unveiling of the cast bronze statue, which depicts Schmidt sitting on a bench and holding a Loyola basketball, fell on what would have been the beloved sister's 107th birthday and a little less than a year since Schmidt's death at age 106 on Oct. 9, 2025. Known to all as Sister Jean, Schmidt received international attention and acclaim during the Loyola Ramblers' appearance during the 2018 NCAA March Madness tournament, the year she served as the team's chaplain at age 98.

Tom Hitcho, Loyola senior associate athletics director and longtime friend of Sr. Jean Schmidt, was the first to sit next to the statue after it was unveiled Aug. 21, 2026, at Loyola University Chicago. (Courtesy of Loyola University Chicago)

But during the statue unveiling ceremony, university officials and members of her congregation, the Sisters of Charity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, praised Schmidt for being more than a dedicated basketball fan. "Sister Jean's ministry of presence was a gift to generations of Ramblers," said Loyola President Mark Reed, who praised Schmidt's compassion, joy and concern and care for students and staff. In her remarks, Sr. LaDonna Manternach, president of the Sisters of Charity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, recalled Schmidt's love of Loyola students. "A good listener, she inspired many to pursue their dreams with purpose. Her deep trust in God guided her life and encouraged others to trust their own journey. "

title: As Nepal identifies those killed in the floods , questions grow over China reporting
full_text:
BEIJING — Shortly after the deadly flash floods hit the border of Nepal and China on Aug. 26, Nepalese authorities released a list of names, ages and nationalities of hundreds of missing foreigners. In contrast, Chinese authorities took five days to disclose that the 261 foreigners missing in Tibet come from 23 countries.

Twelve days on, very little is known about the victims in Tibet as Chinese authorities have restricted reporting on the floods.

To date, Nepal has reported over 1,300 dead and nearly 5,000 missing, while China is reporting over 40 dead and more than 500 missing.

"Xinhua (state-run news agency) and (state broadcaster) CCTV have total information dominance," said David Bandurski in Taipei with the China Media Project, which monitors news censorship in China.

These outlets are expected to "guide public opinion," he said.

While China has always censored information, controls have tightened steadily over the last decade, he said to levels that are "unprecedented."

No independent access

Rights groups that have been closely following the disaster relief say the lack of independent access to the area of the flooding in Gyirong County in Tibet is striking.

"This is in contrast to the Nepal side of the border where there was immediate access given for journalists, for other observers, for international humanitarian relief organizations," said Ryan Fioresi of the DC-based International Campaign for Tibet.

To report on the rescue efforts in Nepal, NPR was able to check in with international aid agencies on the ground and speak with a rescue pilot . Nepal's police, disaster management authority and the tourism board have also been providing regular updates on their social media feeds.

Whereas in China, the government restricts foreign journalists from entering the politically sensitive region.

It took more than a week of repeated requests from multiple international media outlets before the Chinese government allowed foreign journalists in Tibet.

Dar Yasin / AP / AP People take part in a candlelight vigil for victims of the floods in Nepal and Tibet, at Durbar Square in Kathmandu, Nepal, Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026.

However, it was limited to a small number of foreign outlets in a carefully arranged visit. NPR was not granted access.

The International Campaign for Tibet claims at least 300 homes were destroyed in Gyirong County, and Fioresi said the casualty count could be "much higher" than the dozens reported by Chinese officials so far.

He also said Tibetans in the worst affected areas were relocated to "tightly controlled holding areas."

"Their communications with the outside world have been extremely limited and curtailed," Fioresi said, adding that it hampers local rescue efforts.

China's foreign ministry has not responded to NPR's request for comment.

However, in an earlier briefing with reporters in Beijing, foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun denied China was understating the number of missing and dead, saying China has been "open, transparent and timely in information release."

"Smear and disinformation is most unwelcome at a time of disaster response," Guo said.

How different Chinese media are covering the tragedy

China's commercial media, which were still subject to censorship but had more leeway, would have sent journalists to a disaster site quickly in the past, according to Rose Luqiu, an associate professor of journalism at Hong Kong Baptist University who studies Chinese propaganda and censorship.

She said she saw the Beijing News and Southern Weekly had tried to do some of their own reporting.

ARUN SANKAR / AFP / AFP China Fire and Rescue personnel arrive at Trishuli camp after inspecting the tunnel site in Rasuwa, in the aftermath of flash floods in Nepal's Nuwakot district on August 31, 2026. Rescuers struggled on August 31 through mud and debris for a sixth day, as the number of missing people soared to nearly 5,000 since tsunami-like glacial floods roared down from the China-Nepal border, creating an "unimaginable" disaster.

"For example they tried to interview tourists. Not victims or those directly impacted in the local villages but they're trying to … provide some more information," she said.

In the 2008 Sichuan earthquake, various Chinese media outlets sent hundreds of journalists to the scene "in direct violation of an explicit ban from the central propaganda department of the Communist Party," Bandurski said.

This time, he said, the Southern Metropolis Daily, known for its journalistic investigations, ran only one front page cover on the floods in the days after the disaster, and it was an article reprinted from the official Xinhua news agency.

"They didn't do additional reporting," Bandurski said, adding that it was unusual for the paper.

Bandurski said his team saw the same pattern in other commercial Chinese media outlets.

"Xi Jinping has reined in the [commercial] press, such as it was developing in the 2000s," he said. "We see a total control of the narrative and basic news and information."

Foreign ministry spokesperson Guo has denied China deletes videos and first-hand accounts online.

Niranjan Shrestha / AP / AP A Buddhist monk offers prayers for the departed soul of the victims of flash flood on the bank of Trishuli river in Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal, Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026.

But many of the videos that were circulating widely after the floods were being actively deleted, according to Bandurski.

Recently the Chinese police penalized 10 people for spreading what they called misinformation about the floods.

Chinese state media, such as Xinhua, CCTV and Tibet Daily, have sent journalists with rescue teams, sometimes hiking overnight with them at high altitudes, sleeping openly under the rain, to reach the worst affected area at the Gyirong-Rasuwa border crossing.

The focus of their coverage is on the rescue teams, logistics of the operations and how government leaders are reacting quickly to the disaster, according Luqiu.

She said there are state media reports on people affected by the floods, but compared with the reports on the rescue operations, "the situation about the victims and the village members is relatively very small."

NPR's Diaa Hadid in Mumbai, and Mamita Bhandari in Kathmandu contributed to this report.

title: Nepal holds a day of mourning after floods kill at least 1 , 300 people
full_text:
KATHMANDU, Nepal — Nepal held a day of mourning Monday to remember those killed in the Aug. 26 floods, with flags lowered at government offices and families concluding mourning rituals.

Monday was the 13th day since the flooding which killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal and Tibet and left some 5,000 missing, including foreigners, according to Nepal's disaster management agency.

In predominantly Hindu Nepal, mourning periods last 13 days, during which close family members stay home and relatives visit to pay their respects. Rituals are held on the final day to pray for the souls of the departed.

Several people whose relatives remain missing performed symbolic funerals. Cremation is an important final rite in Hindu tradition, and performing the ceremony even without the bodies of their loved ones provided some families a sense of spiritual release.

The government had declared Monday an official day of mourning and ordered flags at government offices lowered to half-staff.

Meanwhile, search efforts continued for the missing, but some protested that not enough was being done.

In Kathmandu, relatives gathered near the offices of the prime minister and key ministries to demand the government speed up search and rescue efforts for hundreds of people who had been working at hydropower plants and were either swept away by the rushing Bhotekhoshi River or buried under debris.

Sumana Shrestha stood with family members holding a poster with the photo of her 55-year-old husband, who has not been heard from since the day of the flood.

Her husband, a consulting geologist, had promised to return home after his shift at the project office for the Trishuli hydropower plant on the day of the flood. The 2 1/2-story office was completely buried by debris.

"We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already," she said. "The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle."

Another protester, Mahesh Prasad Shrestha, held a photograph of his brother Niraj Shrestha, a 52-year-old engineer who worked at the same site. He said authorities only sent a small excavator by helicopter on the sixth or seventh day after the disaster, adding: "They should have ordered big helicopters from places like China or India to fly in equipment."

Candlelight vigils were held in several places in Kathmandu in memory of the people who lost their lives during the flooding.

Rescue efforts have focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said. Specialized rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects.

Two Nepalese workers were rescued from the plant Friday, and rescuers pulled out a Chinese man from the facility on Saturday.

Nepal continued rescue and relief operations on Monday as the death toll from devastating flash floods and mountain collapses rose sharply, with thousands of people still missing and authorities warning of the wider impact of the disaster on communities and the economy.

Authorities said the death toll in Nepal had risen to 1,356 on Monday as more bodies were recovered from flood-hit areas. A separate report put the combined death toll from the August 26 glacial and mountain collapse along the China-Nepal border at at least 1,385 across Nepal and China, with more than 5,500 people missing in the two countries.

Hundreds of hydropower workers are among those missing, while rescue teams have continued searching affected areas for survivors.

Nepal observed a national day of mourning on Monday, the 13th day since the Rasuwa flash flood disaster. The country honoured more than 1,340 people killed in one of its deadliest natural disasters in recent history.

Rescue operations continue

Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet said rescue efforts were continuing at the same pace as they had since the first day of the disaster.

"Our focus is on search and rescue at three levels -- on ground, by air, and in the tunnels. We are making sure that no one is still stranded," Basnet told AFP on Monday.

The rescue of three workers trapped deep inside tunnels has raised hopes that more survivors could be found. Two Nepali workers were rescued on Friday, followed by a Chinese worker on Saturday.

Foreign experts from China, India and South Korea are assisting Nepali rescue teams. Australian tunnel expert Arnold Dix, who played a key role in the rescue of 41 workers trapped inside the Silkyara tunnel in Uttarakhand in 2023, is also advising teams in Nepal.

Dix described the current disaster as an unprecedented challenge, with several search operations taking place simultaneously inside hydropower tunnels.

"We are facing something I have never faced before," Dix, president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, said in a social media post.

"Not one rescue, but multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties, and lives that may still be saved."

"We are measured not only by the lives we save, but by the lives we refuse to abandon," Dix said.

He added, "Silkyara taught me never to confuse unlikely with impossible."

Calls for climate justice

President Ramchandra Paudel appealed to the international community to take concrete steps towards ensuring "climate justice" for Nepal and other countries bearing the impact of climate change.

His appeal came as rescue and relief operations continued across flood-affected areas.

Sharmila Shrestha, who lost her home and was separated from her baby for several days, was reunited with the child at a crowded shelter. In Rasuwa district, 16-year-old Sameer Tamang recalled the destruction caused by the Bhotekoshi River.

"In a single moment, the disaster took away my sisters," he said.

Nepal has also sought to reassure international tourists that the country remains open for travel as authorities assess the potential impact of the floods on the crucial autumn tourism season.

The Bhotekoshi flash floods have raised concerns about disruption to tourism and the sector's recovery.

Meanwhile, Nepal Police urged people not to keep, sell or distribute gold, silver, cash and other valuables recovered after the August 26 floods. Police asked anyone finding such items to hand them over to the nearest police office.

The government is continuing rescue, relief and recovery operations as teams search for people still missing in flood-hit communities and hydropower tunnels.

title: Gurkha Fire to host exclusive menu to fundraise for Nepal floods relief after raising more than £2 , 000
full_text:
A Nepalese restaurant has rallied to raise thousands of pounds in just two days to support relief efforts following devastating Himalayan floods.

Gurkha Fire owners and chefs Keshav and Raju Kandel say they are overwhelmed by the support after the disaster hit their home country.

Raju and Keshav Kandel who run Gurkha Fire, a Nepalese restaurant in Chatham, say they were urged to start a fundraiser by customers who wanted to help

As news reports of the situation came in, customers began asking how they could help and where to send funds for rescue efforts and rebuilding.

It prompted the pair to set up a JustGiving page with a target of £1000, with all funds going towards the Nepalese prime minister’s natural disasters fund.

Within two days it had already hit more than double the original goal and patrons were asking for more ways they could contribute.

The Chatham restaurant will now be hosting a special fundraising event on September 15 with a set menu where proceeds will again go towards relief efforts in their native Nepal.

The award-winning culinary pair, who opened Gurkha Fire in 2024 after decades of experience in the industry, say the response has been incredible.

Gurkha Fire is a popular Nepalese restaurant in Chatham and has been a regular at the Kent and Medway Food and Drinks awards. Photo: Google Maps

Raju said: “Everyone knows there was a big flood in Nepal and lots of people have lost their lives, lost families, lost homes.

“Our customer encouraged us to find ways they could support them, so we started this fundraiser and now we’re hosting a charity dinner as well.”

Keshav added: “It's really melted our hearts the way people are supporting us and want to help and have encouraged others in the local community to support the relief.

“This is all thanks to them, so it's really a very good feeling.”

The devastating flash floods struck at the Nepal-Tibet border on the morning of August 26 and has killed more than 1,300 people and destroyed more than 8,000 homes.

Gurkha Fire will be holding a special fundraiser with a menu exclusive to the event. The proceeds will go to the relief fund

Raju continued: “It was shocking news for us. No one was expecting these things.

“When we see the news on socials and TV, we immediately tried to contact our relatives, friends and families, but some of our relatives are still missing.

“So we still are just hoping they will be back but we’re not sure. Lots of people are still missing and more than 1,300 people already confirmed to have died.”

Keshav said: “At first I thought the videos were AI created, I just couldn’t believe it.

“One minute everything was perfect and after one minute, everything was a disaster.”

Devastating floods hit Nepal and Keshav said when he first saw the images he couldn’t believe what he was seeing was real. Photo: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP

The fundraising event on September 15 will feature a new dish for the restaurant which will be closer to the traditional Kathmandu style in honour of the victims of the tragedy.

The thali which will be served is a plate with a variety of flavours all in one dish and will be exclusive to the charity night.

Funds will go towards the continuing search and rescue operations, moving survivors to safe locations, and long-term rehabilitation.

More information and bookings for the event can be found at the restaurant’s website here. Donations can also be made via the JustGiving page here.

The Medway Towns have a connection with Nepal through the Gurkhas. In the restaurant, Gurkha Victoria Cross winners are displayed.

Medway has a key connection with Nepal through the Gurkhas, a unique unit in the Army with a reputation of being among the finest, and some families have been settled in the area for more than 200 years.

Elsewhere in the county, vigils have been held for the victims of the floods, including in Dartford as senior nurse at Darent Valley Hospital Sarada Simkhada is among the missing.

Mrs Simkhada travelled to Nepal on August 22 for a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a sacred mountain in Hinduism.

She last contacted her husband on August 25, the day before the disaster, and has not been heard from since.

Community members and civic leaders gathered at Dartford Civic Centre to show their solidarity with Nepal. Picture: Justine Larter

Nepal Red Cross Society teams are providing emergency shelter, food, drinking water, blankets and first aid supplies.

They are also supporting search and rescue operations and helping people locate missing relatives.

The British Red Cross has launched an appeal to support those affected in Nepal and people facing other emergencies worldwide.

title: Nepal floods : loss , dignity and the power of solidarity

Nepal’s floods: loss, dignity and the power of solidarity As Nepal recovers from devastating floods, children face loss, uncertainty and displacement. Dr Unni Krishnan, Plan International’s Humanitarian Director, reflects on what survivors need most and why dignity must guide recovery efforts. Communities have been destroyed by the flash floods in Nepal. Photo credit: Ganesh Jee.

In Nepal, I have witnessed both profound loss and extraordinary solidarity in the aftermath of the devastating flash floods. Across affected communities, families are grieving loved ones, searching for answers and trying to rebuild their lives. At the same time, neighbours, volunteers and humanitarian responders are coming together to support those most affected.

The longest wait

Every time a search-and-rescue helicopter lands, families watch without blinking. For some, it carries the possibility of a miracle: a loved one rescued and finally coming home. For others, it may bring news that ends days of agonising uncertainty.

Since the Bhote Koshi River surged on 26 August, families have searched army camps, hospitals and police stations daily. More than 11,000 people have been rescued, but thousands remain missing. More than 1,000 have died and 1.6 million have been affected.

Across northern Nepal, homes, schools, roads, bridges and markets have been swept away or buried beneath mud and debris.

In Bidur, I visited a relief centre where 56 children were sheltering with families and volunteers. Some had lost their parents. Some were still waiting for news. All had been separated from the people, places and routines that made them feel safe.

Their fear was impossible to miss. They had witnessed the flood come with a force they could neither comprehend nor withstand. Now, every rainfall and darkening sky causes fresh anxiety.

The floodwaters are receding, but thousands of families remain suspended between hope and heartbreak. They are waiting for answers, stability and for life to make sense again.

Children eat a nutritious meal at relief centre in Nuwakot district. Photo credit: Plan International.

Recovery must begin with dignity

When everything you own has been swept away, where do you begin?

At the relief centre, volunteers told us that many children arrived with nothing but the clothes on their backs. Families were trying to work out how to make a simple meal for their children.

“Disasters affect everyone, but not equally. Poverty, age, gender and disability can determine who suffers most and who finds it hardest to recover.” Dr Unni Krishnan, Plan International’s Humanitarian Director

In disasters, needs are immense. But the first question should not be what aid organisations have available. It should be what people need most. That distinction matters.

Humanitarian aid is not about distributing whatever happens to be in a warehouse. It is about listening to communities and providing support that is useful, appropriate and dignified.

Disasters affect everyone, but not equally. Poverty, age, gender and disability can determine who suffers most and who finds it hardest to recover. Across the affected areas, communities need access to clean water, sanitation facilities and essential supplies, including dignity kits for women and girls.

Children face risks, especially when they are separated from family members. While there are currently no reports of exploitation or abuse in the areas I visited, experience from previous disasters shows that risks can increase when families are displaced and protective systems are disrupted.

For the children I met, the psychological scars may outlast the physical destruction. They have watched floodwaters swallow homes and, in some cases, people they love. Most are living with the constant fear that the water could return.

Psychological first aid, safe spaces for children, and access to education are critical. Together they provide stability, routine and a sense of normality during recovery.

Dr Unni Krishnan assesses the damage in Nuwakot district. Photo credit: Plan International.

Nepal will need sustained support from donors and the international community. Local communities and volunteers, who are invariably the first responders, must be supported as partners, not treated as recipients of help.

This disaster is also a reminder of the importance of preparedness. As climate-related hazards intensify, early warning systems and anticipatory action are vital. One teacher, after receiving an early warning, moved more than 1,000 children to higher ground in time. That is the power of preparedness.

Humanitarian action is guided by the principle that assistance should be provided according to need. But dignity demands something more. People, including children, must have a voice in decisions that affect their lives.

The question here is not simply whether we help, it is how we help. Are we supporting people to regain a sense of safety, choice and control over their own recovery?

The power of solidarity

Local volunteers, community organisations, the army, police, government agencies and international humanitarian organisations have worked side by side to rescue survivors and reach isolated communities. Many are supporting others while coping with losses of their own.

This spirit extends far beyond Nepal. I was deeply moved to learn that schoolchildren in Nepal have collected money for the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund. Thousands of miles away, a 6-year-old girl in London, set up a pop-up fundraiser and raised enough money to provide around 10 dignity kits (which contain vital supplies for young girls).

These children remind us you are never too young or too far away to make a difference.

People may never meet, speak the same language or share the same experiences, yet they can still choose to stand with one another.

The floods have destroyed homes, separated families and taken lives. They have also revealed something powerful: the extraordinary human capacity to support one another when crisis strikes.

In moments of disaster, compassion can be as important as practical assistance. It reassures survivors that they have not been forgotten and reminds all of us that we share a common humanity.

Dignity, solidarity and hope will be essential to Nepal’s recovery. They are not extras to be delivered after the emergency response. They must be at the heart of it from the very beginning.

title: Nepal holds a day of mourning after floods kill at least 1 , 300 people - Boston News , Weather , Sports
full_text:
KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Nepal held a day of mourning Monday to remember those killed in the Aug. 26 floods, with flags lowered at government offices and families concluding mourning rituals.

Monday was the 13th day since the flooding which killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal and Tibet and left some 5,000 missing, including foreigners, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

In predominantly Hindu Nepal, mourning periods last 13 days, during which close family members stay home and relatives visit to pay their respects. Rituals are held on the final day to pray for the souls of the departed.

Several people whose relatives remain missing performed symbolic funerals. Cremation is an important final rite in Hindu tradition, and performing the ceremony even without the bodies of their loved ones provided some families a sense of spiritual release.

The government had declared Monday an official day of mourning and ordered flags at government offices lowered to half-staff.

Meanwhile, search efforts continued for the missing, but some protested that not enough was being done.

In Kathmandu, relatives gathered near the offices of the prime minister and key ministries to demand the government speed up search and rescue efforts for hundreds of people who had been working at hydropower plants and were either swept away by the rushing Bhotekhoshi River or buried under debris.

Sumana Shrestha stood with family members holding a poster with the photo of her 55-year-old husband, who has not been heard from since the day of the flood.

Her husband, a consulting geologist, had promised to return home after his shift at the project office for the Trishuli hydropower plant on the day of the flood. The 2 1/2-story office was completely buried by debris.

“We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already,” she said. “The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle.”

Another protester, Mahesh Prasad Shrestha, held a photograph of his brother Niraj Shrestha, a 52-year-old engineer who worked at the same site. He said authorities only sent a small excavator by helicopter on the sixth or seventh day after the disaster, adding: “They should have ordered big helicopters from places like China or India to fly in equipment.”

Candlelight vigils were held in several places in Kathmandu in memory of the people who lost their lives during the flooding.

Rescue efforts have focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said. Specialized rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects.

Two Nepalese workers were rescued from the plant Friday, and rescuers pulled out a Chinese man from the facility on Saturday.

KATHMANDU - Nepal held a national day of mourning Monday for victims of devastating glacial floods, as families of missing hydropower workers feared trapped in tunnels prayed rescuers might yet find them alive.

The August 26 glacial and mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border killed at least 1,398 people, with more than 5,500 missing, including around 800 foreigners.

Flags flew at half-mast, with candlelight vigils planned later in the day, following traditional Hindu mour­ning rituals on the 13th day after death.

SPIRITUAL RITES Buddhist monks offer prayers for flash flood victims at Trishuli in Nepal's Nuwakot district on Sept. 7, 2026. AFP Photo

Hundreds of hydropower workers are among the missing, but the rescue of three of them from deep inside tunnels -- two Nepalis on Friday and a Chinese man on Saturday -- have buoyed hopes that more could still be alive.

Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP on Monday rescue efforts were continuing “with the same tempo we had on day one”.

“Our focus is on search and rescue at three levels -- on ground, by air, and in the tunnels,” he said.

‘Hope’

Families of some of the missing workers who gathered in the capital Kathmandu said the ­government must move faster.

“We have a lot of hope,” said Reena Amatya Shrestha, whose brother is among the missing.

Australian tunnel rescue expert Arnold Dix, who is advising Nepali teams, said the operation presented an unprecedented challenge.

“We are facing something I have never faced before,” said Dix, president of the International Tunneling and Underground Space Association, in a post on social media.

“Not one rescue, but multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties, and lives that may still be saved.”

Foreign experts, including from China, India and South Korea, are aiding Nepali teams in rescue efforts.

“We are measured not only by the lives we save, but by the lives we refuse to abandon,” said Dix, a key adviser during the Indian rescue of 41 men trapped for 17 days inside the collapsed Silkyara tunnel in Uttarakhand state in 2023.

Advertisement

‘Help Nepal’

With mortuaries overflowing, Nepal has buried hundreds of bodies in mass graves after taking DNA samples for future identification, according to police

Only around 100 bodies have been identified and handed over to families.

While the exact cause of the glacial collapse is unclear, climate change is accelerating glacial melting worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.

The disaster has come just ahead of the anniversary of last year’s September 8-9 mass anti-corruption protests that toppled the government, and the young government now faces the enormous task of rebuilding communities and critical infrastructure.

A UN preliminary assessment estimated building damage from Nepal’s floods at $158 million alone, warning that total losses -- inclu­ding damage to roads and bridges, agricultural land and humanitarian costs -- would be far higher.

The United Nations has appealed for $50 million to help more than 84,000 people.

“My plea to the international community is -- this is the time to help Nepal,” UN country chief Lila Pieters Yahia told AFP.
