title: Colchester Nepalese Society launches flood disaster appeal
full_text:
At least 1,300 people died in the August 26 floods, which were likely caused by a glacier collapse, and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

The large flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border destroyed villages, roads and bridges.

Udaibahadur Gurung, chairman of the Colchester Nepalese Society, told the Gazette on August 27 that thankfully he did not know of anyone directly caught up in the incident.

August - Nepalese policemen watch as earthmovers clear the debris of flash flooding in Nepal's Nuwakot district (Image: AP/PA /Niranjan Shrestha))

Mr Gurung has now been able to launch a GoFundMe Page with a £49,000 target to help the agencies which are “working hard on the ground” and the long road to recovery in Nepal.

The society has raised £12,000 so far, including £2,786 donated through its online fundraising page. The rest was collected in person.

Mr Gurung said: “We are very grateful for the support.

“I am feeling more confident than before I started. It is very good that people are chipping in money.

Awful - a drone view shows houses damaged by flash floods surrounded by sludge, mud and debris along the swollen Trishuli River in Devighat, Nepal, Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Rajesh Kumar Singh) (Image: AP/PA)

“I hope I will be able to get to the target as this has been the worst disaster to strike Nepal since the devastating earthquake of 2015.”

Latest rescue efforts have taken place at the Trishuli hydropower project where a Chinese national was pulled out alive from a tunnel.

The Nepalese Army said the man was pulled alive from a 738ft tunnel and is undergoing a health assessment.

About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects across Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in various tunnels, according to authorities.

Appealing for more support, Mr Gurung said: “The Nepali government has declared the affected districts disaster zones.

August - Rescuers use an earthmover to carry a victim of flash flooding to safety along the Trishuli River in Nepal's Nuwakot district (Image: AP/PA /Niranjan Shrestha))

In this photo provided by the Nepal Army, a Chinese national is seen after being rescued by soldiers during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli-3A hydropower project in Nepal's Rasuwa district, Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026. (Nepal Army via AP) (Image: AP/PA)

“International support is arriving, including emergency assistance from India, the United States, and South Korea, as well as satellite mapping teams from the United Nations and the European Union.

“But the need on the ground for shelter, clean water, medical care, and the long road of rebuilding to come will far outstrip what any single response can provide.

“Colchester Nepalese Society, representing the Nepalese and Gurkha community here in Colchester, is asking for your help.

“Many of us have family, friends and roots in the very communities affected by this tragedy, and we are determined to do everything we can to support them.”

The Colchester Nepalese Society will be holding a vigil at the Castle Methodist Church in Maidenburgh Street to light candles in remembrance of the people who have died and been displaced.

A charity curry night will also be held. Both will take place this month once dates have been organised.

The Gurkha Brigade is also raising funds to support those affected by the disaster.

Poster - The Gurkha Brigade's appeal which is separate to the Colchester Nepalese Society's efforts (Image: The Gurkha Brigade)

Colchester Council deputy leader David King said: "'The Gurkhas and the garrison are a huge part of our city and our history.

"Please support this appeal and the official fundraiser from the Brigade of Gurkhas.

"To show our respect compassion and care for the people of Nepal as they try to console their own and rebuild and recover from their terrible times. It will take many years.

"We can start now. To show some love and make a difference, please donate. It will be hugely appreciated in Nepal and here in Colchester by their friends and family and compatriots."

You can donate to the Colchester Nepalese Society's fundraiser at gofundme.com/f/nepal-flood-relief-2026-help-the-communities-of-rasuwa.

title: Nepal holds a day of mourning after floods kill at least 1 , 300 people
full_text:
KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Nepal held a day of mourning Monday to remember those killed in the Aug. 26 floods, with flags lowered at government offices and families concluding mourning rituals.

Monday was the 13th day since the flooding, which killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal and Tibet and left some 5,000 missing, including foreigners, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

In predominantly Hindu Nepal, mourning periods last 13 days, during which close family members stay home and relatives visit to pay their respects. Rituals are held on the final day to pray for the souls of the departed.

Several people whose relatives remain missing performed symbolic funerals. Cremation is an important final rite in Hindu tradition, and performing the ceremony even without the bodies of their loved ones provided some families a sense of spiritual release.

The government had declared Monday an official day of mourning and ordered flags at government offices lowered to half-staff.

Meanwhile, search efforts continued for the missing, but some protested that not enough was being done.

In Kathmandu, relatives gathered near the offices of the prime minister and key ministries to demand the government speed up search and rescue efforts for hundreds of people who had been working at hydropower plants and were either swept away by the rushing Bhotekhoshi River or buried under debris.

Sumana Shrestha stood with family members holding a poster with the photo of her 55-year-old husband, who has not been heard from since the day of the flood.

Her husband, a consulting geologist, had promised to return home after his shift at the project office for the Trishuli hydropower plant on the day of the flood. The 2 1/2-story office was completely buried by debris.

“We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already,” she said. “The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle.”

Another protester, Mahesh Prasad Shrestha, held a photograph of his brother Niraj Shrestha, a 52-year-old engineer who worked at the same site. He said authorities only sent a small excavator by helicopter on the sixth or seventh day after the disaster, adding: “They should have ordered big helicopters from places like China or India to fly in equipment.”

Candlelight vigils were held in several places in Kathmandu in memory of the people who lost their lives during the flooding.

Rescue efforts have focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said. Specialized rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects.

Two Nepalese workers were rescued from the plant Friday, and rescuers pulled out a Chinese man from the facility on Saturday.

Binaj Gurubacharya, The Associated Press

title: Nepal floods : Toll rises to 1 , 356 , search stepped up for 5 , 000 missing
full_text:
Nepal grapples with the devastating aftermath of flash floods, as the death toll climbs, thousands remain missing, and recovery efforts face immense challenges, prompting international calls for climate justice and national unity.

IMAGE: A joint team of India and Nepal works to construct the road towards the flood-hit hydropower tunnel as part of rescue operations, at Chilime in Rasuwa, Nepal, September 7, 2026. Photograph: Indian Embassy, Kathmandu/ANI Photo

Key Points Nepal's flash flood death toll has surged to 1,356, with 4,994 people, including 589 foreign nationals, still missing.

Identification of recovered bodies is a significant challenge due to severe damage, decomposition, and being swept far downstream.

President Ramchandra Paudel has appealed to the international community for climate justice and urged national unity for relief efforts.

International assistance, including experts from India and China, is aiding search and rescue operations, particularly for 121 men trapped in hydropower project tunnels.

Nepal has launched a 'Nepal Calling' campaign to reassure international tourists and prevent the floods from derailing its crucial autumn tourism season.

The death toll from the devastating flash floods in Nepal surged to 1,356 on Monday as more bodies were recovered from the affected areas, authorities said.

Rescue teams continued to search for 4,994 people, including at least 589 foreign nationals, who remain missing, while 13,396 people have been rescued so far, according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

The flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal.

The Bhotekoshi River, which flows south from the Himalayan border region, carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.

The disaster also killed at least 43 people on the Chinese side, while more than 500 people remain missing in Tibet, according to Chinese media reports.

Challenges In Body Identification

In Nepal, 363 bodies have been recovered in Chitwan district, 223 in Nawalparasi East, 221 in Nawalparasi West, 197 in Nuwakot, 169 in Rasuwa, 75 in Gorkha, 70 in Dhading and 38 in Tanahu, according to NDRRMA.

Identification of bodies has emerged as a massive challenge.

Only 98 bodies were identified as of Monday, and handed over to the families, according to NDRRMA.

Most bodies recovered after being swept downstream severely damaged, decomposed or recovered only in parts. Police have said that bodies carried far from the disaster sites and those that remained in water and mud have made identification particularly difficult.

Nepal Police has been collecting DNA samples from relatives of missing people to help identify unclaimed bodies and human remains recovered after the floods.

More than 1,000 unidentified bodies have been buried after DNA samples were collected to facilitate their identification in the future, officials said.

Hospitals struggled to cope with the growing number of unidentified bodies.

Large crowds continued to gather at medical facilities, carrying photographs of missing relatives and scrutinising images of the dead displayed on the walls.

President's Appeal And National Mourning

Nepal President Ramchandra Paudel on Monday visited flood-affected areas of Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts to take stock of the situation and review rescue and relief operations.

According to the President's Secretariat, he was briefed by senior officers on search and rescue operations, relief distribution, holding centres and rehabilitation efforts.

In a televised address to the nation after visiting the flood-hit areas, Paudel appealed to the international community to take concrete action to ensure climate justice for the Himalayan nation and other countries bearing the brunt of climate change.

The president also called on all Nepalese political parties and citizens to unite for relief efforts instead of blaming one another or engaging in confrontation. Nepal on Monday observed a national day of mourning on the 13th day of the disaster, with the national flag flown at half-mast at government offices across the country and at Nepali diplomatic missions abroad.

The mourning was observed in keeping with the traditional Hindu practice of marking the 13th day following a death.

The government has declared September 7 a national day of mourning to honour the victims of the catastrophic floods.

International Support And Ongoing Search

"Our thoughts are with the bereaved families and all those affected. India stands with Nepal in this difficult time and will continue to support Nepal's efforts towards search, rescue and relief," the Indian Embassy in Nepal said in a post on X.

Several families of people missing since the August 26 floods gathered at Maitighar Mandala area in Kathmandu on Monday, carrying placards bearing photographs of their loved ones and urging the government to step up efforts to locate them.

Thirteen days after the disaster, the families said they were still seeking clear information about the whereabouts of the missing and the progress of search and rescue operations.

NDRRMA executive chief Dharma Raj Uprety said the government has deployed security personnel round-the-clock for search, rescue and relief operations.

He further said relief had reached most of the affected areas, while efforts were continuing to deliver food and other essential supplies to locations accessible only by helicopter.

Around 3,500 people were staying in government-run holding centres across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading as of Monday, according to the NDRRMA.

But many others displaced by the floods have sought shelter wherever they could, including schools, temples, monasteries, empty office buildings, community buildings and tents set up in forested areas.

Hydropower Project Rescues And Tourism Revival

Major rescue operations are also underway at hydropower projects in flood-affected districts, where 121 men are believed to be trapped in underground tunnels.

The Nepali Army on Monday said search and rescue operations inside the tunnels would continue until a breakthrough is achieved, unless the government directs otherwise.

Brigadier General Subash Jung Thapa said rescue teams were conducting continuous searches inside the tunnels.

He further said, Army personnel, along with representatives of the Rasuwagadhi hydropower project, have reached the damaged powerhouse and the "control point" while searching for possible survivors.

Nepali Army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet said the rescue operation had been divided into three areas -- air, ground and tunnel searches -- with the Army working alongside other security agencies.

Teams of experts from India and China are assisting their Nepali counterparts in these operations. Australian tunnel expert Arnold Dix, who helped rescue 41 workers from India's Silkyara tunnel in 2023, is also assisting in the search for people believed to be trapped inside the Chilime hydropower project tunnel.

Meanwhile, reconstruction efforts have gathered pace, with authorities working to restore the flood-damaged Krishnabhir section of the Prithvi Highway in Dhading, where a 252-metre temporary track has been opened to reconnect the key Kathmandu-western Nepal road link.

Repairs are also underway on other damaged roads and crucial bridges. Nepal has also stepped up efforts to reassure international tourists that the country remains open for travel, as it seeks to prevent the recent flash floods from derailing its crucial autumn tourism season and undoing a fragile recovery in the sector.

Tourism Minister Khadak Raj Poudel has launched a social media campaign under the hashtag "Nepal Calling", telling foreign tourists that the country remains open and its Himalayan trekking routes are ready to receive visitors.

"Nepal is still open... Our Himalayan trekking routes are still waiting for you," he said in a video message posted on social media.

Tourism contributes about 6.7 percent to Nepal's GDP directly and indirectly and provides more than one million jobs.

Fall in the number of foreign tourist arrivals could have a wider economic impact, affecting hotels, trekking agencies, guides, porters, airlines, restaurants and transport operators.

title: Nepal Floods Disaster : 1 , 356 Dead , 5 , 000 Missing as India - Nepal Team Battles Mud - Choked Chilime Tunnel
full_text:
The search for survivors in Nepal has moved underground.

An India-Nepal technical team has established safety-rope connectivity inside the mud-choked Chilime tunnel, allowing rescuers and equipment to enter one of the most difficult sites created by the August 26 floods.

A large mud pump and generator have been transported to the tunnel to remove slush, while controlled rock blasting is being used to build a temporary access road for heavy machinery.

Above ground, the scale of the disaster continues to expand.

The death toll has reached 1,356, according to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Nearly 5,000 people remain missing, including 587 foreign nationals and approximately 100 security personnel and government officials.

More than 13,000 people have been rescued.

Nepal observed a day of national mourning on Monday, with flags lowered at government offices and diplomatic missions. But in Chilime and across the flood-ravaged districts, mourning remains suspended between identification and hope.

Thousands of families still do not know whether they are waiting for a survivor or a body.

What Is Happening Inside the Chilime Tunnel?

Indian Ambassador to Nepal Naveen Srivastava said the joint technical team was making steady progress despite challenging conditions.

“Safety rope connectivity to induct the team into the tunnel was successfully achieved,” he said in a social-media update. “A large mud pump and a generator were brought in to clear slush and mud from the tunnel.”

Rescuers are also constructing an approach road through controlled blasting, enabling larger equipment to reach the site.

The safety rope is crucial because the flooded tunnel presents several simultaneous risks. Rescuers must move through mud and debris with limited visibility while guarding against unstable surfaces, water accumulation, falling material and further movement in the surrounding landscape.

The authorities have not disclosed how many people may be trapped inside the tunnel or how far rescue teams have penetrated. The operation should therefore not be interpreted as confirmation that survivors or bodies have been located.

At this stage, progress means access. Every metre cleared gives the teams another place to search.

Why Has the Rescue Become So Difficult?

The floods did not create a single, clearly defined disaster site.

They damaged roads, bridges, settlements, hydropower installations and other infrastructure across several districts. Search teams are operating along river systems, inside tunnels and beneath enormous deposits of mud and debris.

Australian tunnelling expert Arnold Dix, who helped advise rescuers during the 2023 Silkyara tunnel operation in Uttarakhand, described the Nepal emergency as unlike anything he had previously encountered.

“Not one rescue, but multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties and lives that may still be saved,” Dix wrote from the field.

The Silkyara operation involved 41 workers trapped inside a defined tunnel space. Nepal’s rescuers are confronting multiple possible entrapment zones across a landscape altered by water, landslides and destroyed access routes.

The location of the missing may itself be uncertain.

Where Have the Bodies Been Recovered?

The official district-wise toll places Chitwan at the centre of the recovery operation, with 363 bodies found there.

Nawalparasi East has reported 223 bodies, followed by Nawalparasi West with 221, Nuwakot with 197 and Rasuwa with 169. Gorkha has reported 75 deaths, Dhading 70 and Tanahun 38.

Together, these figures account for the official toll of 1,356.

The recovery geography also demonstrates how far the disaster travelled. The Bhotekoshi flood devastated parts of Rasuwa before the impact spread into downstream areas along the Trishuli river system, including Nuwakot and Dhading.

Homes and roads were destroyed, communities were displaced and electricity, water supply and transport links were disrupted.

The largest concentrations of missing people have been reported in Nuwakot and Rasuwa. Around 2,340 people remain unaccounted for in Nuwakot and approximately 1,967 in Rasuwa.

How Many People Have Been Rescued?

Nepal’s disaster authority said 13,396 people had been rescued by Monday.

More than 21,400 security personnel have been deployed across the affected areas, including 7,912 Nepal Police personnel, 9,287 soldiers and 4,203 members of the Armed Police Force.

The official update said treatment had been provided to 6,676 injured people through hospitals and medical teams operated by the Nepali Army and Armed Police Force.

Another 3,533 people are staying at 39 holding centres. Nuwakot accounts for 2,651 of them, while 669 are in Rasuwa and 213 in Dhading.

The government has released emergency cash support to the most severely affected districts and local administrations. Search operations, relief distribution and restoration work are proceeding simultaneously, stretching personnel and equipment across a wide disaster zone.

Why Has DNA Become Central to the Operation?

Floodwater, mud and prolonged exposure can make visual identification difficult or impossible.

Nepal’s disaster authority said the recovered remains include unidentified bodies and human remains. Only 98 bodies had been handed over to families at the time of its update.

An Indian forensic team working at two Kathmandu laboratories has processed more than 1,200 DNA samples and generated approximately 292 DNA profiles, according to India’s Ministry of External Affairs.

Processing a sample and producing a usable profile are different stages. A sample may be damaged, incomplete or require repeated laboratory work before forensic scientists can extract sufficient genetic information for comparison.

Families searching for missing relatives have been asked to provide DNA samples, photographs and documents establishing kinship through the relevant district police offices.

The profiles obtained from relatives can then be compared with those generated from unidentified remains. For thousands of families, rescue has therefore entered its most painful phase: proving identity when recognition is no longer possible.

What About Indians Missing in China?

A parallel identification effort is under way across the border.

The Indian Embassy in Beijing has asked relatives of Indian nationals missing in China following the August 26 mudslide and flash flood to submit DNA data.

This is connected to the same wider Himalayan weather disaster but is distinct from the forensic operation taking place in Kathmandu.

Chinese authorities have agreed to receive DNA information relating to the missing Indians. Families have been asked to submit the data in the internationally recognised Combined DNA Index System, or CODIS, format to the Indian Embassy, which will forward it for comparison.

The request indicates that the search is no longer confined to national boundaries. Floods and mudslides across the Himalayan region affected Nepal as well as adjoining territory controlled by China, leaving foreign workers, travellers and local communities caught across different jurisdictions.

Why Is Nepal Observing National Mourning?

Nepal’s Cabinet declared Monday a day of national mourning for those killed in the floods.

The national flag was flown at half-mast at government institutions, embassies and diplomatic missions around the world.

The observance came as the country struggled to establish the disaster’s final human cost. With 4,994 people still missing, the confirmed toll is likely to remain provisional.

The large number of unidentified victims also means many families have been denied the rituals that ordinarily follow death. Nepal is mourning 1,356 confirmed lives. Thousands more remain suspended in official records under one word: missing.

What Happens Next?

The immediate priorities are gaining deeper access to the Chilime tunnel, reaching isolated communities, clearing transport routes and identifying the recovered bodies.

The tunnel operation will depend on whether pumps can remove mud and water faster than they re-enter, whether the access road can support heavy equipment and whether the internal structure remains safe for rescuers.

Across the wider disaster zone, authorities must continue matching DNA, supporting displaced residents and restoring roads, power and drinking-water supplies.

The number rescued—13,396—demonstrates the scale of the mobilisation. The number missing—4,994—defines everything still unfinished.

In Chilime, a rope now extends into the darkness. Behind it will come rescuers, pumps and machinery. For the families waiting outside, it carries something far more fragile. A route towards an answer.

title: Nepal holds a day of mourning after floods kill at least 1 , 300 people
full_text:
Nepal held a day of mourning Monday to remember those killed in the Aug. 26 floods, with flags lowered at government offices and families concluding mourning rituals.

Monday was the 13th day since the flooding which killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal and Tibet and left some 5,000 missing, including foreigners, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

In predominantly Hindu Nepal, mourning periods last 13 days, during which close family members stay home and relatives visit to pay their respects. Rituals are held on the final day to pray for the souls of the departed.

Several people whose relatives remain missing performed symbolic funerals. Cremation is an important final rite in Hindu tradition, and performing the ceremony even without the bodies of their loved ones provided some families a sense of spiritual release.

The government had declared Monday an official day of mourning and ordered flags at government offices lowered to half-staff.

Meanwhile, search efforts continued for the missing, but some protested that not enough was being done.

RELATED STORY | Two workers rescued alive from Nepal tunnel 9 days after floods

In Kathmandu, relatives gathered near the offices of the prime minister and key ministries to demand the government speed up search and rescue efforts for hundreds of people who had been working at hydropower plants and were either swept away by the rushing Bhotekhoshi River or buried under debris.

Sumana Shrestha stood with family members holding a poster with the photo of her 55-year-old husband, who has not been heard from since the day of the flood.

Her husband, a consulting geologist, had promised to return home after his shift at the project office for the Trishuli hydropower plant on the day of the flood. The 2 1/2-story office was completely buried by debris.

“We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already,” she said. "The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle."

Another protester, Mahesh Prasad Shrestha, held a photograph of his brother Niraj Shrestha, a 52-year-old engineer who worked at the same site. He said authorities only sent a small excavator by helicopter on the sixth or seventh day after the disaster, adding: “They should have ordered big helicopters from places like China or India to fly in equipment.”

Candlelight vigils were held in several places in Kathmandu in memory of the people who lost their lives during the flooding.

Rescue efforts have focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said. Specialized rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects.

Two Nepalese workers were rescued from the plant Friday, and rescuers pulled out a Chinese man from the facility on Saturday.

The Anak Krakatau volcano erupted on Saturday, grounding at least 200 flights across six Indonesian airports including Jakarta's main international hub and stranding hundreds of thousands of tourists.

Nepal has fallen silent for a national day of mourning as families mark 13 days since catastrophic floods tore through the Himalayas, killing more than 1300 people and leaving thousands more missing.

Flags were lowered to half-mast at government offices on Monday as families completed traditional Hindu mourning rituals for those killed in the August 26 disaster.

But for thousands of families, there is still no body to farewell.

About 5000 people remain missing across Nepal and Tibet, including foreigners, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency, as increasingly desperate relatives demand more be done to find their loved ones.

Several families performed symbolic funerals on Monday despite their relatives remaining missing, allowing them to complete important final rites without their bodies.

In predominantly Hindu Nepal, mourning traditionally lasts 13 days, with rituals performed on the final day to pray for the souls of the dead.

Camera Icon Mourners across Nepal lit candles to mark the 13th day of mourning for victims of the floods. Credit: AAP

But while the country mourned, anger was also growing.

Families gathered near government offices in Kathmandu demanding authorities ramp up search efforts, particularly around devastated hydropower projects where hundreds of workers remain unaccounted for.

Sumana Shrestha has not heard from her 55-year-old husband since the flood buried the two-and-a-half-storey building where he worked at the Trishuli hydropower plant.

“We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already,” she said.

“The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle.”

Authorities say rescue operations are focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped inside tunnels.

Teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States are searching debris, damaged buildings and tunnels, with glimmers of hope emerging in recent days.

Two Nepalese workers were pulled alive from a hydropower tunnel on Friday, while a Chinese man was rescued on Saturday.

Among those still desperately waiting for news are Australian families.

Newcastle father-of-two Bhavin Patel has spent almost two weeks searching for his wife Reshma, a Sydney council worker who disappeared while returning from a walking tour in Tibet.

He has chartered a helicopter, tracked her last phone signal and repeatedly approached authorities for information.

“She is my life,” Mr Patel told AAP.

“I am not going without her.”

Camera Icon Bhavin Patel has tirelessly searched Nepal's disaster zone for his missing wife, Reshma. Credit: AAP

Reshma was travelling back towards Kathmandu with the Isha Foundation when an immigration building near the Nepal-Tibet border was overwhelmed by the flood.

Mr Patel later flew over the site, seeing exposed earth where the building had stood, but was unable to land because of dangerous terrain.

“I felt like... if they give me permission to land, I might rescue her,” he said.

He is now calling for Australia to pressure Beijing for greater co-operation and information from the Chinese-controlled Tibetan side of the border.

“I can feel she’s alive, that she’s safe somewhere,” he said.

“Our government is trying, but it’s not enough.”

A group of Australian families has also called for greater transparency from tour operators and authorities as 36 Australians remain among the missing.

Australia has deployed a disaster assistance response team and specialist resources to Kathmandu and committed $11 million to the response.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese acknowledged the agonising wait facing families on Monday.

“This is now very much a race against time,” Mr Albanese told Parliament.

title: Two More Rescued in Nepal as Flood Toll Tops 1 , 398
full_text:
Two weeks after a glacier collapse on the flank of Langtang Lirung sent a wall of ice, rock and mud through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli valleys, Nepal's government has begun the arithmetic of rebuilding — and the numbers are outrunning the country's ability to pay for them. Officials in Kathmandu now expect a formal Post-Disaster Needs Assessment, due within five weeks, to put losses at least 30% above the initial estimate of 400 billion rupees, implying a reconstruction bill of $4 billion to $5 billion for a country whose debt has already swelled since the 2015 earthquake. The official toll on the Nepali side stands at 1,377 confirmed dead, 5,326 missing and 6,827 injured, with no new survivors reported since the weekend rescues that briefly turned recovery back into rescue.

Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told the Kathmandu Post that the government prefers grants and aid over loans, and on Tuesday instructed senior diplomats to press that preference with foreign governments and institutions. "Given the way the loan portion is ballooning compared to our GDP, if we are able to generate grants and aid in a considerable amount, it would be easier for us," he said, while acknowledging that declining loans is "not a declared policy." Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said grants were always preferred but could not meet all of Nepal's needs. Govinda Raj Pokharel, who oversaw the needs assessment after the 2015 earthquake, was blunter: in the current financial architecture, he said, "it is almost impossible to receive sufficient grants," and Nepal should reach out to wealthy individuals and philanthropies while also considering soft loans. The National Planning Commission's assessment will form the basis for a donor conference; the government also plans to file a claim with the global Loss and Damage Fund, arguing that climate change contributed to the flood's severity. A senior official said the sum sought there might be symbolic but could "open more avenues for us to claim compensation."

The scale of the damage explains the gap. Initial assessments count 7,570 houses destroyed or damaged and 32,933 people directly affected across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts. The Nepal Electricity Authority says 13 hydropower projects were hit, removing an estimated 431 megawatts from the grid and damaging projects under construction with a further 470 megawatts of capacity; the Independent Power Producers' Association puts losses at a dozen plants in Rasuwa and Nuwakot alone at 25 to 30 billion rupees, a figure it says is provisional because its members are still occupied with searches. Along the Trishuli, whole commercial strips such as Trishuli Bazar stand as gutted concrete frames, the ground floors sheared away or buried under gray sludge, and rescuers say the riverbed rose 30 to 50 feet in places, shifting the river's course over what were once tunnel entrances. The needs assessment is expected to recommend changes to settlement patterns, river-basin planning and the relocation of people from high-risk areas — recommendations that would require funding beyond reconstruction itself.

The search has not formally ended. Prime Minister Balendra Shah declared a shift toward rehabilitation last week after teams entered the last of the hydropower sites where active operations were under way and found no one; the weekend rescues of two hydropower workers from the Trishuli 3A tunnel, a Chinese worker from a flooded tunnel in Rasuwa, and a 60-year-old woman from a collapsed building in Nuwakot forced crews to keep listening at tunnel mouths. At least 557 workers remain missing from Trishuli 3A, about 115 of them believed to have been in the main tunnel when the water hit, and roughly 900 hydropower workers across a dozen projects are still out of contact. One of the rescued men told rescuers that more people remained alive in the tunnel; no further survivors have been reported. The Electricity Authority has asked relatives of missing workers to submit DNA samples, and mass burials with forensic documentation continue in the Devghat forest in Chitwan, nearly 200 kilometers downstream, where the river continues to return bodies.

The missing include, by the government's count, 147 officials — police, soldiers, customs and immigration staff, teachers and local representatives — as well as some 622 students and roughly 300 trade and transport workers who were at the Gyirong border crossing when the surge struck within minutes of the collapse. Hundreds of foreign nationals remain listed as unaccounted for on the Nepali side, among them dozens of Americans the U.S. State Department has said it continues to track, along with citizens of Ukraine, Malaysia, Britain and Canada. On the Chinese side, where 16 deaths and 546 missing were reported, Reuters described search teams picking through the ruins of the Gyirong port, once the busiest land crossing between the two countries; Chinese state media say more than 2,500 rescuers have been deployed there and the road to the border has been largely reopened along a route cut into the riverbank.

Nepal's handling of foreign assistance has been selective by design. The government initially declined offers of foreign search-and-rescue teams, citing the coordination problems of the 2015 earthquake response, before admitting specialists from India, China, Australia and South Korea for tunnel rescues, DNA testing and forensic work. More than 9,300 Nepali soldiers remain deployed for medical care, road clearance and patrols, and army engineers have been erecting temporary iron bridges to reconnect communities cut off since the flood destroyed their crossings. The Kathmandu Post reported Tuesday that the collapse of the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir, the main road west from the capital, has engineers urging urgent stabilization and a permanent tunnel or bridge, and that tourist hubs across the country have emptied in what should be peak trekking season — a second economic blow for a country where tourism is a principal source of foreign exchange.

The danger upstream has not passed. The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology has kept the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli under high flash-flood warnings with rain continuing in the upper catchment, and the debris-dammed lake that formed above Gyirong after the collapse remains under watch; Chinese authorities say the risk has been reduced but not removed. A rapid assessment by an international scientific consortium found that pre-event satellite imagery showed visible signs of instability — meltwater discharge and cracks in surrounding bedrock — in the days before the collapse, findings that have renewed calls for early-warning systems and cross-border data sharing. The same corridor flooded fourteen months earlier, killing nine and destroying the friendship bridge at the border.

That history is the subtext of the financing debate. Nepal borrowed heavily to rebuild after 2015 and is now being asked to borrow again for a disaster its officials describe as climate-driven, in a valley where the last flood was still being repaired when this one arrived. Whether donors treat the Bhotekoshi flood as a one-time catastrophe to be funded with grants, or as the first installment of a recurring bill to be met with loans, will be decided at the donor conference the needs assessment is meant to prepare — and it will shape not only what Nepal rebuilds but where, and whether the settlements along the Trishuli are rebuilt at all.

title: Omaha Nepalese community feels impact of deadly floods
full_text:
OMAHA, Neb. (WOWT) - More than 1,200 people are confirmed dead and more than 4,000 remain missing following floods near the Nepal-China border, according to the United Nations.

Members of Omaha’s Nepalese community are hoping for good news about family and friends still unaccounted for.

Community leaders wait for updates

Yadu Sapkota, president of the Nebraska Nepalese Society, said the wait for information continues more than a week after the floods hit.

“Today is the ninth day, still family members are waiting, maybe. They hope that they will be back,” Sapkota said.

Sapkota is waiting for an update on a childhood friend and his middle school teacher. No one has heard from them since the floods.

Flooding described as sudden

The U.S. Geological Society said the speed of the water combined with 30-foot waves washed out towns within minutes.

Subash Baniya, healthcare coordinator with the Nebraska Nepalese Society, said the flooding caught people off guard.

“That wasn’t something that people were anticipating or like anything like that, because it happened out of nowhere,” Baniya said.

UNL student reflects on nearby hometown

Sandeep Sharma, a Ph.D. student at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and president of the Nepalese Student Association at UNL, was born in Nuwakot, nine miles from the flood site.

“You really can’t not look at all of those, like, videos or not feel for the families that have had their family members missing or look at their stories and see how difficult it is,” Sharma said.

Society organizes relief efforts

The Nebraska Nepalese Society has created GoFundMe pages, reposted flyers for missing people and spread awareness about Nepal this week.

“I think one of the biggest things that we have seen in a crisis like this is how different communities and people from all over the world have really come together to help people in need of this crisis,” Sharma said.

“It has been a really humbling experience for all of us because there are different communities, different people really trying their best in order to help and support these victims and the families impacted,” Sharma said.

title: How two men survived nine days in a Nepal flood tunnel
full_text:
NUWAKOT, Nepal: A delirious Kabir Maharjan drifted in and out of consciousness in a pool of muddy water in complete darkness, trapped for nine days in a tunnel beneath the wreckage of Nepal's worst flood disaster in decades.

When he finally awoke at a hospital after a miracle rescue, he did not recognise his wife. Confused, he asked her why she had not given him a bed sooner.

When he finally awoke at a hospital after a miracle rescue, he did not recognise his wife. Confused, he asked her why she had not given him a bed sooner.

At 7:30 a.m. (0145 GMT) on the day of the disaster, Maharjan called his wife before his shift at the Upper Trishuli 3A hydropower project.

“I have to go inside the tunnel,” he told her. “There won’t be any network inside.”

Around 60 minutes later, a glacier collapsed at the Langtang Lirung mountain some 25 miles upstream, causing a landslide so powerful that it formed a wall of water that flattened villages and submerged a network of 12 hydropower projects with nearly 900 workers inside.

In the capital Kathmandu, electricity department officials were monitoring the projects' power supplies on their screens. Then the fields started going blank — one after another, stations disappearing from the control panels, falling like dominoes.

SurajDahal, an engineer at the Nepal Electricity Authority who led parts of the rescue effort, said he was not immediately alarmed because "floods are normal" in Nepal.

They soon understood otherwise. Because the 3A station manager was abroad, it took officials two extra minutes to reach out on call to theroughly 40 workers estimated to be inside. By then, at least two hydropower projects upriver had already been hit.

At 9:15 a.m. — two minutes after Maharjan's wife, Hira Shova Maharjan, had tried and failed to reach him —officials gave the final order to 3A:"Evacuate!"

Sah, who worked in the power house's control room, sped from floor to floor, warning colleagues individually, he later told rescuers.

Outside the tunnels, evacuating workers tried to run away from the flood, but were not fast enough. Officials pointed to footage showing a group of roughly 30 workers swept away by a wave many times their height.

Rescuers later identified an escape ladder which, had workers known of it, could have saved as many as two-thirds of those inside,said Dahal.

But they "didn't know where to go," he said.

Of the tunnel's four access routes, engineering drawings seen by Reuters showed one ran more than 180 meters to the underground powerhouse — but rescuers believed it was fully flooded, offering no hope of survivors.

Neupane instead turned his attention to a shorter cable-duct tunnel that sloped upward and was less exposed to the floodwaters. It was there that Maharjan and Sah had taken shelter, just 160 meters from the exit — "at the corner, at the edge of the tunnel," as Maharjan would later describe it to his wife.

When Hira Shova first heard about the flood, she assumed the powerhouse would be safe.

Officials believed that oxygen pockets scattered through the wreckage might help some workers survive.

Lawmaker and engineer Sagar Dhakal, along with Neupane, reached the site by army helicopterthe day after the disaster. They found heavy machinery couldn't move in immediately; the debris was too saturated.

"Everything you drop on that place just goes under," said Prakash Pokhrel, a geologist with Nepal's disaster management authority.

Crews first had to build a stable platform before any excavation could begin.

Serious digging didn't start until three days after the disaster. All four tunnels were blocked — mud, rock, timber and debris, some of it buried under 15 to 30 meters (49 to 98 feet) of landslide material. Rescuers turned to drilling, controlled blasting and heavy equipment to inch a path forward.

A breakthrough came when a 5-inch borehole drilled from above finally confirmed the tunnel's true alignment, giving crews a fixed point to dig toward.

Rain made everything worse. Several nights, downpours refilled the excavated shaft with fresh water and debris, undoing hours of work in minutes. When they called out for survivors, nobody answered.

Then the rain came again, triggering a partial collapse that briefly trapped several rescuers themselves. The operation stalled for hours before colleagues talked them back inside, and crews reinforced the passage with metal sheeting and gabion wire.

At 4 a.m. on the 10th day, Dahal got a call from a heavy equipment operator: the rescuers had heard something. A noise. Maybe a survivor. Maybe just an echo of the rescuers' own voices calling into the dark.

On the ground, Ganga Baral, who led the rescue team, said they began to hear noises as they drilled into the tunnel.

Another 5 to 10 meters of mud-choked passage stood between them and the survivor. By 7 a.m., soldiers broke open a small hole.

From inside came a single word:"hunuhuncha", which loosely translates to "we are here".

Neither man could stand when rescuers finally pulled them from the tunnel. Sah, his face caked in mud, had to be carried out on a rescuer's back. He managed to lift one hand toward a camera. Maharjan, with more severe injuries, went out on a stretcher.

Dhakal, who ran the operation from outside but never entered the tunnel himself, wept when the two men emerged. "I couldn't hold my tears," he said.

When Hira Shova walked into the hospital room, he did not recognise her.

“Where am I?” he asked her.

But she was just thrilled to get him back alive.

"He is blessed with another life."

title: Omaha Nepalese community feels impact of deadly floods
full_text:
OMAHA, Neb. (WOWT) - More than 1,200 people are confirmed dead and more than 4,000 remain missing following floods near the Nepal-China border, according to the United Nations.

Members of Omaha’s Nepalese community are hoping for good news about family and friends still unaccounted for.

Community leaders wait for updates

Yadu Sapkota, president of the Nebraska Nepalese Society, said the wait for information continues more than a week after the floods hit.

“Today is the ninth day, still family members are waiting, maybe. They hope that they will be back,” Sapkota said.

Sapkota is waiting for an update on a childhood friend and his middle school teacher. No one has heard from them since the floods.

Flooding described as sudden

The U.S. Geological Society said the speed of the water combined with 30-foot waves washed out towns within minutes.

Subash Baniya, healthcare coordinator with the Nebraska Nepalese Society, said the flooding caught people off guard.

“That wasn’t something that people were anticipating or like anything like that, because it happened out of nowhere,” Baniya said.

UNL student reflects on nearby hometown

Sandeep Sharma, a Ph.D. student at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and president of the Nepalese Student Association at UNL, was born in Nuwakot, nine miles from the flood site.

“You really can’t not look at all of those, like, videos or not feel for the families that have had their family members missing or look at their stories and see how difficult it is,” Sharma said.

Society organizes relief efforts

The Nebraska Nepalese Society has created GoFundMe pages, reposted flyers for missing people and spread awareness about Nepal this week.

“I think one of the biggest things that we have seen in a crisis like this is how different communities and people from all over the world have really come together to help people in need of this crisis,” Sharma said.

“It has been a really humbling experience for all of us because there are different communities, different people really trying their best in order to help and support these victims and the families impacted,” Sharma said.

title: Omaha Nepalese community feels impact of deadly floods
full_text:
OMAHA, Neb. (WOWT) - More than 1,200 people are confirmed dead and more than 4,000 remain missing following floods near the Nepal-China border, according to the United Nations.

Members of Omaha’s Nepalese community are hoping for good news about family and friends still unaccounted for.

Community leaders wait for updates

Yadu Sapkota, president of the Nebraska Nepalese Society, said the wait for information continues more than a week after the floods hit.

“Today is the ninth day, still family members are waiting, maybe. They hope that they will be back,” Sapkota said.

Sapkota is waiting for an update on a childhood friend and his middle school teacher. No one has heard from them since the floods.

Flooding described as sudden

The U.S. Geological Society said the speed of the water combined with 30-foot waves washed out towns within minutes.

Subash Baniya, healthcare coordinator with the Nebraska Nepalese Society, said the flooding caught people off guard.

“That wasn’t something that people were anticipating or like anything like that, because it happened out of nowhere,” Baniya said.

UNL student reflects on nearby hometown

Sandeep Sharma, a Ph.D. student at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and president of the Nepalese Student Association at UNL, was born in Nuwakot, nine miles from the flood site.

“You really can’t not look at all of those, like, videos or not feel for the families that have had their family members missing or look at their stories and see how difficult it is,” Sharma said.

Society organizes relief efforts

The Nebraska Nepalese Society has created GoFundMe pages, reposted flyers for missing people and spread awareness about Nepal this week.

“I think one of the biggest things that we have seen in a crisis like this is how different communities and people from all over the world have really come together to help people in need of this crisis,” Sharma said.

“It has been a really humbling experience for all of us because there are different communities, different people really trying their best in order to help and support these victims and the families impacted,” Sharma said.

title: Nepal holds a day of mourning after floods kill at least 1 , 300 people
full_text:
Nepal held a day of mourning Monday to remember those killed in the Aug. 26 floods, with flags lowered at government offices and families concluding mourning rituals.

Monday was the 13th day since the flooding which killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal and Tibet and left some 5,000 missing, including foreigners, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

In predominantly Hindu Nepal, mourning periods last 13 days, during which close family members stay home and relatives visit to pay their respects. Rituals are held on the final day to pray for the souls of the departed.

Several people whose relatives remain missing performed symbolic funerals. Cremation is an important final rite in Hindu tradition, and performing the ceremony even without the bodies of their loved ones provided some families a sense of spiritual release.

The government had declared Monday an official day of mourning and ordered flags at government offices lowered to half-staff.

Meanwhile, search efforts continued for the missing, but some protested that not enough was being done.

In Kathmandu, relatives gathered near the offices of the prime minister and key ministries to demand the government speed up search and rescue efforts for hundreds of people who had been working at hydropower plants and were either swept away by the rushing Bhotekhoshi River or buried under debris.

Sumana Shrestha stood with family members holding a poster with the photo of her 55-year-old husband, who has not been heard from since the day of the flood.

Her husband, a consulting geologist, had promised to return home after his shift at the project office for the Trishuli hydropower plant on the day of the flood. The 2 1/2-story office was completely buried by debris.

“We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already,” she said. "The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle."

Another protester, Mahesh Prasad Shrestha, held a photograph of his brother Niraj Shrestha, a 52-year-old engineer who worked at the same site. He said authorities only sent a small excavator by helicopter on the sixth or seventh day after the disaster, adding: “They should have ordered big helicopters from places like China or India to fly in equipment.”

Candlelight vigils were held in several places in Kathmandu in memory of the people who lost their lives during the flooding.

Rescue efforts have focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said. Specialized rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects.

Two Nepalese workers were rescued from the plant Friday, and rescuers pulled out a Chinese man from the facility on Saturday.

Two workers were rescued after spending nine days trapped inside a hydroelectric plant tunnel on Nepal's Trishuli River following deadly flooding and a mudslide.

title: How the Nepal - Tibet disaster became the latest victim of China  Clean Internet  campaign | China

The flooding disaster is an example of the increasing use by Chinese authorities of “Clean Internet 2026”, the latest version of a long-running campaign by the Ministry of Public Security that criminalises anything officials regard as false information, which includes unofficial accounts of the floods.

It follows a well-established playbook in which authorities promote official narratives, suppress independent accounts, discourage efforts to look back at the causes of a disaster and punish those who post claims that differ from the government-approved narrative.

While earlier versions of the campaign focused on cybercrime and hacking, it is increasingly being used to target what the authorities call “rumours” which include unofficial information about the disaster.

“The campaign serves a dual purpose. Tackling genuine problems like fraud and misinformation while tightening control over public narratives,” says Tencho Gyatso from the International Campaign for Tibet, a US based Tibetan advocacy group. “That dual purpose is what makes it more nuanced and challenging to criticise.”

In the hours after the floods, researchers say they saw a huge surge in interest across Chinese social media. The topic was trending, but then fell away as comments were removed in real time.

View image in fullscreen Flowers are placed on mud as a tribute at the disaster-hit area at Gyirong Port. Photograph: Tingshu Wang/Pool Reuters/AP

Screenshots seen by the Guardian show the Chinese app WeChat restricting posts about the floods. In one case, a user was notified by WeChat that a post about the flooding had been reported and then deleted for containing “politically sensitive content”. Another was stopped from being shared. It was said to be “unavailable due to policy violation” and that it contained “prohibited content”.

“[The trend] was constantly shifting and being manipulated because there was real interest,” says David Bandurski, director of the China Media Project, a research group that monitors Chinese media. “A ‘crackdown’ is not the right word, because they don’t crack down. It’s a consistent, persistent, everyday application of a policy of public-opinion guidance.”

On 30 August, four days after the disaster, police in Tibet reported 10 cases under the Clean Internet 2026 campaign relating to “rumours” about the disaster. In the majority of cases there were claims that more than 1,000 people had been swept away in the floods. So far, Chinese authorities have released a death toll of 43. Human rights and Tibetan advocacy groups have accused the Chinese government of concealing the true scale of the death toll.

The police notice said that spreading of “rumours” “misleads the public and disrupts online order” and it intended to “ensure that disaster relief work proceeds smoothly”.

A user from Jiangxi, a province 3,000km away from the disaster, posted on a video platform claiming “the number of missing people had risen to 826”. According to the police report the user faced “administrative punishment” without specifying what that involved.

‘Proving that the state is working hard’

One former Chinese state media journalist, who agreed to speak on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisals, says control in times of crisis also works through simple omission of information as much as suppression: “Official news coverage devotes enormous space to proving that the state is working hard, but gives very little information answering the most basic questions: who is missing? “Controls have become much stricter, especially regarding the internet, though there are nuances, as there are still ways to bypass restrictions. For instance, by posting quickly or using veiled language to get content through,” they say.

But allowing some reporting can serve the interests of central authorities, says one former CGTN editor who worked at the broadcaster during the Covid pandemic and who also asked not to be named for fear of reprisals.

Bandurski says: “The [Communist] party sees itself in a global public-opinion struggle. It is wrestling with the world fighting to get its view out. This is how China sees information globally, in a very, very oppositional framework.”

The night before the survivors were found, rescuers hit a wall of mud-clogged debris they couldn't move. Dhakal's crew improvised, tapping a natural channel some 15 meters above the tunnel and forcing water through it with a high-pressure jet that cleared 4 to 5 meters in minutes during testing.

Then the rain came again, triggering a partial collapse that briefly trapped several rescuers themselves. The operation stalled for hours before colleagues talked them back inside, and crews reinforced the passage with metal sheeting and gabion wire.

At 4 a.m. on the 10th day, Dahal got a call from a heavy equipment operator: the rescuers had heard something. A noise. Maybe a survivor. Maybe just an echo of the rescuers' own voices calling into the dark.

On the ground, Ganga Baral, who led the rescue team, said they began to hear noises as they drilled into the tunnel.

Again and again, they cut their machines' engines to listen. "We would call out, 'Where are you? Are you there?'" Baral said. "Sometimes it felt like there was a person alive trying to communicate with us."

They still couldn't make out words — but they now estimated the source was just 15 to 20 meters away. Then, in the beam of a light, they saw a hand.

Another 5 to 10 meters of mud-choked passage stood between them and the survivor. By 7 a.m., soldiers broke open a small hole.

From inside came a single word: "hunuhuncha", which loosely translates to "we are here".

INTO THE LIGHT

Neither man could stand when rescuers finally pulled them from the tunnel. Sah, his face caked in mud, had to be carried out on a rescuer's back. He managed to lift one hand toward a camera. Maharjan, with more severe injuries, went out on a stretcher.

"Mummy, Papa is back!" his sons shouted when they heard.

Dhakal, who ran the operation from outside but never entered the tunnel himself, wept when the two men emerged. "I couldn't hold my tears," he said.

The following day Chinese national Lu Haitao was found in the tunnel of a separate station, the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project.

At the hospital, doctors operated on a deep, infected wound on Maharjan's leg, his wife said.

When Hira Shova walked into the hospital room, he did not recognise her.

“Where am I?” he asked her.

But she was just thrilled to get him back alive.

"He is blessed with another life."

title: How two men survived nine days in a Nepal flood tunnel
full_text:
A delirious Kabir Maharjan drifted in and out of consciousness in a pool of muddy water in complete darkness, trapped for nine days in a tunnel beneath the wreckage of Nepal's worst flood disaster in decades.

When he finally awoke at a hospital after a miracle rescue, he did not recognise his wife. Confused, he asked her why she had not given him a bed sooner.

Maharjan was one of hundreds of hydropower workers believed to have been buried when a glacier collapsed above Nepal's Trishuli valley on August 26, unleashing a wall of mud and water that killed more than 1,300 people and left thousands missing across Nepal and neighbouring Tibet.

He and mechanical foreman Sanjay Sah survived in an air-filled chamber, said lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane, a veteran tunnel engineer who helped lead the rescue effort.

Their rescue against the odds has given hope to search teams working at the sites along the devastated valley that some of the 121 workers still believed to be trapped in tunnels as of Monday are still alive.

Reuters has reconstructed the full story of the men's survival and the frantic effort to save them through exclusive interviews with a dozen people, including the previously unreported accounts shared by relatives, engineers, government officials and rescuers directly involved in the operation and a review of site documents, maps, and internal conversations between rescuers.

THE MORNING

At 7:30 a.m. (0145 GMT) on the day of the disaster, Maharjan called his wife before his shift at the Upper Trishuli 3A hydropower project.

“I have to go inside the tunnel,” he told her. “There won’t be any network inside.”

Around 60 minutes later, a glacier collapsed at the Langtang Lirung mountain some 25 miles upstream, causing a landslide so powerful that it formed a wall of water that flattened villages and submerged a network of 12 hydropower projects with nearly 900 workers inside.

Survivors rescued from Nepal’s power project

Two people were pulled out alive on September 4 from a tunnel linked to the Upper Trishuli 3A hydropower station in Nepal, nine days after a glacier collapse burried the area under mud.

In the capital Kathmandu, electricity department officials were monitoring the projects' power supplies on their screens. Then the fields started going blank — one after another, stations disappearing from the control panels, falling like dominoes.

Suraj Dahal, an engineer at the Nepal Electricity Authority who led parts of the rescue effort, said he was not immediately alarmed because "floods are normal" in Nepal.

They soon understood otherwise. Because the 3A station manager was abroad, it took officials two extra minutes to reach out on call to the roughly 40 workers estimated to be inside. By then, at least two hydropower projects upriver had already been hit.

At 9:15 a.m. — two minutes after Maharjan's wife, Hira Shova Maharjan, had tried and failed to reach him — officials gave the final order to 3A: "Evacuate!"

Sah, who worked in the power house's control room, sped from floor to floor, warning colleagues individually, he later told rescuers.

Outside the tunnels, evacuating workers tried to run away from the flood, but were not fast enough. Officials pointed to footage showing a group of roughly 30 workers swept away by a wave many times their height.

Rescuers later identified an escape ladder which, had workers known of it, could have saved as many as two-thirds of those inside, said Dahal.

But they "didn't know where to go," he said.

Of the tunnel's four access routes, engineering drawings seen by Reuters showed one ran more than 180 meters to the underground powerhouse — but rescuers believed it was fully flooded, offering no hope of survivors.

Neupane instead turned his attention to a shorter cable-duct tunnel that sloped upward and was less exposed to the floodwaters. It was there that Maharjan and Sah had taken shelter, just 160 meters from the exit — "at the corner, at the edge of the tunnel," as Maharjan would later describe it to his wife.

FEAR OF THE WORST

For the next nine days, the air pocket that had saved their lives became their prison. Sah said he recited Hindu prayers to keep his courage. Maharjan sipped the same muddy water he slept in to stay alive, his wife said.

When Hira Shova first heard about the flood, she assumed the powerhouse would be safe.

She tried calling her husband, colleagues, anyone who might know something. No one answered.

When officials later showed her photographs of where the site entrance once stood — now a bare riverbank — she told herself, "he couldn't possibly be alive".

"Deep down in my heart, a terrible hopelessness was setting in," she recalled, but to her sons, 15 and 10, she kept up a brave front.

title: Nepal holds a day of mourning after floods kill at least 1 , 300 people
full_text:
Nepal held a day of mourning Monday to remember those killed in the Aug. 26 floods, with flags lowered at government offices and families concluding mourning rituals.

Monday was the 13th day since the flooding which killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal and Tibet and left some 5,000 missing, including foreigners, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

In predominantly Hindu Nepal, mourning periods last 13 days, during which close family members stay home and relatives visit to pay their respects. Rituals are held on the final day to pray for the souls of the departed.

Several people whose relatives remain missing performed symbolic funerals. Cremation is an important final rite in Hindu tradition, and performing the ceremony even without the bodies of their loved ones provided some families a sense of spiritual release.

The government had declared Monday an official day of mourning and ordered flags at government offices lowered to half-staff.

Meanwhile, search efforts continued for the missing, but some protested that not enough was being done.

In Kathmandu, relatives gathered near the offices of the prime minister and key ministries to demand the government speed up search and rescue efforts for hundreds of people who had been working at hydropower plants and were either swept away by the rushing Bhotekhoshi River or buried under debris.

Sumana Shrestha stood with family members holding a poster with the photo of her 55-year-old husband, who has not been heard from since the day of the flood.

Her husband, a consulting geologist, had promised to return home after his shift at the project office for the Trishuli hydropower plant on the day of the flood. The 2 1/2-story office was completely buried by debris.

“We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already,” she said. "The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle."

Another protester, Mahesh Prasad Shrestha, held a photograph of his brother Niraj Shrestha, a 52-year-old engineer who worked at the same site. He said authorities only sent a small excavator by helicopter on the sixth or seventh day after the disaster, adding: “They should have ordered big helicopters from places like China or India to fly in equipment.”

Candlelight vigils were held in several places in Kathmandu in memory of the people who lost their lives during the flooding.

Rescue efforts have focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said. Specialized rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects.

Two Nepalese workers were rescued from the plant Friday, and rescuers pulled out a Chinese man from the facility on Saturday.

Two workers were rescued after spending nine days trapped inside a hydroelectric plant tunnel on Nepal's Trishuli River following deadly flooding and a mudslide.
